q: Under Article 1768 of the Civil Code, a partnership:
choices: Has no personality apart from the partners
Has a juridical personality separate and distinct from that of each partner, even if the registration requirement of Art. 1772 was not complied with
Exists only if registered with the SEC
hints: Partnerships are juridical persons too.
Non-registration does not destroy the personality.
why: Art. 1768: the partnership has a juridical personality separate and distinct from each partner, even if it failed to comply with Art. 1772 (public instrument and SEC recording).

q: Ana and Ben orally agreed to contribute P1 million each to open a cafe and share the profits. They never executed a public instrument or recorded anything with the SEC. When the cafe incurred debts, a supplier sued the partnership. The partners argue that the partnership does not legally exist because it was never registered. Are they correct?

alac.answer: No, the partners are not correct. The partnership exists and has juridical personality.
alac.basis: Article 1767 of the Civil Code defines a partnership as a contract by which two or more persons bind themselves to contribute money, property, or industry to a common fund, with the intention of dividing the profits among themselves. Article 1768 provides that the partnership has a juridical personality separate and distinct from that of each partner, even in case of failure to comply with the requirements of Article 1772. Article 1772 provides that failure to execute a public instrument and record it with the SEC shall not affect the liability of the partnership and its members to third persons.
alac.application: Here, Ana and Ben agreed to contribute money to a common fund with the intention of dividing profits, so a partnership was formed. Their failure to execute a public instrument and register with the SEC does not negate its existence or its liability to third persons.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the partnership exists, may be sued by the supplier, and the partners are liable as provided by law.

keyPoints: Elements of partnership (Art. 1767)
Juridical personality despite non-registration (Art. 1768)
Non-compliance does not affect liability to third persons (Art. 1772)

q: Under Article 1769 of the Civil Code, which of the following is prima facie evidence that a person is a partner in a business?
choices: Receipt of a share of the profits of the business, unless received as wages, rent, interest, or the like
hints: Co-ownership and sharing gross returns do not by themselves establish a partnership.
Sharing net profits is a strong sign.
why: Art. 1769: co-ownership and sharing of gross returns do not of themselves establish a partnership; receipt of a share of the profits is prima facie evidence of partnership, unless received as payment of a debt, wages, annuity, interest, or consideration for goodwill.

q: Carlo and Dina inherited a building in common. They lease it out and divide the rentals equally. Carlo's creditor claims that Carlo and Dina are partners, so the building is partnership property answerable for Carlo's debts in a particular way. Are they partners?

alac.answer: No, Carlo and Dina are mere co-owners, not partners.
alac.basis: Article 1769(2) of the Civil Code provides that co-ownership or co-possession does not of itself establish a partnership, whether such co-owners or co-possessors do or do not share any profits made by the use of the property. Article 1767 requires an intention to contribute to a common fund for the purpose of dividing profits from a business.
alac.application: Here, Carlo and Dina became co-owners by inheritance, not by agreeing to form a business. Leasing the building and dividing the rentals is merely the use of co-owned property. There is no showing that they intended to form a partnership.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, they are co-owners, not partners, and the rules on co-ownership, not partnership, govern Carlo's share.

keyPoints: Co-ownership does not of itself establish a partnership (Art. 1769(2))
Even if profits from the property are shared
Intent to form a partnership is lacking

q: Under Article 1825 of the Civil Code, a person who represents himself, or consents to being represented, as a partner, when he is not, is liable:
choices: To any person to whom the representation was made and who, on the faith of it, gave credit to the apparent partnership
hints: This is partnership by estoppel.
The creditor relied on the representation.
why: Art. 1825: one who represents himself or consents to being represented as a partner is liable to persons who gave credit on the faith of that representation (partnership by estoppel).

q: Eddie, a well-known businessman, allowed his friend Fred to tell suppliers that Eddie was Fred's partner in a hardware store, though Eddie was not. Relying on this, a supplier extended P2 million in credit to the store. When the store failed, the supplier sued Eddie. Is Eddie liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Eddie is liable to the supplier as a partner by estoppel.
alac.basis: Article 1825 of the Civil Code provides that when a person, by words spoken or written or by conduct, represents himself, or consents to another representing him to anyone, as a partner in an existing partnership or with persons not actual partners, he is liable to any such persons to whom the representation has been made, who has, on the faith of such representation, given credit to the actual or apparent partnership.
alac.application: Here, Eddie consented to Fred's representing him as a partner to suppliers. The supplier, relying on that representation and on Eddie's reputation, extended P2 million in credit to the store.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Eddie is liable to the supplier as a partner by estoppel, even though he was not a real partner.

keyPoints: Partnership by estoppel (Art. 1825)
Consent to being represented as a partner
Credit given on the faith of the representation

q: Under Article 1843 of the Civil Code, a limited partnership must have:
choices: One or more general partners and one or more limited partners
hints: Limited partners are not bound by partnership obligations.
Someone must have unlimited liability.
why: Art. 1843: a limited partnership has one or more general partners and one or more limited partners; limited partners are not bound by the obligations of the partnership. Art. 1776 classifies partnerships as universal or particular, and general or limited.

q: In "Gomez and Santos Ltd.," a limited partnership, Gomez is the general partner and Santos is a limited partner. Santos's surname was put in the firm name, and a creditor who did not know Santos was only a limited partner extended credit. When the partnership's assets proved insufficient, the creditor sued Santos personally. Is Santos liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Santos is liable as a general partner to that creditor.
alac.basis: Article 1843 of the Civil Code provides that limited partners as such shall not be bound by the obligations of the partnership. However, Article 1846 provides that the surname of a limited partner shall not appear in the partnership name unless it is also the surname of a general partner or the business was previously carried on under that name, and that a limited partner whose surname appears contrary to this rule is liable as a general partner to partnership creditors who extend credit without actual knowledge that he is not a general partner.
alac.application: Here, Santos is a limited partner, and his surname is not that of the general partner, yet it appears in the firm name. The creditor extended credit without knowing that Santos was only a limited partner.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Santos is liable as a general partner to that creditor.

keyPoints: Limited partners not bound by partnership obligations (Art. 1843)
Limited partner's surname in the firm name (Art. 1846)
Liable as general partner to creditors without knowledge

q: Under Article 1810 of the Civil Code, the property rights of a partner are:
choices: His rights in specific partnership property, his interest in the partnership, and his right to participate in management
The right to sell partnership property alone
hints: There are three property rights.
A partner's right in specific property is limited.
why: Art. 1810: a partner's property rights are his rights in specific partnership property, his interest in the partnership, and his right to participate in the management. His right in specific property is not separately assignable or attachable for his personal debts (Art. 1811).

q: Gerry, a partner in a trucking partnership, owes a personal debt to Hilda. Hilda obtained a judgment and levied on one of the partnership's trucks, claiming it as Gerry's share. Is the levy proper?

alac.answer: No, the levy on the partnership truck is not proper.
alac.basis: Article 1811 of the Civil Code provides that a partner is co-owner with his partners of specific partnership property, but a partner's right in specific partnership property is not subject to attachment or execution, except on a claim against the partnership. Article 1810 lists, as a separate property right, the partner's interest in the partnership, which may be charged by his personal creditors.
alac.application: Here, the truck is specific partnership property, and Hilda's claim is for Gerry's personal debt, not a claim against the partnership. She cannot levy on the truck. Her remedy is to proceed against Gerry's interest in the partnership, his share of the profits and surplus.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the levy on the truck should be lifted, and Hilda may instead seek a charging order on Gerry's interest in the partnership.

keyPoints: Partner's right in specific property not subject to execution for personal debts (Art. 1811)
Personal creditor may proceed against the partner's interest
Partnership property answers only for partnership claims

q: Under Article 1822 of the Civil Code, the partnership is liable for loss caused to a third person by the wrongful act of a partner when the partner acted:
choices: In the ordinary course of the partnership's business or with the authority of his co-partners
Outside the business, on a personal errand
hints: A partner is an agent of the partnership.
The act must be connected with the business.
why: Art. 1822: where, by any wrongful act or omission of a partner acting in the ordinary course of the business or with the authority of his co-partners, loss is caused to a non-partner, the partnership is liable to the same extent as the partner.

q: Ivan, a partner in a courier partnership, was delivering a package for the partnership when he negligently crashed into Jun's car. Jun sued the partnership. The partnership argues that only Ivan, who was negligent, is liable. Is the partnership liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the partnership is liable to Jun.
alac.basis: Article 1822 of the Civil Code provides that where, by any wrongful act or omission of any partner acting in the ordinary course of the business of the partnership or with the authority of his co-partners, loss or injury is caused to any person not a partner, the partnership is liable therefor to the same extent as the partner so acting.
alac.application: Here, Ivan was delivering a package for the partnership, which is in the ordinary course of the courier business, when his negligence damaged Jun's car. Jun is not a partner.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the partnership is liable to Jun to the same extent as Ivan.

keyPoints: Partnership liable for partner's wrongful acts in the ordinary course of business (Art. 1822)
Third person not a partner
Same extent as the acting partner

q: Under Article 1808 of the Civil Code, a capitalist partner who, without stipulation allowing it, engages for his own account in the same kind of business as the partnership:
choices: Pays a fine to the SEC
Must bring his profits to the common fund and personally bear all losses
hints: Partners owe each other loyalty.
Industrial partners have a stricter rule (Art. 1789).
why: Art. 1808: capitalist partners cannot engage for their own account in the same kind of business as the partnership unless stipulated; a violator must bring his profits into the common fund and bear all losses personally.

q: The partners of a printing partnership agreed that profits would be shared "40% to Kris, 40% to Lito, and 20% to Mila," but said nothing about losses. Mila is an industrial partner who contributed only services. The partnership lost P1 million. How should the losses be shared?

alac.answer: Kris and Lito should share the losses equally, P500,000 each, and Mila bears none.
alac.basis: Article 1797 of the Civil Code provides that losses and profits shall be distributed in conformity with the agreement; if only the share in the profits has been agreed upon, the share in the losses shall be in the same proportion; but the industrial partner shall not be liable for the losses. Article 1799 voids any stipulation excluding a partner from any share in profits or losses, but the exemption of the industrial partner from losses is provided by law.
alac.application: Here, the partners agreed only on profits. Losses would follow the same proportion, but Mila, as an industrial partner, is not liable for losses. Kris and Lito had equal profit shares (40% each), so they share the P1 million loss equally between them.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Kris and Lito each bear P500,000 of the loss, and Mila bears nothing as between the partners.

keyPoints: Losses follow the agreed profit shares if only profits are stipulated (Art. 1797)
Industrial partner not liable for losses among partners
Remaining capitalist partners share in their proportion

q: Under Article 1816 of the Civil Code, partners are liable for partnership contracts to third persons:
choices: Solidarily, before the partnership assets are exhausted
Pro rata with all their property, after all partnership assets have been exhausted, including industrial partners
hints: Partners' liability is subsidiary and joint (pro rata).
Industrial partners are included as to third persons.
why: Art. 1816: all partners, including industrial ones, are liable pro rata with all their property, after all partnership assets have been exhausted, for partnership contracts; Art. 1817 voids stipulations to the contrary except among partners.

q: A partnership of three partners, including one industrial partner, owes P900,000 to a bank under a loan in the partnership's name. Its assets of P300,000 were exhausted. The partnership agreement says the industrial partner is "not liable for any partnership debts." How much can the bank collect from each partner?

alac.answer: The bank can collect the P600,000 balance pro rata, P200,000 from each partner, including the industrial partner.
alac.basis: Article 1816 of the Civil Code provides that all partners, including industrial ones, shall be liable pro rata with all their property and after all the partnership assets have been exhausted, for contracts entered into in the name and for the account of the partnership. Article 1817 provides that any stipulation against this liability shall be void, except as among the partners.
alac.application: Here, the partnership's assets of P300,000 were exhausted, leaving P600,000 unpaid. The three partners, including the industrial partner, are liable pro rata to the bank. The stipulation exempting the industrial partner binds only the partners among themselves, not the bank.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the bank may collect P200,000 from each partner; the industrial partner may then seek reimbursement from the others under their agreement.

keyPoints: Pro rata liability of all partners after exhaustion of assets (Art. 1816)
Industrial partners included as to third persons
Contrary stipulation void except among partners (Art. 1817)

q: Under Article 1829 of the Civil Code, upon dissolution, the partnership:
choices: Is not terminated, but continues until the winding up of partnership affairs is completed
Is automatically liquidated by the SEC
hints: Dissolution is different from termination.
Winding up comes between them.
why: Art. 1828: dissolution is the change in relation of the partners caused by any partner ceasing to be associated in carrying on the business; Art. 1829: on dissolution the partnership continues until winding up is completed.

q: A partnership at will (with no fixed term) had three partners. Nora, acting in good faith, notified the others that she was withdrawing from the partnership. The others continued the business without liquidation. What is the effect of Nora's withdrawal, and what may she claim?

alac.answer: Nora's withdrawal dissolved the partnership; she may have the value of her interest ascertained and paid as an ordinary creditor.
alac.basis: Article 1830(1)(b) of the Civil Code provides that dissolution is caused, without violation of the agreement, by the express will of any partner, who must act in good faith, when no definite term or particular undertaking is specified. Article 1841 provides that when a partner retires and the business is continued without settlement of accounts, the retiring partner may have the value of his interest at the date of dissolution ascertained and receive it as an ordinary creditor, with interest or, at his option, the profits attributable to the use of his right in the property.
alac.application: Here, the partnership had no fixed term, and Nora withdrew in good faith, which caused its dissolution without violating the agreement. The others continued the business without liquidating.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Nora may claim the value of her interest as of the dissolution, as an ordinary creditor, with interest or a share in the profits.

keyPoints: Partnership at will dissolved by any partner's good-faith express will (Art. 1830(1)(b))
Dissolution is not termination (Art. 1829)
Retiring partner's claim when the business continues (Art. 1841)

q: Under Section 2(a) of the Insurance Code, a contract of insurance is an agreement whereby one undertakes, for a consideration, to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability arising from:
hints: Insurance covers risk.
Willful acts of the insured are not covered (Sec. 89).
why: Insurance Code Sec. 2(a): insurance is an agreement whereby one undertakes for a consideration to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability arising from an unknown or contingent event.
cite: Insurance Code (PD 612, as amended by RA 10607), Sec. 2(a)

q: Oscar insured his warehouse against fire. He later set it on fire himself to collect the insurance. Separately, his employee's carelessness caused a fire in another insured building. Can Oscar recover for either fire?

alac.answer: Oscar cannot recover for the fire he set, but he can recover for the fire caused by his employee's negligence.
alac.basis: Section 2(a) of the Insurance Code defines insurance as an agreement to indemnify another against loss arising from an unknown or contingent event. Section 89 provides that an insurer is not liable for a loss caused by the willful act or through the connivance of the insured, but he is not exonerated by the negligence of the insured, or of the insurance agents or others.
alac.application: Here, the first fire was Oscar's own willful act, not a contingent event, so the insurer is not liable. The second fire was caused by the negligence of his employee, which does not exonerate the insurer.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Oscar may recover for the second building but not for the warehouse he burned.

keyPoints: Insurance covers unknown or contingent events (Sec. 2(a))
No liability for loss caused by the insured's willful act (Sec. 89)
Negligence of the insured or others does not exonerate the insurer

q: Under Section 10 of the Insurance Code, every person has an insurable interest in the life and health of:
choices: Himself, his spouse and his children, and persons on whom he depends or in whom he has a pecuniary interest, among others
hints: Insurable interest prevents wagering.
A creditor has an insurable interest in the debtor's life.
why: Insurance Code Sec. 10: insurable interest in life exists in oneself, spouse and children; persons on whom one depends for education or support or in whom one has a pecuniary interest; persons under a legal obligation to him; and persons on whose life an estate or interest depends.

q: Pablo sold his house to Quina, delivered it, and received full payment. A month later, without Quina's knowledge, the old fire policy Pablo had taken out still being in force in his name, the house burned. Pablo claims the insurance. Can he recover?

alac.answer: No, Pablo cannot recover.
alac.basis: Section 13 of the Insurance Code provides that every interest in property, or any relation thereto, of such nature that a contemplated peril might directly damnify the insured, is an insurable interest. Section 18 provides that no contract or policy of insurance on property shall be enforceable except for the benefit of some person having an insurable interest in the property insured. Section 25 declares void any policy executed by way of gaming or wagering.
alac.application: Here, Pablo had already sold, delivered and been fully paid for the house. At the time of the fire, the loss could no longer damnify him; he had no insurable interest. The policy cannot be enforced for his benefit.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Pablo cannot recover under the policy.

keyPoints: Insurable interest in property: peril might directly damnify the insured (Sec. 13)
Policy enforceable only for one with insurable interest (Sec. 18)
No interest after sale, delivery and full payment

q: Under Section 27 of the Insurance Code, a concealment:
choices: Whether intentional or unintentional, entitles the injured party to rescind the contract
Only allows the insurer to increase the premium
hints: Good faith does not cure a material concealment.
Materiality is judged by its influence on the insurer (Sec. 31).
why: Insurance Code Sec. 26: concealment is a neglect to communicate what a party knows and ought to communicate; Sec. 27: whether intentional or unintentional, it entitles the injured party to rescind.

q: When applying for health insurance, Rita did not disclose that she had been diagnosed with diabetes two years earlier, honestly thinking it was not important since she felt well. The insurer would have charged a higher premium had it known. After a claim, the insurer discovered the diagnosis and sought to rescind. Can it rescind?

alac.answer: Yes, the insurer may rescind the policy.
alac.basis: Section 26 of the Insurance Code defines concealment as a neglect to communicate that which a party knows and ought to communicate. Section 27 provides that a concealment, whether intentional or unintentional, entitles the injured party to rescind. Section 31 provides that materiality is determined by the probable and reasonable influence of the facts upon the party to whom the communication is due in forming his estimate of the proposed contract.
alac.application: Here, Rita knew of her diabetes diagnosis and did not disclose it. It was material because it would have led the insurer to charge a higher premium. Her good faith does not matter, since even an unintentional concealment allows rescission.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the insurer may rescind the policy, subject to the rule that rescission must be exercised before an action on the policy is commenced.

keyPoints: Concealment: neglect to communicate known material facts (Sec. 26)
Intentional or unintentional, allows rescission (Sec. 27)
Materiality judged by influence on the insurer (Sec. 31)

q: Under Section 45 of the Insurance Code, if a representation is false in a material point, the injured party may rescind the contract:
choices: From the time when the representation becomes false
Only if the insurer is paid
hints: Representations may be affirmative or promissory.
A representation is false when facts fail to correspond with it.
why: Insurance Code Sec. 45: if a representation is false in a material point, whether affirmative or promissory, the injured party may rescind from the time the representation becomes false.

q: In 2022, Sam took out a life policy, falsely stating in his application that he had never been hospitalized; in fact he had been confined for a heart condition. He paid premiums regularly and died in 2025. The insurer, discovering the false statement, refuses to pay, claiming the policy is rescindable. Will its defense succeed?

alac.answer: No, the insurer's defense will not succeed because of the incontestability rule.
alac.basis: Section 45 of the Insurance Code allows rescission when a representation is false in a material point. However, Section 48 provides that after a policy of life insurance payable on the death of the insured shall have been in force during the lifetime of the insured for a period of two years from the date of its issue or last reinstatement, the insurer cannot prove that the policy is void ab initio or rescindable by reason of the fraudulent concealment or misrepresentation of the insured.
alac.application: Here, Sam's statement was a material misrepresentation. But the life policy was in force during his lifetime for about three years, more than two years from issuance, before he died. The policy has become incontestable.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the insurer can no longer rescind or contest the policy on the ground of misrepresentation and must pay the proceeds.

keyPoints: Material false representation allows rescission (Sec. 45)
Incontestability after two years in force during the insured's lifetime (Sec. 48)
Insurer must pay

q: Under Section 49 of the Insurance Code, the policy of insurance is:
choices: Any oral promise of the agent
The written instrument in which a contract of insurance is set forth
hints: The policy is the written contract.
Riders must be properly referred to in the policy (Sec. 50).
why: Insurance Code Sec. 49: the written instrument in which a contract of insurance is set forth is called a policy of insurance; Sec. 50 requires riders and endorsements to be mentioned in the blank spaces of the policy to bind the insured.

q: After a car accident, Tina's insurer denied her claim, citing an exclusion rider pasted on her policy. The rider's title was not written or mentioned anywhere in the blank spaces of the policy. Is Tina bound by the rider?

alac.answer: No, Tina is not bound by the rider.
alac.basis: Section 50 of the Insurance Code provides that any rider, clause, warranty or endorsement purporting to be part of the contract of insurance and which is pasted or attached to the policy is not binding on the insured, unless the descriptive title or name of the rider is also mentioned and written on the blank spaces provided in the policy.
alac.application: Here, the exclusion rider was merely pasted on Tina's policy; its title was not mentioned or written in the blank spaces of the policy. The law protects the insured from riders she may not have known were part of her contract.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the rider does not bind Tina, and the insurer cannot deny her claim on the basis of it.

keyPoints: Policy is the written instrument (Sec. 49)
Attached riders bind only if their title is written in the policy's blank spaces (Sec. 50)
Unmentioned rider does not bind the insured

q: Under Section 74 of the Insurance Code, the violation of a material warranty by either party:
choices: Entitles the other party to rescind
hints: Warranties are statements or promises in the policy.
They may be express or implied (Sec. 67).
why: Insurance Code Sec. 74: the violation of a material warranty or other material provision of a policy by either party entitles the other to rescind.

q: Uma's fire policy on her store contains an express warranty that "no fireworks or explosives shall be stored on the premises." She later began storing fireworks for the holidays, and a fire broke out, though not caused by the fireworks. The insurer seeks to rescind. Can it?

alac.answer: Yes, the insurer may rescind for violation of a material warranty.
alac.basis: Section 71 of the Insurance Code provides that a statement in a policy, of a matter relating to the risk, as fact, is an express warranty. Section 74 provides that the violation of a material warranty or other material provision of a policy, on the part of either party, entitles the other to rescind.
alac.application: Here, the warranty against storing fireworks is an express warranty in the policy concerning the risk, and it is material, since fireworks greatly increase the fire hazard. Uma violated it by storing fireworks, regardless of whether they caused this particular fire.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the insurer is entitled to rescind the policy.

keyPoints: Express warranty in the policy (Sec. 71)
Violation of a material warranty allows rescission (Sec. 74)
Causal connection with the loss not required

q: Under Section 77 of the Insurance Code, as a rule, an insurance policy is valid and binding only when:
choices: The premium has been paid, except in cases such as the grace period for life policies or a 90-day credit extension to licensed intermediaries
hints: This is the cash-and-carry rule.
There are limited exceptions.
why: Insurance Code Sec. 77: notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, no policy is valid and binding until the premium has been paid, except for life or industrial life policies within the grace period, or a 90-day credit extension under broker or agency agreements, among others.

q: Victor applied for fire insurance on his house; the insurer issued the policy, and the agent agreed that Victor could pay the premium "next week." Two days later, before any payment, the house burned. The policy contains no acknowledgment of premium payment. Can Victor recover?

alac.answer: No, Victor cannot recover.
alac.basis: Section 77 of the Insurance Code provides that, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, no policy or contract of insurance issued by an insurance company is valid and binding unless and until the premium has been paid, except in specified cases such as the grace period for life policies or a ninety-day credit extension to duly licensed intermediaries. Under Section 79, an acknowledgment of payment in the policy is conclusive evidence of payment.
alac.application: Here, no premium was paid before the fire. The agent's informal agreement to defer payment is an "agreement to the contrary" that the law disregards, and it is not one of the recognized exceptions. The policy also does not acknowledge payment of the premium.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the policy never became binding, and Victor cannot recover.

keyPoints: Cash-and-carry rule: no binding policy until premium is paid (Sec. 77)
Contrary agreements are disregarded
Acknowledgment of payment in the policy would be conclusive (Sec. 79)

q: Under Section 90 of the Insurance Code, in case of loss under a fire insurance policy, the insurer is exonerated if:
choices: Written notice of the loss is not given without unnecessary delay
hints: Notice lets the insurer investigate promptly.
Defects not objected to are waived (Sec. 92).
why: Insurance Code Sec. 90: in fire insurance, the insurer is exonerated if written notice of the loss is not given without unnecessary delay; Secs. 92-93: defects and delay are waived if the insurer fails to object promptly or caused the delay.

q: Wendy's insured store burned. She gave prompt written notice, but her proof of loss lacked a required fire department certificate. The insurer kept silent about the missing certificate for months, then denied the claim for incomplete proof. Is the denial valid?

alac.answer: No, the denial is not valid; the defect was waived.
alac.basis: Section 92 of the Insurance Code provides that all defects in a notice of loss, or in preliminary proof thereof, which the insured might remedy, and which the insurer omits to specify to him, without unnecessary delay, as grounds of objection, are waived. Section 93 likewise provides that delay in presenting notice or proof of loss is waived if the insurer omits to take objection promptly and specifically on that ground.
alac.application: Here, Wendy gave prompt written notice. Her proof of loss had a defect she could have remedied, the missing certificate, but the insurer did not specify it as an objection without unnecessary delay; it stayed silent for months.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the insurer waived the defect and cannot deny the claim on that ground.

keyPoints: Prompt written notice of fire loss required (Sec. 90)
Remediable defects not promptly specified are waived (Sec. 92)
Insurer's silence for months is a waiver

q: Under Section 95 of the Insurance Code, double insurance exists where:
choices: Two people insure the same property for different interests
The same person is insured by several insurers separately in respect to the same subject and interest
One insurer issues two policies to different persons
hints: Same insured, same subject, same interest, several insurers.
Over-insurance is when the total exceeds the value.
why: Insurance Code Sec. 95: double insurance exists where the same person is insured by several insurers separately in respect to the same subject and interest.

q: Xena insured her P2 million building against fire with Insurer A for P2 million and with Insurer B for P1 million (both open, unvalued policies). Fire totally destroyed it. How much can she recover in total, and from whom?

alac.answer: Xena can recover a total of P2 million, the actual loss, and may claim from the insurers in the order she chooses, up to each one's liability.
alac.basis: Section 95 of the Insurance Code provides that double insurance exists where the same person is insured by several insurers separately in respect to the same subject and interest. Section 96 provides that where the insured is over-insured by double insurance, the insured may claim payment from the insurers in such order as he may select, up to the amount for which they are severally liable; where the policy is unvalued, any sum received under any other policy shall be deducted against the full insurable value. The insured cannot recover more than the loss, and insurers who pay contribute ratably among themselves.
alac.application: Here, Xena is insured for P3 million in total on a building worth P2 million, so she is over-insured by double insurance. Since insurance is a contract of indemnity, she can recover only her actual loss of P2 million. She may choose, for example, to collect P2 million from Insurer A, or P1 million from B and P1 million from A.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Xena can recover only P2 million in total, in the order she chooses, and the insurers will settle their ratable shares between themselves.

keyPoints: Double insurance: same insured, subject and interest, several insurers (Sec. 95)
Over-insured: claim in any order up to each insurer's liability (Sec. 96)
Total recovery limited to the actual loss (indemnity)

q: Under Section 97 of the Insurance Code, a contract of reinsurance is one by which:
choices: An insurer procures a third person to insure him against loss or liability by reason of the original insurance
The insured buys a second policy
hints: Reinsurance is insurance of an insurer.
The original insured is not a party to it.
why: Insurance Code Sec. 97: reinsurance is a contract by which an insurer procures a third person to insure him against loss or liability by reason of the original insurance; Sec. 99: it is presumed a contract of indemnity against liability.

q: Insurer Y reinsured part of a large fire policy it issued on Zaldy's factory with Reinsurer R. When the factory burned and Insurer Y delayed payment, Zaldy sued Reinsurer R directly. Insurer Y had also not disclosed to R that the factory had an unrepaired faulty wiring report. What are the rights of the parties?

alac.answer: Zaldy cannot sue Reinsurer R directly; and R may rescind the reinsurance for Insurer Y's non-disclosure.
alac.basis: Section 97 of the Insurance Code defines reinsurance as a contract by which an insurer procures a third person to insure him against loss or liability by reason of the original insurance; it is a contract between the insurer and the reinsurer, and the original insured has no interest in it. Section 98 provides that where an insurer obtains reinsurance, except under automatic treaties, he must communicate all the representations of the original insured and all the knowledge and information he possesses which are material to the risk.
alac.application: Here, the reinsurance is a contract between Insurer Y and Reinsurer R, so Zaldy, a stranger to it, must claim from Insurer Y. As for Reinsurer R, Insurer Y failed to disclose the faulty wiring report, information material to the risk, in violation of its duty under Section 98.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Zaldy's remedy is against Insurer Y, and Reinsurer R may rescind the reinsurance contract for concealment.

keyPoints: Reinsurance insures the insurer (Sec. 97)
Original insured has no interest in it
Insurer must disclose all material information to the reinsurer (Sec. 98)

q: Under Section 48 of the Insurance Code, whenever the insurer has a right to rescind a contract of insurance, that right must be exercised:
choices: Within ten years of the loss
Before the commencement of an action on the contract
hints: Rescission must come first.
For life policies, the two-year incontestability period also applies.
why: Insurance Code Sec. 48: the insurer's right to rescind must be exercised previous to the commencement of an action on the contract; after two years in force during the insured's lifetime, a life policy becomes incontestable.

q: After her husband's death, Anna sued the insurer to collect on a one-year-old life policy. Only in its answer to her complaint did the insurer allege concealment and ask for rescission of the policy. Can the insurer still rescind?

alac.answer: No, the insurer can no longer rescind the policy.
alac.basis: Section 48 of the Insurance Code provides that whenever a right to rescind a contract of insurance is given to the insurer, such right must be exercised previous to the commencement of an action on the contract. Rescission raised for the first time after the insured's beneficiary has sued is too late.
alac.application: Here, although the policy was in force for only one year, so the incontestability period had not lapsed, the insurer did not rescind before Anna filed her action on the policy. It raised rescission only in its answer, after the action had commenced.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the insurer lost its right to rescind and cannot avoid liability on the ground of concealment.

keyPoints: Right to rescind must be exercised before an action on the policy (Sec. 48)
Raising it only in the answer is too late
Separate from the two-year incontestability rule

q: Under Article 1732 of the Civil Code, a common carrier is one engaged in the business of carrying passengers or goods or both, for compensation:
choices: Offering its services to the public, whether regularly or occasionally
hints: The test is offering services to the public.
An occasional or unlicensed carrier may still be a common carrier.
why: Art. 1732 defines common carriers as those engaged in carrying passengers or goods for compensation, offering their services to the public; a carrier remains common even if carriage is occasional, ancillary or without a certificate of public convenience (De Guzman v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-47822, December 22, 1988).
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1732; De Guzman v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-47822, December 22, 1988

q: Ben, a junk dealer, uses his two trucks to haul his own goods to Manila and, on the way back, regularly offers to carry other people's goods for a fee. He has no certificate of public convenience. When goods he carried were lost, he argued he is not a common carrier. Separately, a shipowner chartered its entire vessel to one company for a voyage. Are Ben and the shipowner common carriers?

alac.answer: Ben is a common carrier; the shipowner, as to the charterer, acts as a private carrier.
alac.basis: Article 1732 of the Civil Code defines common carriers as those engaged in the business of carrying goods for compensation, offering their services to the public. In De Guzman v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-47822, December 22, 1988, the Supreme Court held that a person who carries goods for others for compensation, even only on backhauls, occasionally, and without a certificate of public convenience, is a common carrier. In Home Insurance Co. v. American Steamship Agencies, Inc., G.R. No. L-25599, April 4, 1968, the Court held that a common carrier that charters its entire vessel to a single party for a voyage acts as a private carrier as to that party.
alac.application: Here, Ben regularly offers to carry other people's goods for a fee, so he offers his services to the public, though only on return trips and without a certificate. The shipowner chartered the whole vessel to one company, so as to that charterer it acted as a private carrier, governed by the ordinary diligence agreed upon.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ben is a common carrier bound to extraordinary diligence, while the shipowner is a private carrier with respect to the charterer.

keyPoints: Common carrier: offers services to the public for compensation (Art. 1732)
Occasional or unlicensed carriage still qualifies (De Guzman v. CA)
Charter of the entire vessel: private carrier as to the charterer (Home Insurance v. American Steamship)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1732; De Guzman v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-47822, December 22, 1988; Home Insurance Co. v. American Steamship Agencies, Inc., G.R. No. L-25599, April 4, 1968

q: Under Article 1733 of the Civil Code, common carriers are bound to observe:
choices: Extraordinary diligence in the vigilance over goods and for the safety of passengers
hints: The duty comes from the nature of the business and public policy.
For passengers, it is the utmost diligence of very cautious persons (Art. 1755).
why: Art. 1733: common carriers, from the nature of their business and for reasons of public policy, must observe extraordinary diligence over goods and for the safety of passengers.

q: A ferry's ticket states, "The carrier is not liable for injuries to passengers, who travel at their own risk." A passenger was injured when the ferry's railing, which had been rusting for months, gave way. The carrier invokes the ticket stipulation. Is it valid?

alac.answer: No, the stipulation is void, and the carrier is liable.
alac.basis: Article 1733 of the Civil Code requires common carriers to observe extraordinary diligence for the safety of passengers. Article 1755 requires them to carry passengers safely as far as human care and foresight can provide, using the utmost diligence of very cautious persons. Article 1757 provides that this responsibility cannot be dispensed with or lessened by stipulation, by the posting of notices, by statements on tickets, or otherwise.
alac.application: Here, the ticket stipulation tries to exempt the carrier entirely from liability for injuries to passengers, which the law forbids. The railing had been rusting for months, showing a lack of the utmost diligence required.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the stipulation is void, and the carrier is liable for the passenger's injuries.

keyPoints: Extraordinary diligence for passengers (Arts. 1733, 1755)
Cannot be dispensed with by stipulation or ticket statements (Art. 1757)
Rusting railing shows negligence

q: Under Article 1734 of the Civil Code, which of the following is a defense of a common carrier for loss of goods?
choices: Flood, storm, earthquake or other natural disaster, when it is the proximate and only cause
Theft by a stranger without force
hints: Art. 1734 lists five exempting causes.
The natural disaster must be the only cause (Art. 1739).
why: Art. 1734: carriers are not liable if the loss is due only to natural disaster, act of the public enemy in war, act or omission of the shipper, character of the goods or defective packing, or order of competent public authority.

q: A trucking company's truck carrying a shipper's appliances was hijacked by armed men who overpowered the driver and his helper at gunpoint. The goods were never recovered. The shipper sues the carrier. Is the carrier liable?

alac.answer: No, the carrier is not liable if it shows the hijacking was by armed men with grave force it could not resist.
alac.basis: Under Articles 1734 and 1735 of the Civil Code, common carriers are presumed at fault for loss of goods unless the loss is due to the causes in Article 1734 or they prove extraordinary diligence. Article 1745(6) declares unreasonable a stipulation that the carrier is not responsible for loss due to theft or robbery unless committed with grave or irresistible threat, violence or force, implying that robbery with such force exempts the carrier. In De Guzman v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-47822, December 22, 1988, the Supreme Court held that a carrier is not liable for goods lost to armed hijackers who used grave or irresistible force.
alac.application: Here, the goods were taken by armed men who overpowered the crew at gunpoint. That is a robbery committed with grave or irresistible threat and force, which no degree of diligence could have prevented.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the carrier is exempt from liability for the hijacked goods.

keyPoints: Presumption of fault for loss of goods (Arts. 1734-1735)
Robbery with grave or irresistible force is a valid defense (Art. 1745(6); De Guzman v. CA)
Ordinary theft would not exempt
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 1734, 1735 and 1745; De Guzman v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-47822, December 22, 1988

q: Under Article 1736 of the Civil Code, the extraordinary responsibility of a common carrier over goods lasts:
choices: Until the goods arrive at the port
From the time the goods are unconditionally placed in its possession and received for transportation until delivered, actually or constructively, to the consignee
Only while the goods are in transit
hints: The duty begins at receipt and ends at delivery.
Delivery may be actual or constructive.
why: Art. 1736: the carrier's extraordinary responsibility lasts from the time the goods are unconditionally placed in its possession and received for transportation until delivered to the consignee or person entitled to receive them.

q: A shipping line delayed a cargo of rice for a week without justification. During the delay, a typhoon sank the vessel, and the rice was lost. The carrier invokes the typhoon as a natural disaster. Is it liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the carrier is liable.
alac.basis: Article 1734(1) of the Civil Code exempts a common carrier from liability for loss due to flood, storm or other natural disaster, but Article 1739 requires that the natural disaster be the proximate and only cause of the loss and that the carrier exercise due diligence to prevent or minimize loss. Article 1740 provides that if the common carrier negligently incurs in delay in transporting the goods, a natural disaster shall not free such carrier from responsibility.
alac.application: Here, the carrier delayed the cargo for a week without justification, which is negligent delay. The typhoon struck during that delay. Under Article 1740, the natural disaster does not free it from responsibility.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the shipping line is liable for the loss of the rice.

keyPoints: Natural disaster must be the proximate and only cause (Art. 1739)
Negligent delay: natural disaster does not exempt (Art. 1740)
Carrier liable

q: In the Philippines, how does the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act (COGSA) relate to the Civil Code for goods shipped from a foreign port to the Philippines?
choices: COGSA replaces the Civil Code entirely
The Civil Code applies primarily (as the law of the country of destination), and COGSA applies suppletorily
Only the Code of Commerce applies
hints: Art. 1753: the law of the destination governs.
Art. 1766: special laws apply in matters not regulated by the Code.
why: Under Arts. 1753 and 1766 of the Civil Code, the law of the country of destination governs the carrier's liability; for goods coming to the Philippines, the Civil Code applies primarily, and COGSA (Commonwealth Act No. 65) suppletorily, e.g., on the package limitation and the one-year period to sue.
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 1753 and 1766; Carriage of Goods by Sea Act (Commonwealth Act No. 65)

q: Goods shipped from Japan to Manila were found damaged upon discharge. The bill of lading did not declare their value. The consignee filed suit against the shipping line 15 months after delivery. The carrier argues that the claim is barred and, in any case, that its liability is limited. Decide.

alac.answer: The claim is barred by the one-year period under COGSA; if it had been timely, the carrier's liability would be limited per package absent a declared value.
alac.basis: Under Articles 1753 and 1766 of the Civil Code, the Civil Code governs the liability of a carrier for goods transported to the Philippines, and special laws apply suppletorily. The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act (Commonwealth Act No. 65), applied suppletorily, provides that the carrier and the ship shall be discharged from all liability for loss or damage unless suit is brought within one year after delivery of the goods, and limits the carrier's liability per package unless the shipper declared a higher value in the bill of lading.
alac.application: Here, the goods were shipped from a foreign port to Manila, so the Civil Code applies primarily and COGSA suppletorily, since the Civil Code does not fix a special prescriptive period for this claim. The suit was filed 15 months after delivery, beyond the one-year period. Even if timely, no value was declared, so the package limitation would apply.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the consignee's action is barred by prescription.

keyPoints: Civil Code primarily, COGSA suppletorily for inbound sea cargo (Arts. 1753, 1766)
One-year period after delivery to sue under COGSA
Package limitation unless value is declared
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 1753 and 1766; Carriage of Goods by Sea Act (Commonwealth Act No. 65)

q: Under the Montreal Convention of 1999, to which the Philippines is a party, a claim for damage to checked baggage or cargo in international air carriage requires:
choices: A written complaint to the carrier within the periods fixed by the Convention, and suit within two years
Only an oral complaint at any time
hints: Air carriage has its own uniform rules.
Time limits for complaint and suit are strict.
why: The Montreal Convention governs international air carriage of passengers, baggage and cargo: the carrier is liable for damage to baggage and cargo within liability limits expressed in Special Drawing Rights; written complaints must be made within the periods fixed for damage or delay; the right to damages is extinguished if suit is not brought within two years.
cite: Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air (Montreal Convention, 1999)

q: Goods shipped by air from Singapore to Manila under an international air waybill arrived damaged. The consignee made a timely written complaint but sued the airline only after three years. The airline invokes the Montreal Convention. Will the suit prosper?

alac.answer: No, the suit will not prosper because it was filed after the two-year period.
alac.basis: The Montreal Convention of 1999, to which the Philippines is a party, governs the international carriage of cargo by air. It makes the carrier liable for damage to cargo during carriage by air, subject to limits expressed in Special Drawing Rights, and provides that the right to damages shall be extinguished if an action is not brought within two years from the date of arrival at the destination or from the date the aircraft ought to have arrived.
alac.application: Here, the carriage from Singapore to Manila is international carriage by air governed by the Convention. Although the consignee complained in writing on time, it sued only after three years, beyond the two-year period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the consignee's right to damages was extinguished, and the suit must be dismissed.

keyPoints: Montreal Convention governs international air cargo
Carrier liable within SDR limits
Two-year period to sue; right extinguished after

q: Under Article 1756 of the Civil Code, in case of death or injury to passengers, common carriers are:
choices: Liable only if the passenger proves negligence
Presumed at fault or negligent, unless they prove extraordinary diligence
hints: The burden shifts to the carrier.
Contrast with quasi-delict, where the victim proves negligence.
why: Art. 1756: in case of death or injury to passengers, common carriers are presumed at fault unless they prove they observed extraordinary diligence as prescribed in Arts. 1733 and 1755.

q: While riding a bus, Celia was stabbed by another passenger. The conductor had noticed the attacker acting threateningly toward her for several minutes but did nothing. Celia sues the bus company. Is it liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the bus company is liable.
alac.basis: Article 1763 of the Civil Code provides that a common carrier is responsible for injuries suffered by a passenger on account of the wilful acts or negligence of other passengers or of strangers, if the common carrier's employees, through the exercise of the diligence of a good father of a family, could have prevented or stopped the act or omission. Article 1756 presumes the carrier at fault for injuries to passengers.
alac.application: Here, the injury was caused by another passenger, but the conductor saw the attacker acting threateningly for several minutes and did nothing. With ordinary diligence, he could have intervened, alerted the driver, or stopped the bus to prevent the attack.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the bus company is liable to Celia for her injuries.

keyPoints: Carrier presumed at fault for injury to passengers (Art. 1756)
Liable for acts of other passengers if its employees could have prevented them with ordinary diligence (Art. 1763)
Conductor's inaction

q: Under the Montreal Convention, the carrier's liability for death or bodily injury of a passenger in international air carriage:
choices: Is strict up to a threshold amount in Special Drawing Rights, and above that the carrier is liable unless it proves the damage was not due to its negligence
Is limited to the ticket price
Is unlimited and requires proof of negligence for all amounts
hints: The Convention uses a two-tier system.
The first tier does not depend on fault.
why: Montreal Convention: for passenger death or injury caused by an accident on board or in embarking or disembarking, the carrier is strictly liable up to a threshold in SDRs; above it, the carrier is liable unless it proves the damage was not due to its negligence or was solely due to a third party.

q: During an international flight from Tokyo to Manila, Dante fell and was injured when the aircraft hit severe turbulence after the seatbelt sign had been switched off by the crew without checking weather reports. He sues the airline for damages above the Convention's strict-liability threshold. Can he recover the excess?

alac.answer: Yes, Dante may recover above the threshold unless the airline proves the injury was not due to its negligence.
alac.basis: Under the Montreal Convention of 1999, to which the Philippines is a party, the carrier is liable for damage sustained in case of bodily injury of a passenger caused by an accident on board the aircraft. For damages up to a threshold set in Special Drawing Rights, the carrier cannot exclude or limit its liability; for damages above that amount, the carrier is not liable only if it proves that the damage was not due to its negligence or other wrongful act or omission, or was solely due to that of a third party.
alac.application: Here, Dante's injury from turbulence on board is an accident covered by the Convention, so the airline is liable up to the threshold regardless of fault. For the excess, the burden is on the airline to prove it was not negligent; but the crew switched off the seatbelt sign without checking weather reports, which points to negligence.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dante may recover even above the threshold, since the airline is unlikely to prove the absence of negligence.

keyPoints: Accident on board covered by the Montreal Convention
Strict liability up to the SDR threshold
Above it: carrier liable unless it proves no negligence

q: Under Section 3.1 of the General Banking Law of 2000, banks are entities engaged in:
choices: The lending of funds obtained in the form of deposits
hints: The two key acts are taking deposits and lending them.
Banks are classified in Sec. 3.2.
why: GBL Sec. 3.1: banks are entities engaged in the lending of funds obtained in the form of deposits; Sec. 3.2 classifies them into universal, commercial, thrift, rural, cooperative and Islamic banks, and others the Monetary Board may determine.

q: Lending Co. regularly accepts money from the public, calling it "investment placements" withdrawable on demand with interest, and uses the money to grant loans. It has no authority from the Bangko Sentral. Is it engaged in banking, and may it do so?

alac.answer: Yes, Lending Co. is engaged in banking, and it may not do so without Bangko Sentral authority.
alac.basis: Section 3.1 of the General Banking Law of 2000 defines banks as entities engaged in the lending of funds obtained in the form of deposits. Section 6 provides that no person or entity shall engage in banking operations or quasi-banking functions without authority from the Bangko Sentral, and that whether a person is performing banking functions without authority shall be decided by the Monetary Board.
alac.application: Here, Lending Co. receives money from the public, repayable on demand with interest, which are deposits in substance whatever they are called, and lends those funds. That is banking. It has no Bangko Sentral authority.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Lending Co. is engaged in unauthorized banking, which the Monetary Board may determine and stop.

keyPoints: Bank: lends funds obtained as deposits (Sec. 3.1)
Substance over label
Banking requires Bangko Sentral authority (Sec. 6)
cite: General Banking Law of 2000 (RA 8791), Secs. 3 and 6

q: Under Section 79 of the General Banking Law, a trust entity is:
choices: Any person who holds property for another
A stock corporation or person duly authorized by the Monetary Board to engage in trust business
hints: Trust business needs Monetary Board authority.
Quasi-banks borrow through deposit substitutes.
why: GBL Sec. 79: only a stock corporation or a person authorized by the Monetary Board may engage in trust business; it is called a trust entity. Quasi-banks borrow funds through deposit substitutes for re-lending (Sec. 4); banks lend funds obtained as deposits (Sec. 3.1).
cite: General Banking Law of 2000 (RA 8791), Secs. 3, 4 and 79

q: Fin Corp. issues promissory notes to 25 investors, assigned with recourse, to raise funds that it re-lends to small businesses. It does not accept deposits. A regulator asks: is Fin Corp. a bank, a quasi-bank or a trust entity?

alac.answer: Fin Corp. is a quasi-bank, not a bank or a trust entity.
alac.basis: Under the General Banking Law of 2000, banks are entities engaged in the lending of funds obtained in the form of deposits (Section 3.1). Quasi-banks are entities engaged in the borrowing of funds through the issuance, endorsement or assignment with recourse or acceptance of deposit substitutes for purposes of re-lending or purchasing receivables (Section 4). A trust entity is a stock corporation or person authorized by the Monetary Board to engage in trust business (Section 79).
alac.application: Here, Fin Corp. does not accept deposits, so it is not a bank. It borrows from the public through promissory notes assigned with recourse, which are deposit substitutes, in order to re-lend the funds. It does not hold property in trust for others.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Fin Corp. is a quasi-bank and needs Bangko Sentral authority to perform quasi-banking functions.

keyPoints: Bank: lends funds obtained as deposits (Sec. 3.1)
Quasi-bank: borrows through deposit substitutes to re-lend (Sec. 4)
Trust entity: authorized to engage in trust business (Sec. 79)
cite: General Banking Law of 2000 (RA 8791), Secs. 3, 4, 6 and 79

q: Because of the fiduciary nature of banking recognized in Section 2 of the General Banking Law, banks must observe:
choices: High standards of integrity and performance, a degree of diligence higher than that of a good father of a family
hints: Section 2 uses the word fiduciary.
The Supreme Court requires the highest degree of diligence.
why: GBL Sec. 2 recognizes the fiduciary nature of banking requiring high standards of integrity and performance; the Supreme Court requires banks to treat depositors' accounts with meticulous care (Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 88013, March 19, 1990).
cite: General Banking Law of 2000 (RA 8791), Sec. 2; Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 88013, March 19, 1990

q: Due to a teller's error, a bank failed to credit Gina's P100,000 deposit to her current account. Her checks issued to suppliers were then dishonored for insufficient funds, embarrassing her business. The bank corrected the error days later and argues that it acted in good faith. Is the bank liable for damages?

alac.answer: Yes, the bank is liable for damages.
alac.basis: Section 2 of the General Banking Law of 2000 recognizes the fiduciary nature of banking that requires high standards of integrity and performance. In Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 88013, March 19, 1990, the Supreme Court held that a bank which, through negligence, failed to credit a deposit and dishonored the depositor's checks is liable for damages, because the bank must treat the accounts of its depositors with meticulous care, whatever the amount involved.
alac.application: Here, the bank's teller failed to credit Gina's deposit, causing the dishonor of her checks and injury to her business reputation. Good faith does not excuse the negligence of a bank, whose business is impressed with public interest and whose duty to depositors is fiduciary.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the bank is liable to Gina for damages, which may include moral and exemplary damages.

keyPoints: Fiduciary nature of banking (GBL Sec. 2)
Meticulous care over depositors' accounts (Simex v. CA)
Negligent dishonor of checks gives rise to damages
cite: General Banking Law of 2000 (RA 8791), Sec. 2; Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 88013, March 19, 1990

q: Under Article 1980 of the Civil Code, fixed, savings and current deposits of money in banks are governed by the provisions on:
hints: The bank becomes the debtor of the depositor.
The bank may use the money.
why: Art. 1980: bank deposits are governed by the rules on simple loan; the bank becomes the owner of the money and the depositor's creditor (Guingona, Jr. v. City Fiscal of Manila, G.R. No. L-60033, April 4, 1984).
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1980; Guingona, Jr. v. City Fiscal of Manila, G.R. No. L-60033, April 4, 1984

q: Hector's savings deposit of P2 million in a bank was lost when the bank's manager misappropriated depositors' funds. Hector filed a complaint for estafa against the bank's president, arguing that the bank received the money in trust for him. Will the estafa complaint prosper on that theory?

alac.answer: No, the theory that the bank held the money in trust will not support estafa.
alac.basis: Article 1980 of the Civil Code provides that fixed, savings, and current deposits of money in banks shall be governed by the provisions concerning simple loan. In Guingona, Jr. v. City Fiscal of Manila, G.R. No. L-60033, April 4, 1984, the Supreme Court held that a bank deposit is a loan; the bank acquires ownership of the money and becomes the depositor's debtor, so its failure to return the deposit gives rise to civil liability, not estafa based on a trust.
alac.application: Here, Hector's savings deposit made the bank his debtor, not his trustee or agent. The bank owned the money and was obliged only to pay an equal amount. Hector's remedy against the bank is a civil action to collect the debt.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the estafa complaint on the theory of a trust will not prosper, although Hector may sue to recover his deposit, and the manager who misappropriated funds may face separate liability.

keyPoints: Bank deposits are simple loans (Art. 1980)
Bank becomes owner of the money and debtor of the depositor
Non-return is a civil obligation (Guingona v. City Fiscal)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1980; Guingona, Jr. v. City Fiscal of Manila, G.R. No. L-60033, April 4, 1984

q: Under Section 36 of the General Banking Law, a bank director may borrow from his bank only:
choices: With the approval of the president alone
If the loan is below P1 million without approval
With the written approval of the majority of all the directors, excluding the director concerned
hints: This is the DOSRI rule.
The interested director cannot approve his own loan.
why: GBL Sec. 36: no director or officer may borrow from the bank or be its obligor except with the written approval of the majority of all the directors, excluding the director concerned (except fringe benefit loans to officers).

q: Ivy, a bank loan officer, accepted a "thank you" gift of P50,000 from a borrower whose loan she had recommended for approval. Separately, Jose, a bank director, borrowed P5 million from the bank with only the president's verbal approval. What violations, if any, were committed?

alac.answer: Both Ivy and Jose violated the General Banking Law.
alac.basis: Section 55.1(c) of the General Banking Law of 2000 prohibits any director, officer, employee or agent of a bank from accepting gifts, fees, or commissions or any other form of remuneration in connection with the approval of a loan or other credit accommodation. Section 36 prohibits a director or officer from borrowing from the bank except with the written approval of the majority of all the directors, excluding the director concerned.
alac.application: Here, Ivy accepted P50,000 from a borrower in connection with a loan she recommended; the label "thank you" does not change its nature. Jose borrowed P5 million with only the president's verbal approval, not the written approval of the majority of the directors excluding himself.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ivy committed a prohibited transaction under Section 55, and Jose's loan violated the DOSRI rule of Section 36; both are subject to the penalties of the law.

keyPoints: No gifts in connection with loan approval (Sec. 55.1(c))
DOSRI loans need written approval of majority of directors, excluding the director (Sec. 36)
Verbal approval of the president is not enough
cite: General Banking Law of 2000 (RA 8791), Secs. 36 and 55

q: Under Section 1 of RA 1405, the purpose of the Law on Secrecy of Bank Deposits is to:
choices: Encourage people to deposit their money in banks and discourage private hoarding
Allow banks to charge higher fees
hints: Confidence in banks attracts deposits.
The deposits are then used for loans that help the economy.
why: RA 1405 Sec. 1: the policy is to encourage people to deposit their money in banks and to discourage private hoarding, so that the money may be used by banks in authorized loans.
cite: Law on Secrecy of Bank Deposits (RA 1405), Sec. 1

q: A senator proposes abolishing bank secrecy entirely so that all deposits may be examined by any government office on request. In a policy debate, you are asked: what is the purpose of bank secrecy under RA 1405, and why does that purpose matter?

alac.answer: Bank secrecy aims to encourage deposits and discourage hoarding, so that deposited funds can be used for loans that support economic development.
alac.basis: Section 1 of RA 1405 declares the policy of the Government to give encouragement to the people to deposit their money in banking institutions and to discourage private hoarding so that the same may be properly utilized by banks in authorized loans to assist in the economic development of the country. Section 2 makes deposits absolutely confidential, subject only to the exceptions provided by law.
alac.application: Here, removing all secrecy could make people fear exposure and keep their money outside banks. That would reduce the funds available for lending and weaken the economy, the very harm the law seeks to prevent. Narrow exceptions, such as those in RA 1405 and the Anti-Money Laundering Act, balance this policy against the needs of justice.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the purpose of bank secrecy is to promote deposits and their productive use, and any reform should keep targeted exceptions rather than abolish confidentiality.

keyPoints: Policy: encourage deposits, discourage hoarding (Sec. 1)
Deposits fund authorized loans for economic development
Absolute confidentiality subject to legal exceptions (Sec. 2)
cite: Law on Secrecy of Bank Deposits (RA 1405), Secs. 1 and 2

q: Under Section 3 of RA 1405, it is unlawful for any official or employee of a bank to:
choices: Disclose to any person other than those mentioned in Section 2 any information concerning deposits
Disclose deposit information to the depositor
Report a covered transaction to the AMLC
hints: Section 3 lists the prohibited act.
Penalties are in Section 5.
why: RA 1405 Sec. 3: it is unlawful for any bank official or employee to disclose information concerning deposits to persons other than those mentioned in Sec. 2; Sec. 5 penalizes violations with imprisonment of up to five years or a fine, or both.
cite: Law on Secrecy of Bank Deposits (RA 1405), Secs. 3 and 5

q: Karen, a bank teller, told her friend, a reporter, the balance of a celebrity's savings account, and the reporter published it. No court order or written consent of the celebrity existed. What liability, if any, does Karen face?

alac.answer: Karen is criminally liable for violating RA 1405.
alac.basis: Section 3 of RA 1405 makes it unlawful for any official or employee of a banking institution to disclose to any person other than those mentioned in Section 2 any information concerning deposits. Section 5 provides that any violation shall subject the offender, upon conviction, to imprisonment of not more than five years or a fine of not more than twenty thousand pesos, or both.
alac.application: Here, Karen, a bank employee, disclosed the celebrity's deposit balance to a reporter, who is not among the persons or cases allowed by Section 2. There was neither written permission of the depositor nor a court order.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Karen may be prosecuted and penalized under Sections 3 and 5 of RA 1405, without prejudice to civil liability for damages.

keyPoints: Prohibited disclosure by bank officials and employees (Sec. 3)
No exception applies
Penalty: imprisonment up to five years or fine, or both (Sec. 5)
cite: Law on Secrecy of Bank Deposits (RA 1405), Secs. 2, 3 and 5

q: Which of the following is an exception under Section 2 of RA 1405 that allows the examination of peso bank deposits?
choices: A request by the depositor's neighbor
Cases where the money deposited is the subject matter of the litigation
A request by a private creditor
hints: Section 2 lists four exceptions.
Others come from later laws, such as the AMLA.
why: RA 1405 Sec. 2: deposits may be examined upon written permission of the depositor, in impeachment cases, upon court order in bribery or dereliction of duty cases of public officials, or where the money deposited is the subject matter of the litigation. Later laws, such as the AMLA, add exceptions.
cite: Law on Secrecy of Bank Deposits (RA 1405), Sec. 2

q: Leo sued his former business partner Mario to recover P10 million that Mario allegedly took from their partnership and deposited in his personal account in Bank X. Leo asked the court to order Bank X to disclose Mario's account records. Mario invokes RA 1405. Should the court grant Leo's request?

alac.answer: Yes, the court may order the examination of the account, because the money deposited is the subject matter of the litigation.
alac.basis: Section 2 of RA 1405 provides that all deposits are absolutely confidential and may not be examined except upon written permission of the depositor, in cases of impeachment, upon order of a competent court in cases of bribery or dereliction of duty of public officials, or in cases where the money deposited or invested is the subject matter of the litigation.
alac.application: Here, Leo's action seeks to recover the very P10 million that Mario allegedly deposited in Bank X. The deposit is therefore the subject matter of the litigation, not merely evidence of Mario's general wealth.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court may order Bank X to disclose the records of the account insofar as they relate to the money in issue.

keyPoints: Absolute confidentiality of deposits (Sec. 2)
Exception: money deposited is the subject matter of the litigation
Examination limited to the deposit in issue
cite: Law on Secrecy of Bank Deposits (RA 1405), Sec. 2

q: Does the garnishment of a judgment debtor's peso bank deposit violate RA 1405?
choices: No; garnishment does not involve an examination or inquiry prohibited by the law, as held in China Banking Corp. v. Ortega
Only if the deposit exceeds P1 million
hints: Garnishment merely sets the money aside to satisfy a judgment.
Foreign currency deposits follow a stricter rule (RA 6426).
why: In China Banking Corporation v. Ortega, G.R. No. L-34964, January 31, 1973, the Supreme Court held that a bank may be required to disclose whether a judgment debtor has a deposit, for purposes of garnishment, without violating RA 1405, since garnishment is not the inquiry the law forbids.
cite: China Banking Corporation v. Ortega, G.R. No. L-34964, January 31, 1973

q: A foreign tourist was convicted of a serious crime against a Filipino child and ordered to pay damages, but he left the country. His only asset in the Philippines is a US dollar deposit in a local bank. The bank refuses to honor a writ of garnishment, citing the Foreign Currency Deposit Act (RA 6426), which exempts foreign currency deposits from garnishment. Must the bank comply?

alac.answer: Yes, under the ruling in Salvacion, the bank must honor the garnishment in this case.
alac.basis: Section 8 of RA 6426 provides that foreign currency deposits are absolutely confidential and exempt from attachment, garnishment, or any other order or process of any court. However, in Salvacion v. Central Bank of the Philippines, G.R. No. 94723, August 21, 1997, the Supreme Court held that this exemption cannot be invoked by a transient foreigner to defeat a judgment for damages in favor of a victim, because applying the law in that way would bring about an injustice its framers never intended.
alac.application: Here, the judgment debtor is a transient foreign tourist who committed a crime against a Filipino child and left the country, leaving his dollar deposit as his only asset. Refusing garnishment would let him use the law to escape his civil liability.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the bank must honor the writ of garnishment against the dollar deposit.

keyPoints: Foreign currency deposits generally exempt from garnishment (RA 6426, Sec. 8)
Exception for a transient foreigner's deposit to satisfy a judgment for the victim (Salvacion v. Central Bank)
Garnishment of peso deposits does not violate RA 1405 (China Banking v. Ortega)
cite: Foreign Currency Deposit Act (RA 6426), Sec. 8; Salvacion v. Central Bank of the Philippines, G.R. No. 94723, August 21, 1997

q: Under Section 15 of the New Central Bank Act, the Monetary Board shall, among others:
choices: Issue rules and regulations it considers necessary for the discharge of the responsibilities and powers of the Monetary Board and the Bangko Sentral
hints: The Monetary Board is the policy-making body of the BSP.
Its rules are reported to the President and Congress.
why: RA 7653 Sec. 15: the Monetary Board issues rules and regulations, directs the management and operations of the BSP, and establishes its personnel system; its rules are reported to the President and Congress within 15 days.
cite: New Central Bank Act (RA 7653, as amended by RA 11211), Sec. 15

q: The Monetary Board issued a circular requiring all banks to adopt stricter cybersecurity controls within six months. A bank challenges the circular, arguing that only Congress may impose such requirements. Is the circular valid?

alac.answer: Yes, the circular is a valid exercise of the Monetary Board's rule-making and supervisory powers.
alac.basis: Section 15(a) of the New Central Bank Act, as amended, empowers the Monetary Board to issue rules and regulations it considers necessary for the effective discharge of the responsibilities and exercise of the powers vested in it and the Bangko Sentral. Section 4 of the General Banking Law of 2000 subjects the operations of banks to Bangko Sentral supervision, including the issuance of rules of conduct and standards of operation.
alac.application: Here, cybersecurity controls protect depositors and the stability of the banking system, which are within the Bangko Sentral's supervisory responsibilities. The circular is a standard of operation issued under the Monetary Board's delegated rule-making power, not an act reserved to Congress.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the circular is valid, provided it is reasonable, published, and reported as required by law.

keyPoints: Monetary Board rule-making power (RA 7653, Sec. 15(a))
Bangko Sentral supervision includes standards of operation (GBL Sec. 4)
Delegated legislation must be reasonable and published
cite: New Central Bank Act (RA 7653, as amended), Sec. 15; General Banking Law of 2000 (RA 8791), Sec. 4

q: Under Section 29 of the New Central Bank Act, a conservatorship of a bank shall not exceed:
hints: A conservator tries to restore viability.
The time limit is short.
why: RA 7653 Sec. 29: the Monetary Board may appoint a conservator when a bank is in a state of continuing inability or unwillingness to maintain adequate liquidity; the conservator may overrule prior management; the conservatorship shall not exceed one year.

q: Bank Y has shown a continuing inability to maintain adequate liquidity, but it is still solvent. The Monetary Board appointed a conservator, who revoked a loan approved by Bank Y's old board in favor of the chairman's relative. The old board says the conservator has no such power. Is the board correct?

alac.answer: No, the old board is not correct; the conservator may revoke the loan approval.
alac.basis: Section 29 of the New Central Bank Act provides that whenever the Monetary Board finds that a bank is in a state of continuing inability or unwillingness to maintain a condition of liquidity deemed adequate to protect the interest of depositors and creditors, it may appoint a conservator with powers to take charge of the assets, liabilities and management, reorganize the management, and exercise all powers necessary to restore its viability. The conservator shall have the power to overrule or revoke the actions of the previous management and board of directors.
