alac.application: Here, Bank Y's continuing liquidity problem justified conservatorship. The conservator's revocation of a loan approved by the old board in favor of the chairman's relative is within the express power to overrule or revoke the actions of previous management, and it helps restore viability.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the conservator validly revoked the loan approval.

keyPoints: Ground: continuing inability or unwillingness to maintain adequate liquidity (Sec. 29)
Conservator may overrule or revoke acts of previous management
Purpose: restore viability; not to exceed one year

q: Under Section 30 of the New Central Bank Act, as amended by RA 11211, when grounds for closure exist, the Monetary Board may forbid the bank from doing business:
choices: Only after one year of conservatorship
Summarily and without need for prior hearing
Only with the consent of the stockholders
hints: The closure must be quick to protect depositors.
This is the close now, hear later doctrine.
why: RA 7653 Sec. 30, as amended: the Monetary Board may summarily and without prior hearing forbid the bank from doing business and designate the PDIC as receiver; the designation of a conservator is not a precondition.
cite: New Central Bank Act (RA 7653), Sec. 30, as amended by RA 11211

q: The Monetary Board closed Bank Z after finding that it had insufficient realizable assets to meet its liabilities, without first giving Bank Z a hearing. Fifteen days after the board of directors received the closure order, a minority stockholder filed a petition for certiorari, alleging denial of due process. Will the petition prosper?

alac.answer: No, the petition will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 30 of the New Central Bank Act, as amended by RA 11211, provides that when a bank has insufficient realizable assets to meet its liabilities, the Monetary Board may summarily and without need for prior hearing forbid it from doing business and designate the PDIC as receiver. The Monetary Board's action is final and executory and may be set aside only on certiorari for excess of jurisdiction or grave abuse of discretion, which petition may only be filed by the stockholders of record representing the majority of the capital stock within ten days from receipt by the board of directors of the order.
alac.application: Here, the closure without prior hearing is expressly allowed and does not violate due process, since the law authorizes summary closure. Moreover, the petition was filed by a minority stockholder, not stockholders representing the majority of the capital stock, and fifteen days after receipt, beyond the ten-day period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the petition for certiorari must be dismissed.

keyPoints: Summary closure without prior hearing is allowed (Sec. 30)
Certiorari only by majority stockholders of record
Within ten days from receipt by the board
cite: New Central Bank Act (RA 7653), Sec. 30, as amended by RA 11211

q: Under Section 30 of the New Central Bank Act, as amended, the receiver of a closed bank is:
choices: Any person chosen by the depositors
hints: PDIC also insures deposits.
For quasi-banks, a different receiver may be designated.
why: RA 7653 Sec. 30, as amended: the Monetary Board designates the PDIC as receiver in the case of banks; for quasi-banks, any person of recognized competence may be designated. The designation of a conservator is not a precondition to receivership.
cite: New Central Bank Act (RA 7653), Sec. 30, as amended by RA 11211

q: Bank W suspended payment of its deposit liabilities for two weeks. The Monetary Board immediately designated the PDIC as receiver without first placing Bank W under conservatorship. Bank W's board argues that conservatorship must come first. Is it correct?

alac.answer: No, Bank W's board is not correct.
alac.basis: Section 30 of the New Central Bank Act, as amended by RA 11211, allows the Monetary Board, when a bank has in any manner suspended the payment of its deposit liabilities, to forbid it from doing business and designate the PDIC as receiver. It expressly provides that the designation of a conservator is not a precondition to the designation of a receiver.
alac.application: Here, Bank W suspended payment of its deposit liabilities, a ground for receivership. The Monetary Board could therefore designate the PDIC as receiver directly, without any prior conservatorship.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the PDIC's designation as receiver is valid.

keyPoints: Suspension of payment of deposit liabilities is a ground (Sec. 30(a))
PDIC designated as receiver for banks
Conservatorship not a precondition to receivership
cite: New Central Bank Act (RA 7653), Sec. 30, as amended by RA 11211

q: After the closure of a bank, under Section 30 of the New Central Bank Act, as amended, the Monetary Board may direct the PDIC to:
choices: Proceed with the liquidation of the closed bank under that section and RA 3591, as amended
Sell the bank to the highest bidder without court approval
hints: Liquidation converts assets to pay creditors.
Creditors file claims in the liquidation proceedings.
why: RA 7653 Sec. 30, as amended: the Monetary Board may direct the PDIC to proceed with the liquidation of the closed bank under that section and RA 3591 (the PDIC Charter).
cite: New Central Bank Act (RA 7653), Sec. 30, as amended by RA 11211

q: After Bank V was closed and placed under liquidation by the PDIC, Nico, a creditor with a final money judgment against Bank V, asked the trial court that decided his case to issue a writ of execution against Bank V's properties. Should the writ issue?

alac.answer: No, the writ should not issue; Nico must file his claim in the liquidation proceedings.
alac.basis: Section 30 of the New Central Bank Act, as amended, provides that the Monetary Board may direct the PDIC to proceed with the liquidation of the closed bank under that section and RA 3591. In liquidation, the assets of the closed bank are held for the benefit of all its creditors and distributed according to the rules on concurrence and preference of credits, so individual creditors may not obtain separate executions that would prejudice the others.
alac.application: Here, Bank V is under liquidation by the PDIC. Allowing Nico to levy on its properties would give him a preference over other creditors, contrary to the purpose of a collective liquidation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Nico should file his claim with the liquidation court, and the trial court should not issue a separate writ of execution.

keyPoints: PDIC directed to liquidate the closed bank (Sec. 30)
Assets held for all creditors
Claims filed in the liquidation proceedings, not by separate execution
cite: New Central Bank Act (RA 7653), Sec. 30, as amended by RA 11211; Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation Charter (RA 3591, as amended)

q: Under Section 5(k) of the PDIC Charter, as amended by RA 11840, the insured deposit is the amount due to any:
choices: Bona fide depositor for legitimate deposits in an insured bank as of the date of closure, up to the maximum insured deposit
Person who claims to be a depositor
hints: Only bona fide depositors and legitimate deposits are covered.
The amount is computed as of the date of closure.
why: RA 3591 Sec. 5(k), as amended by RA 11840: insured deposit means the amount due to any bona fide depositor for legitimate deposits in an insured bank as of the date of closure, up to the maximum insured deposit (P1,000,000 since 15 March 2025, under the PDIC's authority to adjust coverage).
cite: Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation Charter (RA 3591, as amended by RA 11840), Sec. 5(k)

q: Olga held three accounts in a closed bank, all in her own name: a savings account of P400,000, a time deposit of P500,000 and a current account of P300,000. She claims deposit insurance for each account separately. How much is she entitled to?

alac.answer: Olga is entitled to deposit insurance only up to the maximum insured deposit for all her accounts combined.
alac.basis: Section 5(k) of the PDIC Charter, as amended by RA 11840, defines the insured deposit as the amount due to any bona fide depositor for legitimate deposits in an insured bank as of the date of closure, up to the maximum, and provides that in determining the amount due to any depositor, there shall be added together all deposits in the bank maintained in the same right and capacity for his or her benefit.
alac.application: Here, all three accounts are in Olga's name, in the same right and capacity, totaling P1,200,000. They are added together, and the maximum insured deposit applies to the total. With coverage at P1,000,000 (effective 15 March 2025), she may claim P1,000,000; the P200,000 balance may be claimed as an ordinary creditor in the liquidation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Olga cannot claim the maximum for each account separately; her accounts are combined and insured up to the single maximum.

keyPoints: Insured deposit: bona fide depositor, legitimate deposits, as of closure (Sec. 5(k))
Accounts in the same right and capacity are added together
Excess claimed in liquidation
cite: Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation Charter (RA 3591, as amended by RA 11840), Sec. 5(k)

q: Under Section 5(k) of the PDIC Charter, as amended, a joint account held by two natural persons is insured:
choices: Separately from individually-owned accounts, with the maximum insured deposit divided equally unless a different sharing is stipulated
Twice the maximum for each co-owner
hints: Joint accounts are insured separately.
If a juridical person is a co-owner, a presumption applies.
why: RA 3591 Sec. 5(k), as amended: a joint account is insured separately from individual accounts; if held by natural persons, the maximum is divided into equal shares unless stipulated otherwise; if held by a juridical person with natural persons, the maximum is presumed to belong entirely to the juridical person.
cite: Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation Charter (RA 3591, as amended by RA 11840), Sec. 5(k)

q: In a closed bank, Paolo has an individual savings account of P800,000. He also has a joint account "Paolo or Queenie" of P1,400,000 with his sister, with no stipulation on sharing. A third joint account of P600,000 is held by Paolo's corporation "and/or" Paolo. How is the deposit insurance applied, assuming a maximum insured deposit of P1,000,000?

alac.answer: Paolo's individual account is insured up to P800,000; the joint account with Queenie is insured up to P1,000,000, shared equally; and the account with the corporation is presumed to belong entirely to the corporation.
alac.basis: Section 5(k) of the PDIC Charter, as amended by RA 11840, provides that a joint account, regardless of whether the conjunction "and", "or", or "and/or" is used, shall be insured separately from any individually-owned deposit account. If the account is held jointly by two or more natural persons, the maximum insured deposit is divided into equal shares unless a different sharing is stipulated; if held by a juridical person jointly with natural persons, the maximum insured deposit is presumed to belong entirely to the juridical person.
alac.application: Here, Paolo's individual account of P800,000 is fully insured. The joint account with Queenie is insured separately up to P1,000,000, so each gets P500,000, with the P400,000 excess claimable in liquidation. The account of Paolo's corporation and Paolo is presumed to belong entirely to the corporation, which is insured up to P600,000 for it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Paolo receives P800,000 on his individual account and P500,000 as his share of the joint account with Queenie, while the third account is insured for the corporation.

keyPoints: Joint accounts insured separately from individual accounts
Equal division among natural persons absent stipulation
Juridical person with natural persons: presumed to belong to the juridical person
cite: Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation Charter (RA 3591, as amended by RA 11840), Sec. 5(k)

q: Under the PDIC Charter, as amended, splitting of deposits occurs when:
choices: A depositor withdraws part of his deposit
A deposit account is broken down into two or more accounts in the name of other persons, in order to increase deposit insurance coverage
A bank splits into two banks
A depositor opens a joint account with a relative
hints: The purpose is to get more insurance than allowed.
Only the original depositor is paid, up to the maximum.
why: Under RA 3591, as amended (by RA 9576 and RA 10846), splitting is the transfer of a deposit to other accounts or persons within 120 days before closure to increase coverage; the PDIC recognizes only the original depositor up to the maximum, and splitting is penalized.
cite: Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation Charter (RA 3591, as amended by RA 9576 and RA 10846)

q: Two months before Bank U was closed, Rhea, who had a P3 million deposit, transferred P1 million each to new accounts in the names of her two household helpers, who did not own the money, to maximize deposit insurance. After closure, the three of them each claim P1 million in deposit insurance. Will the claims succeed?

alac.answer: No, only Rhea may be paid deposit insurance, up to the maximum insured deposit.
alac.basis: Under the PDIC Charter, RA 3591, as amended by RA 9576 and RA 10846, the splitting of a qualified deposit, meaning the transfer of a deposit into two or more accounts in the names of other persons who are not its beneficial owners within 120 days before the closure of the bank, to increase deposit insurance coverage, is prohibited. The PDIC pays only the bona fide owner of the deposit, up to the maximum, and those who commit splitting may be penalized. Section 5(k), as amended by RA 11840, limits insurance to bona fide depositors for legitimate deposits.
alac.application: Here, Rhea broke her P3 million deposit into accounts in the names of her helpers, who were not the owners, two months before closure, to increase coverage. The helpers are not bona fide depositors, and the transferred deposits are Rhea's.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the PDIC will pay only Rhea, up to the maximum insured deposit, deny the helpers' claims, and Rhea may face liability for splitting.

keyPoints: Splitting: breaking a deposit into accounts of non-owners within 120 days before closure
Only the beneficial owner is insured, up to the maximum
Bona fide depositor requirement (Sec. 5(k))
cite: Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation Charter (RA 3591, as amended by RA 9576, RA 10846 and RA 11840)

q: Under the Anti-Money Laundering Act, as amended, which of the following is NOT required to report covered and suspicious transactions?
choices: Lawyers acting as independent legal professionals as to information covered by professional secrecy
Casinos, as to casino cash transactions
hints: Banks, insurers and casinos are covered persons.
Privileged communications are protected.
why: RA 9160, Sec. 3(a), as amended by RA 10365 and RA 10927, lists covered persons, including banks, insurance companies and casinos; lawyers and accountants acting as independent legal professionals are not required to report information obtained under professional secrecy or privilege.
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended by RA 10365 and RA 10927), Secs. 3(a) and 9(c)

q: A pawnshop and a real estate broker each received large cash payments from a client. The pawnshop owner says AMLA applies only to banks. What are the obligations of covered persons, and is the pawnshop one?

alac.answer: Yes, the pawnshop is a covered person, and it must identify its clients, keep records and report covered and suspicious transactions.
alac.basis: Section 3(a) of the Anti-Money Laundering Act, as amended by RA 10365, provides that covered persons include banks, non-banks, quasi-banks, trust entities, foreign exchange dealers, pawnshops, money changers, remittance companies and others supervised or regulated by the Bangko Sentral, and also includes certain real estate brokers under later amendments. Section 9, as amended, requires covered persons to establish customer identification, keep records, and report to the AMLC all covered transactions and suspicious transactions within five working days from occurrence.
alac.application: Here, the pawnshop is expressly listed as a covered person supervised by the Bangko Sentral. Its large cash receipts must be checked against the thresholds and suspicious circumstances and reported as required. The real estate broker's obligations depend on its coverage under the later amendments (RA 11521).
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the pawnshop owner is wrong; the pawnshop must comply with AMLA's identification, record-keeping and reporting obligations.

keyPoints: Covered persons include pawnshops (Sec. 3(a))
Know your customer and record-keeping (Sec. 9)
Report covered and suspicious transactions within five working days
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended by RA 10365 and RA 11521), Secs. 3(a) and 9

q: Under the AMLA, as amended, a suspicious transaction is one with a covered person:
choices: Regardless of the amount involved, where any of the circumstances listed by law exist, such as no underlying legal or economic justification
Only if it involves foreign currency
Only if a crime is proven
hints: Covered transactions depend on amount; suspicious ones do not.
Look at the circumstances, not the amount.
why: RA 9160 Sec. 3(b-1), inserted by RA 9194: suspicious transactions are transactions with covered institutions, regardless of the amounts involved, where any listed circumstance exists. Covered transactions are cash transactions above P500,000 within one banking day (Sec. 3(b)).
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended by RA 9194 and RA 10927), Sec. 3(b) and (b-1)

q: A jeepney driver with declared income of P20,000 a month deposited P90,000 in cash every day for a week in his bank account, keeping each deposit below P100,000. Must the bank report these transactions to the AMLC, though no single day exceeds P500,000?

alac.answer: Yes, the bank must report the transactions as suspicious transactions.
alac.basis: Section 3(b) of the Anti-Money Laundering Act, as amended, defines a covered transaction as a cash transaction in excess of P500,000 within one banking day. Section 3(b-1), inserted by RA 9194, defines suspicious transactions as transactions with covered institutions, regardless of the amounts involved, where circumstances exist such as that the amount involved is not commensurate with the business or financial capacity of the client, or that the transaction is structured to avoid the reporting requirements.
alac.application: Here, no single day's deposit exceeded P500,000, so the deposits are not covered transactions. But the depositor's daily P90,000 deposits are far beyond his P20,000 monthly income, and the pattern suggests structuring to avoid reporting.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the bank must report the deposits to the AMLC as suspicious transactions within the period required by law.

keyPoints: Covered transaction: cash above P500,000 within one banking day (Sec. 3(b))
Suspicious transaction: regardless of amount (Sec. 3(b-1))
Amount not commensurate with capacity; structuring
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended by RA 9194 and RA 10927), Sec. 3(b) and (b-1)

q: Under the safe harbor provision of the AMLA, covered persons and their officers who report covered or suspicious transactions to the AMLC:
choices: Are liable to the depositor for damages
Shall not be deemed to have violated RA 1405, RA 6426, RA 8791 and similar laws
Must first get the depositor's consent
hints: Reporting is a legal duty.
But tipping off the client is prohibited.
why: RA 9160 Sec. 9(c), as amended: when reporting to the AMLC, covered persons and their officers shall not be deemed to have violated the bank secrecy laws, but they are prohibited from communicating to anyone the fact that a report was made.
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended), Sec. 9(c)

q: A bank reported Sara's unusual cash deposits to the AMLC as a suspicious transaction. A bank officer then called Sara to warn her that a report had been made. Sara later sued the bank for violating bank secrecy by making the report. Decide both issues.

alac.answer: The bank is not liable for making the report, but the officer is liable for telling Sara about it.
alac.basis: Section 9(c) of the Anti-Money Laundering Act, as amended, provides that when reporting covered or suspicious transactions to the AMLC, covered persons and their officers and employees shall not be deemed to have violated RA 1405, RA 6426, RA 8791 and other similar laws, but are prohibited from communicating, directly or indirectly, in any manner or by any means, to any person the fact that a covered or suspicious transaction report was made. Violation of this prohibition is penalized.
alac.application: Here, the bank's report to the AMLC is protected by the safe harbor provision, so it is not a breach of bank secrecy. However, the officer's call to Sara disclosed the fact that a report had been made, which the law expressly prohibits.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Sara's suit against the bank for reporting will fail, but the officer may be held criminally liable for tipping off.

keyPoints: Safe harbor for reporting to the AMLC (Sec. 9(c))
No violation of bank secrecy laws
Tipping off is prohibited and penalized
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended), Sec. 9(c)

q: Under Section 4 of the AMLA, money laundering is a crime whereby:
choices: Taxes are evaded by any means
The proceeds of an unlawful activity are transacted, making them appear to have originated from legitimate sources
hints: Laundering makes dirty money look clean.
Knowledge that the property is proceeds of unlawful activity is required.
why: RA 9160 Sec. 4 (as amended by RA 10365): money laundering is committed by any person who, knowing that any monetary instrument or property represents the proceeds of any unlawful activity, transacts it, converts, transfers, conceals or disguises it, or facilitates the offense, among others.
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended by RA 10365), Sec. 4

q: Tomas, knowing that his brother obtained P20 million from illegal drug sales, agreed to put the money in his own name, buy a building with it, and lease out the building. Has Tomas committed money laundering, though he did not sell drugs himself?

alac.answer: Yes, Tomas committed money laundering.
alac.basis: Section 4 of the Anti-Money Laundering Act defines money laundering as a crime whereby the proceeds of an unlawful activity are transacted, thereby making them appear to have originated from legitimate sources. It is committed by any person who, knowing that any monetary instrument or property represents, involves, or relates to the proceeds of any unlawful activity, transacts or attempts to transact said monetary instrument or property, or converts, transfers, disposes of, conceals or disguises it.
alac.application: Here, Tomas knew the P20 million came from illegal drug sales, an unlawful activity under the law. He put the money in his own name and converted it into a building that earns rent, which disguises its illegal origin and makes it appear legitimate. He need not have committed the drug offense himself.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Tomas is liable for money laundering, separately from his brother's liability for the drug offense.

keyPoints: Money laundering: transacting proceeds of unlawful activity to make them appear legitimate (Sec. 4)
Knowledge of the illegal source
Separate from the predicate offense
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended by RA 10365), Sec. 4

q: Under Section 3(i) of the AMLA, as amended, an unlawful activity (predicate offense) is:
choices: Any act or omission involving or having direct relation to the offenses specifically listed in the law
hints: The law gives a list.
Later laws (such as RA 11930 and RA 12312) added offenses.
why: RA 9160 Sec. 3(i), as amended by RA 10365 and later laws: unlawful activity refers to acts or omissions involving or having direct relation to the listed offenses, such as kidnapping for ransom, drug offenses, graft, plunder, robbery and extortion, swindling, smuggling, fraud, and others added by later laws.
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended by RA 10365, RA 11930 and RA 12312), Sec. 3(i)

q: The AMLC sought to freeze Ursula's bank accounts, alleging that she deposited proceeds of an unlawful activity. Ursula argues that no criminal case for the unlawful activity has been filed, much less a conviction, so there is no predicate offense. Is the lack of a criminal case fatal?

alac.answer: No, a prior criminal case or conviction for the unlawful activity is not required.
alac.basis: Section 3(i) of the Anti-Money Laundering Act, as amended, defines unlawful activity as any act or omission or series or combination thereof involving or having direct relation to the offenses listed in the law. Money laundering is a crime separate and distinct from the unlawful activity, and a freeze order requires only a determination that probable cause exists that the monetary instrument or property is in any way related to an unlawful activity.
alac.application: Here, the AMLC need only show probable cause that Ursula's deposits are related to a listed unlawful activity. The absence of a criminal case or conviction for the predicate offense does not prevent a freeze, and it would not even bar a prosecution for money laundering, which is a separate offense.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ursula's argument fails, and the freeze may issue upon a showing of probable cause.

keyPoints: Unlawful activity: listed offenses (Sec. 3(i))
Money laundering is separate from the predicate offense
Freeze requires probable cause only
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended by RA 10365), Secs. 3(i) and 10

q: Under Section 10 of the AMLA, as amended by RA 10365, a freeze order is issued by:
choices: The Court of Appeals, upon a verified ex parte petition of the AMLC and a finding of probable cause
Any Regional Trial Court upon a depositor's motion
hints: The AMLC applies; a court issues.
It is effective immediately but limited in time.
why: RA 9160 Sec. 10, as amended by RA 10365: upon a verified ex parte petition by the AMLC and a finding of probable cause, the Court of Appeals may issue a freeze order effective immediately, not exceeding six months. Sec. 11 (as amended by RA 10167): the AMLC may inquire into deposits upon order of a competent court on an ex parte application. Sec. 12: civil forfeiture.
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended by RA 10167 and RA 10365), Secs. 10-12

q: The AMLC, without any court order, directed Bank T to let it examine Vic's deposits because it suspected they were proceeds of graft. Bank T refused. Later, the AMLC obtained an ex parte court order to examine the accounts. Vic argues that he should have been notified and heard first. Rule on Bank T's refusal and on Vic's argument.

alac.answer: Bank T validly refused the examination without a court order, and Vic is not entitled to prior notice and hearing on the AMLC's ex parte application.
alac.basis: Section 11 of the Anti-Money Laundering Act, as amended by RA 10167, provides that notwithstanding RA 1405, RA 6426, RA 8791 and other laws, the AMLC may inquire into or examine any particular deposit or investment, including related accounts, upon order of any competent court based on an ex parte application in cases of violations of the Act, when it has been established that there is probable cause that the deposits are related to an unlawful activity or money laundering. The law expressly allows the application to be ex parte.
alac.application: Here, the AMLC first demanded examination without a court order, which is not allowed for graft, an offense outside the few unlawful activities where the law permits inquiry without a court order. Bank T rightly refused. The AMLC's later ex parte application was proper, since the law allows the court to act without notice to Vic to prevent the dissipation of funds.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Bank T's refusal was valid, and the court's ex parte order allowing examination is also valid.

keyPoints: AMLC may inquire into deposits upon court order (Sec. 11, as amended by RA 10167)
Application is ex parte
Probable cause required
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended by RA 10167), Sec. 11

q: Under Section 22 of the IP Code, which of the following is excluded from patent protection?
choices: A new chemical process for making paint
An improvement to a car engine
A new machine for peeling mangoes
hints: Patentable: new, inventive, industrially applicable (Sec. 21).
Business methods and computer programs are excluded.
why: IP Code Sec. 21: a technical solution that is new, involves an inventive step and is industrially applicable is patentable; Sec. 22 excludes discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, schemes and methods of doing business, programs for computers, surgical and diagnostic methods, and plant varieties, among others.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 21 and 22

q: Dr. Wen developed a new surgical technique for heart bypass, and also a new surgical clamp designed for that technique. She had demonstrated the clamp at an international medical conference eight months before filing her patent applications. Which, if any, may be patented?

alac.answer: The clamp may be patented, but the surgical technique may not.
alac.basis: Section 21 of the IP Code provides that any technical solution of a problem which is new, involves an inventive step and is industrially applicable is patentable. Section 22.3 excludes methods for treatment of the human body by surgery or therapy, but this provision shall not apply to products for use in any of these methods. Section 25 provides that disclosure by the inventor during the twelve months preceding the filing date shall not prejudice the applicant on the ground of lack of novelty.
alac.application: Here, the surgical technique is a method for treatment of the human body by surgery, which is excluded. The clamp is a product for use in that method, which is not excluded. Its demonstration by Dr. Wen herself eight months before filing falls within the twelve-month grace period, so it does not destroy novelty.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dr. Wen may obtain a patent for the clamp, if it also involves an inventive step and is industrially applicable, but not for the surgical technique.

keyPoints: Patentability: novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability (Sec. 21)
Surgical methods excluded, but not products used in them (Sec. 22.3)
Twelve-month grace period for the inventor's own disclosure (Sec. 25)
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 21, 22 and 25

q: Under Section 29 of the IP Code, if two persons made the same invention separately and independently, the right to the patent belongs to:
choices: The one who filed first, or who has the earliest filing or priority date
hints: The Philippines follows the first-to-file rule.
Joint inventors own jointly (Sec. 28).
why: IP Code Sec. 28: the right to a patent belongs to the inventor, his heirs or assigns, jointly for joint inventors; Sec. 29: between independent inventors, the first to file (earliest filing or priority date) prevails; Sec. 30: rules for commissioned and employee inventions.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 28-30

q: Xavi, an accountant at a food company, invented a new food-packaging machine on weekends, using the company's workshop and materials. Yuri, the company's research engineer, invented a new preservative as part of his assigned work. Neither had an agreement with the company on inventions. Who owns the patents?

alac.answer: Xavi owns the patent to the packaging machine; the company owns the patent to Yuri's preservative.
alac.basis: Section 30.2 of the IP Code provides that when an employee made an invention in the course of his employment, the patent shall belong to (a) the employee, if the inventive activity is not a part of his regular duties even if the employee uses the time, facilities and materials of the employer; and (b) the employer, if the invention is the result of the performance of his regularly-assigned duties, unless there is an agreement to the contrary.
alac.application: Here, inventing machines is not part of Xavi's regular duties as an accountant, so he owns the patent even though he used the company's workshop and materials. Yuri invented the preservative as part of his assigned research work, and there is no contrary agreement.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Xavi owns the patent to his machine, and the company owns the patent to the preservative.

keyPoints: Employee owns if inventing is not part of regular duties, even using employer's facilities (Sec. 30.2(a))
Employer owns if invention results from regularly-assigned duties (Sec. 30.2(b))
Subject to contrary agreement
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 30

q: Under Section 72 of the IP Code, which act does NOT infringe a patent even without the owner's authorization?
choices: Manufacturing the product for commercial sale
Using the patented invention exclusively for experiments that relate to its subject matter
Selling copies of the patented product made without license
Importing the patented product for sale
hints: Sec. 71 grants exclusive rights; Sec. 72 lists limits.
Experimental use is allowed.
why: IP Code Sec. 71: the patent owner may prevent unauthorized making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product; Sec. 72 lists limitations, such as use after the product is put on the market by the owner, private non-commercial acts, and experimental use. The term is 20 years from filing (Sec. 54).
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 54, 71 and 72

q: Pharma Co. holds a Philippine patent for a drug. A drugstore bought the drug from Pharma Co.'s authorized Philippine distributor and resold it. A university laboratory also made small quantities of the drug solely to study how it works. Pharma Co. sued both for infringement. Will the suits prosper?

alac.answer: No, neither suit will prosper.
alac.basis: Section 71 of the IP Code grants the patent owner the exclusive right to prevent unauthorized persons from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the patented product. Section 72 provides that the owner has no right to prevent third parties from using a patented product which has been put on the market in the Philippines by the owner or with his express consent, after it has been so put on the market, nor acts consisting of making or using exclusively for the purpose of experiments that relate to the subject matter of the patented invention.
alac.application: Here, the drugstore resold drugs that Pharma Co. itself put on the Philippine market through its authorized distributor, so Pharma Co.'s rights over those units were exhausted. The university made small quantities solely to study the drug, which is experimental use.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, neither the drugstore nor the university is liable for infringement.

keyPoints: Exclusive rights of the patent owner (Sec. 71)
Exhaustion after the owner puts the product on the market (Sec. 72.1)
Experimental use exception (Sec. 72.3)
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 71 and 72

q: Under the doctrine of equivalents applied in Godines v. Court of Appeals, an infringement exists when the accused device:
choices: Is sold at a lower price
Performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain substantially the same result
Is made of different materials but has a different function
hints: Literal infringement is not the only kind.
Minor changes do not avoid infringement.
why: IP Code Sec. 76.1 defines patent infringement; under the doctrine of equivalents, a device that performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result infringes (Godines v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 97343, September 13, 1993).
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 76; Godines v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 97343, September 13, 1993

q: Zeny holds a patent for a hand tractor. Alan made hand tractors that are almost identical in design and operation, but with a slightly longer handle and a different color, and sold them under another name. Alan argues that his tractors are not exact copies, so there is no infringement. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Alan is not correct; he infringed Zeny's patent.
alac.basis: Section 76.1 of the IP Code provides that making, using, offering for sale, selling, or importing a patented product without the authorization of the patentee constitutes patent infringement. In Godines v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 97343, September 13, 1993, the Supreme Court applied the doctrine of equivalents: infringement exists when a device appropriates a prior invention by incorporating its innovative concept, and, although with some modification and change, performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result.
alac.application: Here, Alan's hand tractors are almost identical in design and operation to Zeny's patented tractor. A longer handle, a different color and a different name are minor changes that do not alter the function, the way it works, or the result.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Alan is liable for patent infringement, and Zeny may recover damages and obtain an injunction.

keyPoints: Patent infringement defined (Sec. 76.1)
Doctrine of equivalents: same function, same way, same result (Godines v. CA)
Minor modifications do not avoid liability
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 76; Godines v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 97343, September 13, 1993

q: Under Section 105 of the IP Code, an assignment of a patent must be:
choices: In writing, acknowledged before a notary public or other authorized officer, and certified under his hand and seal
hints: Assignment may be of the whole or an undivided share (Sec. 104).
It may also be limited to a territory.
why: IP Code Sec. 104: an assignment may be of the entire right or an undivided share, in which case the parties become joint owners, and may be limited to a territory; Sec. 105: it must be in writing and notarized.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 104 and 105

q: Bea, a patentee, orally agreed to assign to Carl a one-half undivided share in her patent for a water filter, limited to the Visayas. Carl paid but Bea later refused to sign any document, claiming the assignment is invalid. Is the oral assignment valid as an assignment of the patent?

alac.answer: No, the oral assignment is not effective as a patent assignment, although Carl may compel Bea to execute the proper document or recover what he paid.
alac.basis: Section 104 of the IP Code provides that an assignment may be of the entire right, title or interest in the patent, or of an undivided share, in which event the parties become joint owners, and that an assignment may be limited to a specified territory. Section 105 provides that the assignment must be in writing, acknowledged before a notary public or other officer authorized to perform notarial acts, and certified under his hand and official seal.
alac.application: Here, an assignment of a one-half undivided share limited to the Visayas is allowed in substance. But the agreement was only oral, so it does not comply with the form required by Section 105. Since Carl has paid, the agreement may still be enforced between the parties, for example by an action to compel Bea to execute the written and notarized assignment, or Carl may recover the price.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Carl does not yet hold a valid assignment of the patent, but he has remedies to enforce the agreement or recover his payment.

keyPoints: Assignment of the whole or an undivided share; may be territorial (Sec. 104)
Assignment must be written and notarized (Sec. 105)
Remedies between the parties
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 104 and 105

q: Under Section 93 of the IP Code, a compulsory license to exploit a patented invention may be granted, even without the patent owner's agreement, in case of:
choices: National emergency or other circumstances of extreme urgency
The patent owner's refusal to sell to a friend
hints: Voluntary licenses are governed by Secs. 85-92.
Compulsory licensing is an exception for public needs.
why: IP Code Sec. 85: voluntary license contracts (technology transfer arrangements) must comply with the Chapter; Sec. 93: the Director of Legal Affairs may grant a compulsory license on grounds including national emergency, public interest, anti-competitive exploitation, and non-working of the patent.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 85 and 93

q: During a declared national health emergency, the Department of Health found that a patented anti-viral drug is sold at prices far beyond most patients' reach, and the patent owner refused to license local manufacturers. A local drug maker capable of producing the drug applied for a license. May one be granted without the patent owner's consent?

alac.answer: Yes, a compulsory license may be granted.
alac.basis: Section 93 of the IP Code provides that the Director of Legal Affairs may grant a license to exploit a patented invention, even without the agreement of the patent owner, in favor of any person who has shown his capability to exploit the invention, in case of national emergency or other circumstances of extreme urgency, or where the public interest, in particular national security, nutrition, health or the development of other vital sectors, as determined by the appropriate agency, so requires. The patent owner is paid adequate remuneration.
alac.application: Here, there is a declared national health emergency, and the Department of Health has determined that public health requires wider access to the drug. The applicant has shown it is capable of producing the drug.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, a compulsory license may be granted to the local drug maker, subject to the payment of reasonable royalties to the patent owner.

keyPoints: Compulsory license without the owner's consent (Sec. 93)
Grounds: national emergency; public interest including health
Applicant must be capable of exploiting the invention; owner paid remuneration
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 93

q: Under Section 68 of the IP Code, if a person deprived of the patent without his consent or through fraud is declared by final court decision to be the true and actual inventor, the court shall:
choices: Order his substitution as patentee or, at his option, cancel the patent, and award damages if warranted
hints: The true inventor chooses the remedy.
Damages may be awarded.
why: IP Code Sec. 68: the true and actual inventor may be substituted as patentee or, at his option, have the patent cancelled, with damages if warranted; Sec. 67 gives remedies against applications by persons without the right to a patent.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 67 and 68

q: Dina, a technician, stole the design of a solar water pump invented by her employer's research partner, Ed, who was not her employer, and obtained a patent in her own name. Ed proved in court that he is the true and actual inventor. What remedies does Ed have?

alac.answer: Ed may have himself substituted as patentee or, at his option, have the patent cancelled, and he may recover damages.
alac.basis: Section 68 of the IP Code provides that if a person who was deprived of the patent without his consent or through fraud is declared by final court order or decision to be the true and actual inventor, the court shall order his substitution as patentee, or at the option of the true inventor, cancel the patent, and award actual and other damages in his favor if warranted by the circumstances.
alac.application: Here, Dina obtained the patent by stealing Ed's design, so Ed was deprived of the patent without his consent and through fraud. He has been declared by the court to be the true and actual inventor.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ed may choose to be substituted as patentee, or to have Dina's patent cancelled, and may be awarded actual and other damages.

keyPoints: Remedies of the true and actual inventor (Sec. 68)
Substitution as patentee or cancellation, at the inventor's option
Damages if warranted
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 68

q: Under Section 61 of the IP Code, which is a ground for the cancellation of a patent?
choices: What is claimed as the invention is not new or patentable
hints: There are three grounds.
Cancellation may be partial.
why: IP Code Sec. 61: any interested person may petition to cancel a patent on the grounds that the invention is not new or patentable, the patent does not sufficiently disclose the invention, or it is contrary to public order or morality; cancellation may be limited to certain claims.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 61

q: Fe obtained a patent for a "self-cooling bottle," with five claims. Gil, a competitor, proved that claims 1 and 2 describe a bottle sold in Japan years before Fe's application, but claims 3 to 5 describe a new cooling valve. Gil petitioned to cancel the entire patent. How should the petition be resolved?

alac.answer: Only claims 1 and 2 should be cancelled; claims 3 to 5 remain valid.
alac.basis: Section 61.1 of the IP Code provides that any interested person may petition to cancel the patent or any claim thereof, or parts of the claim, on the ground, among others, that what is claimed as the invention is not new or patentable. Section 24.1 provides that prior art consists of everything made available to the public anywhere in the world before the filing date. Section 61.2 provides that where the grounds relate to some of the claims, cancellation may be effected to such extent only.
alac.application: Here, claims 1 and 2 describe a bottle already sold in Japan before Fe's application, so they form part of the prior art and are not new. Claims 3 to 5, covering the new cooling valve, are not affected by that ground.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the patent should be cancelled only as to claims 1 and 2.

keyPoints: Cancellation on lack of novelty (Sec. 61.1(a))
Prior art includes anything public anywhere in the world (Sec. 24.1)
Partial cancellation (Sec. 61.2)
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 24 and 61

q: Under Section 121 of the IP Code, a trade name is:
choices: A sign used by members of an association
The name or designation identifying or distinguishing an enterprise
hints: A mark identifies goods or services; a trade name identifies the business.
A collective mark is used by different enterprises under the owner's control.
why: IP Code Sec. 121.1: a mark is any visible sign capable of distinguishing goods (trademark) or services (service mark); Sec. 121.2: a collective mark distinguishes origin or common characteristics of goods of different enterprises under the owner's control; Sec. 121.3: a trade name identifies or distinguishes an enterprise.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 121

q: "Bayview Coffee Roasters, Inc." has used its business name for years but never registered it with the IPO. A new cafe opened nearby under the name "Bayview Coffee." May Bayview Coffee Roasters stop the new cafe, though its name is unregistered?

alac.answer: Yes, it may stop the new cafe's use of a confusingly similar trade name, even without registration.
alac.basis: Section 121.3 of the IP Code defines a trade name as the name or designation identifying or distinguishing an enterprise. Section 165.2 provides that trade names shall be protected, even prior to or without registration, against any unlawful act committed by third parties, and that any subsequent use of a similar trade name likely to mislead the public shall be deemed unlawful. In Coffee Partners, Inc. v. San Francisco Coffee & Roastery, Inc., G.R. No. 169504, March 3, 2010, the Supreme Court protected a prior user's unregistered trade name against a confusingly similar mark.
alac.application: Here, "Bayview Coffee Roasters" identifies an existing enterprise and has been used for years. The new cafe's "Bayview Coffee," for the same kind of business nearby, is likely to mislead the public.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Bayview Coffee Roasters may sue to stop the new cafe's use of the name, despite the absence of registration.

keyPoints: Trade name defined (Sec. 121.3)
Trade names protected even without registration (Sec. 165.2)
Coffee Partners v. San Francisco Coffee
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 121 and 165; Coffee Partners, Inc. v. San Francisco Coffee & Roastery, Inc., G.R. No. 169504, March 3, 2010

q: Under Section 123.1 of the IP Code, which of the following marks cannot be registered?
hints: Generic terms cannot be monopolized.
A word may be generic for one product but arbitrary for another.
why: IP Code Sec. 123.1(h): a mark consisting exclusively of signs that are generic for the goods it identifies cannot be registered; descriptive marks (j), shapes (k) and color alone (l) may be registered if they have acquired distinctiveness (Sec. 123.2).
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 123

q: Hana applied to register "SUPER SOFT" for tissue paper. The examiner refused it as descriptive. Hana proved that she had sold tissue under "SUPER SOFT" exclusively and continuously for ten years, and that consumers associate it with her product. Should the mark be registered?

alac.answer: Yes, the mark may be registered because it has acquired distinctiveness.
alac.basis: Section 123.1(j) of the IP Code provides that a mark cannot be registered if it consists exclusively of signs that may serve in trade to designate the kind, quality or other characteristics of the goods. However, Section 123.2 provides that nothing shall prevent the registration of any such sign which has become distinctive in relation to the goods for which registration is requested as a result of the use made of it in commerce, and the Office may accept as prima facie evidence of distinctiveness proof of substantially exclusive and continuous use for five years.
alac.application: Here, "SUPER SOFT" describes a quality of tissue paper, so it is descriptive. But Hana used it exclusively and continuously for ten years, more than five, and consumers associate it with her goods. It has acquired a secondary meaning.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the mark should be registered on the basis of acquired distinctiveness.

keyPoints: Descriptive marks not registrable (Sec. 123.1(j))
Exception: acquired distinctiveness through use (Sec. 123.2)
Five years' exclusive and continuous use as prima facie proof
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 123

q: Under Section 123.1(e) of the IP Code, in determining whether a mark is well-known, account shall be taken of:
choices: Only the price of the goods
The knowledge of the relevant sector of the public, rather than of the public at large
hints: Registration in the Philippines is not required for protection against identical or similar goods.
Promotion in the Philippines counts.
why: IP Code Sec. 123.1(e): a mark identical or confusingly similar to a mark well-known internationally and in the Philippines, whether or not registered here, cannot be registered for identical or similar goods; well-known status is judged by the knowledge of the relevant sector of the public. Sec. 123.1(f) extends protection of registered well-known marks to dissimilar goods.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 123.1(e) and (f); Fredco Manufacturing Corporation v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, G.R. No. 185917, June 1, 2011

q: A local company registered "Harvard" with a veritas shield logo for its clothing in the Philippines. Harvard University, which had not registered the mark for clothing here, sought cancellation, proving that its name and logo are known worldwide and in the Philippines. The local company argues that it registered first. Who should prevail?

alac.answer: Harvard University should prevail, and the local company's registration should be cancelled.
alac.basis: Section 123.1(e) of the IP Code provides that a mark cannot be registered if it is identical with or confusingly similar to a mark considered well-known internationally and in the Philippines, whether or not it is registered here, as being already the mark of a person other than the applicant, and used for identical or similar goods. In Fredco Manufacturing Corporation v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, G.R. No. 185917, June 1, 2011, the Supreme Court held that "Harvard" is a well-known mark protected in the Philippines even without registration, and that a local registration of it for clothing may be cancelled.
alac.application: Here, the local company's mark copies Harvard's well-known name and shield, which are known internationally and in the Philippines. Harvard's lack of registration for clothing in the Philippines does not matter, since well-known marks are protected whether or not registered here, and the local company's earlier registration was contrary to the law.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the local company's registration should be cancelled.

keyPoints: Protection of well-known marks whether or not registered here (Sec. 123.1(e))
Relevant sector of the public
Fredco v. Harvard
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 123.1(e); Fredco Manufacturing Corporation v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, G.R. No. 185917, June 1, 2011

q: Under Sections 122, 145 and 146 of the IP Code, rights in a mark are acquired and maintained by:
choices: Valid registration; the registration lasts ten years, renewable for ten-year periods, with a declaration of actual use within one year from the fifth anniversary
hints: The IP Code shifted from use to registration.
Use must still be proved later.
why: IP Code Sec. 122: rights in a mark are acquired through valid registration; Sec. 145: registration remains in force for ten years, provided a declaration of actual use is filed within one year from the fifth anniversary; Sec. 146: renewable for ten-year periods.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 122, 145 and 146

q: Iris registered the mark "IRISSA" for shoes in 2019 but never sold any shoes and filed no declaration of actual use. In 2025, Jun, who had been using "IRISSA" for shoes in good faith since 2017, wants to use and register it. What is the status of Iris's registration, and can Jun continue using the mark?

alac.answer: Iris's registration should be removed for failure to file a declaration of actual use, and Jun, a prior good-faith user, may continue using the mark.
alac.basis: Section 122 of the IP Code provides that rights in a mark are acquired through valid registration. Section 145 provides that a certificate of registration remains in force for ten years, provided the registrant files a declaration of actual use within one year from the fifth anniversary of the registration; otherwise, the mark shall be removed from the Register. Section 159.1 provides that a registered mark shall have no effect against any person who, in good faith, before the filing date, was using the mark for his business.
alac.application: Here, Iris registered in 2019 but filed no declaration of actual use within one year from the fifth anniversary in 2024, so her mark should be removed from the Register. In any case, Jun had used "IRISSA" in good faith since 2017, before Iris's filing date.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Iris's registration should be removed, and Jun may continue using, and apply to register, the mark.

keyPoints: Rights acquired through registration (Sec. 122)
Ten-year term; declaration of actual use after the fifth anniversary (Sec. 145)
Prior good-faith user protected (Sec. 159.1)
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 122, 145 and 159

q: Under Section 147.1 of the IP Code, in case of use of an identical sign for identical goods or services:
choices: A likelihood of confusion shall be presumed
Only criminal action may be filed
Confusion must be proved by surveys
hints: The registered owner has exclusive rights.
Identical sign plus identical goods is the clearest case.
why: IP Code Sec. 147.1: the owner of a registered mark may prevent third parties from using identical or similar signs for identical or similar goods where use would result in a likelihood of confusion, which is presumed for identical signs on identical goods; Sec. 147.2 extends protection of registered well-known marks to dissimilar goods.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 147

q: Kola Corp. owns the registered and well-known mark "KOLA" for soft drinks. Leon began selling "KOLA" cellphone cases, with Kola Corp.'s distinctive red script, suggesting that they are official Kola products. Leon argues that cellphone cases are different from soft drinks, so no infringement exists. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Leon is not correct; Kola Corp. may stop his use of the mark.
alac.basis: Section 147.2 of the IP Code provides that the exclusive right of the owner of a well-known mark which is registered in the Philippines shall extend to goods and services which are not similar to those in respect of which the mark is registered, provided that use of the mark in relation to those goods would indicate a connection between those goods and the owner of the registered mark, and the interests of the owner are likely to be damaged by such use.
alac.application: Here, "KOLA" is registered and well-known. Leon's use of it, in the same distinctive red script, on cellphone cases suggests that they are official Kola products, indicating a connection with Kola Corp. This use is likely to damage Kola Corp.'s interests, such as its reputation and the distinctiveness of its mark.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Kola Corp.'s rights extend to cellphone cases, and it may prevent Leon's use of the mark.

keyPoints: Exclusive rights of the registered owner (Sec. 147.1)
Well-known registered marks protected even for dissimilar goods (Sec. 147.2)
Connection with the owner and likely damage
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 147

q: Under the dominancy test, likelihood of confusion is determined by:
choices: Looking only at the entire packaging including labels and prices
Comparing the prices of the goods
Counting the letters of each mark
Focusing on the similarity of the prevalent or dominant features of the competing marks that might cause confusion
hints: The IP Code adopts the dominancy test (Sec. 155.1).
The holistic test considers the marks as a whole.
why: Under the dominancy test, which the IP Code adopts in Sec. 155.1 ("a dominant feature thereof"), the court focuses on the similarity of the dominant features of the marks (McDonald's Corporation v. L.C. Big Mak Burger, Inc., G.R. No. 143993, August 18, 2004).
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 155; McDonald's Corporation v. L.C. Big Mak Burger, Inc., G.R. No. 143993, August 18, 2004

q: McBurger Corp. owns the registered mark "BIG MAC" for hamburgers. A local chain began selling hamburgers as "BIG MAK," in different packaging, with its own corporate name printed on the wrappers. Using the dominancy test, is there a likelihood of confusion?

alac.answer: Yes, there is a likelihood of confusion under the dominancy test.
alac.basis: Section 155.1 of the IP Code penalizes the use in commerce of any reproduction, copy, or colorable imitation of a registered mark or a dominant feature thereof, where such use is likely to cause confusion. In McDonald's Corporation v. L.C. Big Mak Burger, Inc., G.R. No. 143993, August 18, 2004, the Supreme Court applied the dominancy test, which focuses on the similarity of the dominant features of the marks, and held that "Big Mak" is confusingly similar to "Big Mac" because they are aurally almost identical and used on the same goods, regardless of differences in packaging.
alac.application: Here, "BIG MAK" and "BIG MAC" sound almost the same and are used for the same goods, hamburgers. Under the dominancy test, differences in packaging and the printing of the chain's corporate name do not remove the confusion created by the dominant feature.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, there is a likelihood of confusion, and the local chain's use of "BIG MAK" infringes McBurger Corp.'s mark.

keyPoints: Dominancy test: similarity of dominant features (Sec. 155.1)
Aural similarity on identical goods
McDonald's v. L.C. Big Mak
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 155; McDonald's Corporation v. L.C. Big Mak Burger, Inc., G.R. No. 143993, August 18, 2004

q: Under Section 155 of the IP Code, trademark infringement requires, among others:
choices: That the goods are sold abroad
Use without the registered owner's consent of a reproduction or colorable imitation of the registered mark, likely to cause confusion
Proof of fraudulent intent in all cases
hints: Registration is an element of infringement.
Fraudulent intent is not essential in infringement, unlike unfair competition.
why: IP Code Sec. 155: infringement is the unauthorized use in commerce of a reproduction, counterfeit, copy or colorable imitation of a registered mark or its dominant feature, likely to cause confusion; Sec. 155.2: applying such imitations to labels and packages intended for use in commerce, even without actual sale.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 155

q: Police raided Mel's warehouse and seized thousands of shampoo labels bearing an exact copy of the registered mark "SILKEN," which Mel intended to put on his own shampoo bottles. No shampoo bearing the labels had yet been sold. Mel argues that there is no infringement without actual sale. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Mel is not correct; infringement was committed even without actual sale.
alac.basis: Section 155.2 of the IP Code provides that any person who shall, without the consent of the owner of the registered mark, reproduce, counterfeit, copy or colorably imitate a registered mark or a dominant feature thereof and apply such reproduction to labels, signs, prints, packages, wrappers, receptacles or advertisements intended to be used in commerce upon or in connection with the sale of goods, on which such use is likely to cause confusion, shall be liable for infringement, and the infringement takes place at the moment any of these acts is done, whether or not there is actual sale of goods.
alac.application: Here, Mel reproduced the registered "SILKEN" mark on labels intended to be used on shampoo bottles for sale. That act alone is infringement under Section 155.2, even though no shampoo had yet been sold.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Mel is liable for trademark infringement.

keyPoints: Infringement by reproducing a registered mark on labels for use in commerce (Sec. 155.2)
Committed whether or not there is actual sale
Lack of consent of the registered owner
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 155

q: Under Section 168 of the IP Code, unfair competition consists in:
choices: Using a registered mark with consent
Employing deception or any other means contrary to good faith to pass off one's goods or business as those of another who has established goodwill
hints: The essence is passing off.
Registration of a mark is not required.
why: IP Code Sec. 168: a person who has identified his goods in the public mind has a property right in goodwill, whether or not a registered mark is used; one who passes off his goods as another's by deception or means contrary to good faith commits unfair competition. Unlike infringement, fraudulent intent is essential (Del Monte Corporation v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-78325, January 25, 1990).
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 168; Del Monte Corporation v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-78325, January 25, 1990

q: For years, Nita has sold "Lola's" banana chips in a distinctive yellow bag with a drawing of an old woman, but she never registered any mark. Olie began selling banana chips under "Lolo's" in an almost identical yellow bag with a drawing of an old man, hoping buyers would think they were Nita's. Nita sued for infringement and unfair competition. Which action will prosper?

alac.answer: The action for unfair competition will prosper, but not the action for trademark infringement.
alac.basis: Section 155 of the IP Code requires a registered mark for trademark infringement. Section 168 provides that a person who has identified in the mind of the public the goods he deals in, whether or not a registered mark is employed, has a property right in the goodwill of those goods, and any person who employs deception or other means contrary to good faith to pass off his goods as those of the one having established such goodwill is guilty of unfair competition. In Del Monte Corporation v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-78325, January 25, 1990, the Supreme Court explained that infringement requires a registered mark, while unfair competition requires fraudulent intent to pass off.
alac.application: Here, Nita's mark is unregistered, so infringement will not lie. But Nita established goodwill in "Lola's" banana chips and their distinctive bag, and Olie copied the general appearance of the bag intending buyers to think his chips were Nita's, which is passing off with fraudulent intent.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Nita's action for unfair competition will prosper, while the infringement action will fail.

keyPoints: Infringement requires a registered mark (Sec. 155)
Unfair competition protects goodwill, registered or not (Sec. 168)
Fraudulent intent to pass off (Del Monte v. CA)
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 155 and 168; Del Monte Corporation v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-78325, January 25, 1990

q: Under Section 151 of the IP Code, a petition to cancel a mark registration may be filed at any time if:
choices: The registered mark has become the generic name for the goods, has been abandoned, or was registered fraudulently
hints: The general period is five years from registration.
Some grounds have no time limit.
why: IP Code Sec. 151.1: a petition to cancel may be filed within five years from registration, or at any time if the mark has become generic, has been abandoned, was registered fraudulently or contrary to law, or is used to misrepresent the source of goods.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 151

q: Pat registered the mark "QUICKDRY" for towels in 2015. In 2025, Quin, a competitor, petitioned to cancel the registration, proving that "quickdry" is now commonly used by consumers and the industry to refer to any fast-drying towel. Pat argues that the five-year period to file for cancellation has lapsed. Is the petition timely?

alac.answer: Yes, the petition is timely and may prosper.
alac.basis: Section 151.1 of the IP Code provides that a petition to cancel a mark registration may be filed (a) within five years from the date of registration, or (b) at any time, if the registered mark becomes the generic name for the goods or services for which it is registered, or has been abandoned, or its registration was obtained fraudulently or contrary to the Act.
alac.application: Here, ten years have passed since registration, beyond the general five-year period. But Quin's ground is that "QUICKDRY" has become the generic name for fast-drying towels, a ground for which a petition may be filed at any time.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the petition is timely, and the registration may be cancelled if the mark is proved to have become generic.

keyPoints: Five-year period for cancellation (Sec. 151.1(a))
Any time if the mark becomes generic, abandoned, or fraudulently registered (Sec. 151.1(b))
Genericide
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 151

q: Under Section 175 of the IP Code, which of the following is NOT protected by copyright?
choices: Any official text of a legislative, administrative or legal nature
hints: Works are protected from creation (Sec. 172).
Ideas, news of the day and official texts are unprotected.
why: IP Code Sec. 172: original literary and artistic works are protected from the moment of creation; Sec. 175: no protection extends to ideas, procedures, systems, methods, concepts, principles, discoveries or mere data, news of the day, or official texts of a legislative, administrative or legal nature.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 172 and 175

q: Rico wrote and published a book explaining a new method of bookkeeping, with original forms and illustrations. Sol, after reading it, began using the method in her business and taught it to her staff using her own words and forms. Rico sued Sol for copyright infringement. Will the suit prosper?

alac.answer: No, the suit will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 172 of the IP Code protects original literary and artistic works from the moment of their creation. Section 175 provides that no protection shall extend to any idea, procedure, system, method or operation, concept, principle, discovery or mere data as such, even if they are expressed, explained, illustrated or embodied in a work. In Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc., G.R. No. 148222, August 15, 2003, the Supreme Court held that copyright protects only the expression of a work, not the idea or the useful article described, which may be protected only by a patent.
alac.application: Here, Rico's book, as an expression, is protected. But Sol did not copy his text, forms or illustrations; she used the bookkeeping method itself and taught it in her own words and forms. A method is unprotected by copyright even if explained in a book.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Sol did not infringe Rico's copyright.

keyPoints: Original works protected from creation (Sec. 172)
Ideas, methods and systems unprotected (Sec. 175)
Copyright protects expression, not the idea (Pearl & Dean v. Shoemart)
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 172 and 175; Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc., G.R. No. 148222, August 15, 2003

q: Under Section 178.4 of the IP Code, in the case of a work commissioned and paid for by a person other than the author's employer:
choices: The commissioner owns the work, but the copyright remains with the creator, unless there is a written stipulation to the contrary
The commissioner owns both the work and the copyright
The author owns the work but not the copyright
hints: Owning the object is different from owning the copyright (Sec. 181).
A written stipulation can change the rule.
why: IP Code Sec. 178.1: copyright belongs to the author; Sec. 178.3: employee works follow the regular-duties test; Sec. 178.4: in commissioned works, the commissioner owns the work but the copyright remains with the creator, unless stipulated in writing.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 178

q: Tess, a freelance artist, was commissioned and paid by Uno Corp. to paint a mural for its lobby. Nothing was said about copyright. Uno Corp. later printed the mural's image on its calendars and T-shirts for sale. Tess objects. Who is right?

alac.answer: Tess is right; Uno Corp. owns the mural itself, but the copyright remains with Tess.
alac.basis: Section 178.4 of the IP Code provides that in the case of a work commissioned by a person other than an employer of the author and who pays for it, the person who commissioned the work shall have ownership of the work, but the copyright thereto shall remain with the creator, unless there is a written stipulation to the contrary. Section 181 provides that the copyright is distinct from the property in the material object subject to it.
alac.application: Here, Tess is a freelance artist, not Uno Corp.'s employee, and Uno Corp. commissioned and paid for the mural. Uno Corp. owns the mural as a physical object, but there is no written stipulation transferring the copyright, so it stays with Tess. Reproducing the image on calendars and T-shirts for sale is an exercise of the economic right of reproduction.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Uno Corp. needs Tess's authorization to reproduce the mural, and its unauthorized reproduction infringes her copyright.

keyPoints: Commissioned works: commissioner owns the work, creator keeps the copyright (Sec. 178.4)
Copyright distinct from the material object (Sec. 181)
Reproduction requires the copyright owner's consent
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 178 and 181

q: Under Section 193 of the IP Code, the moral rights of an author include the right to:
choices: Control the price of the work
Require that authorship of the work be attributed to him and to object to any distortion prejudicial to his honor or reputation
hints: Moral rights exist independently of economic rights.
Economic rights are listed in Sec. 177.
why: IP Code Sec. 177: economic rights are the exclusive rights to reproduce, transform, first distribute, rent, publicly display, publicly perform and communicate the work; Sec. 193: moral rights are attribution, alteration before publication or withholding, objection to distortion, and restraint of use of the author's name, independently of economic rights.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 177 and 193

q: Vina sold all the economic rights in her novel to Publisher W. W then released an edition with a new ending, written by another writer, that made the heroine a criminal, and with Vina's name removed from the cover. Vina objects, but W argues that it owns all rights. Who is right?

alac.answer: Vina is right; W violated her moral rights.
alac.basis: Section 193 of the IP Code provides that the author of a work shall, independently of the economic rights in Section 177 or the grant of an assignment or license with respect to such right, have the right to require that the authorship of the work be attributed to him, and to object to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of his work which would be prejudicial to his honor or reputation.
alac.application: Here, Vina assigned only her economic rights, which do not include her moral rights. W removed her name from the cover, violating her right of attribution, and changed the ending in a way that distorts the work and may prejudice her honor or reputation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Vina may assert her moral rights against W, and W's ownership of the economic rights is no defense.

keyPoints: Economic rights (Sec. 177) are distinct from moral rights (Sec. 193)
Moral rights survive assignment of economic rights
Right of attribution and right to object to prejudicial distortion
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 177 and 193

q: Under Section 185 of the IP Code, which factor is considered in determining fair use?
choices: The price of the user's product
The purpose and character of the use, including whether it is commercial or for non-profit educational purposes
hints: There are four factors.
Fair use purposes include criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching and research.
why: IP Code Sec. 185.1: fair use for criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship and research is not infringement; the factors are the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the work, the amount and substantiality of the portion used, and the effect on the potential market for the work (ABS-CBN Corporation v. Gozon, G.R. No. 195956, March 11, 2015).
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 185; ABS-CBN Corporation v. Gozon, G.R. No. 195956, March 11, 2015

q: A law professor photocopied one chapter (about 5%) of a copyrighted textbook for her students' class discussion, free of charge. A review center photocopied the entire textbook and sold the copies to its reviewees. The author sued both. Are their acts fair use?

alac.answer: The professor's use is fair use; the review center's is not.
alac.basis: Section 185.1 of the IP Code provides that the fair use of a copyrighted work for criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching including multiple copies for classroom use, scholarship, research, and similar purposes is not an infringement. The factors include the purpose and character of the use, including whether it is commercial or for non-profit educational purposes; the nature of the work; the amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the work as a whole; and the effect of the use upon the potential market for the work.
alac.application: Here, the professor copied a small portion, one chapter, for classroom use, without charge, for a non-profit educational purpose, with little effect on the book's market. The review center copied the whole book and sold the copies, a commercial use that replaces purchases of the book and harms its market.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the professor's copying is fair use, while the review center is liable for copyright infringement.

keyPoints: Fair use purposes include teaching and classroom copies (Sec. 185.1)
Four factors: purpose, nature, amount, market effect
Commercial copying of the entire work is not fair use
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 185

q: Under Section 184.1 of the IP Code, which act does NOT infringe copyright?
choices: Publishing another's novel under one's own name
Uploading a whole film online for profit
The making of quotations from a published work compatible with fair use and to the extent justified, with the source and author mentioned
hints: Sec. 184 lists statutory limitations.
Mentioning the source is a condition for quotations.
why: IP Code Sec. 184.1 lists acts that are not infringement, such as private and free recitation or performance of a work lawfully made public, quotations compatible with fair use with source and author mentioned, and reproduction by mass media of articles on current topics, among others.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 184

q: At a private family gathering, Xyla's cousins performed a copyrighted song without charge. A church choir also performed the song during a free charity concert for the church. The song's copyright owner demanded royalties from both. Must they pay?

alac.answer: No, neither the family nor the church choir is liable.
alac.basis: Section 184.1(a) of the IP Code provides that the recitation or performance of a work, once it has been lawfully made accessible to the public, if done privately and free of charge or if made strictly for a charitable or religious institution or society, shall not constitute infringement of copyright.
alac.application: Here, the song had been lawfully made public. Xyla's cousins performed it privately at a family gathering, free of charge. The church choir performed it at a free charity concert for the church, which is strictly for a charitable or religious institution.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, both performances fall within the statutory limitation, and no royalties are due.

keyPoints: Statutory limitations on copyright (Sec. 184.1)
Private and free performance
