Performance strictly for a charitable or religious institution
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 184

q: In copyright infringement, according to Habana v. Robles, it is necessary that:
choices: A substantial portion of the work was copied, even if not the whole; intent to pirate is not essential
hints: Copying a substantial part is enough.
Copyright exists from creation; registration is not required.
why: Copyright infringement consists of doing any act within the copyright owner's exclusive rights without consent; in Habana v. Robles, G.R. No. 131522, July 19, 1999, the Supreme Court held that it is enough that a substantial portion was copied, and that animus furandi is not required. Remedies are in Sec. 216.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 177 and 216; Habana v. Robles, G.R. No. 131522, July 19, 1999

q: Yolly wrote a college English textbook. Zeke later published a competing textbook in which many pages, examples and exercises were copied from Yolly's book, with minor changes in wording. Zeke argues that he did not copy the entire book and had no intent to infringe. Is he liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Zeke is liable for copyright infringement.
alac.basis: Section 177.1 of the IP Code gives the copyright owner the exclusive right to carry out, authorize or prevent the reproduction of the work or substantial portion of the work. In Habana v. Robles, G.R. No. 131522, July 19, 1999, the Supreme Court held that infringement exists when a substantial portion of a work is copied, that it is not necessary that the entire work be copied, and that intention to infringe is not an element. Section 216 grants remedies including injunction and damages.
alac.application: Here, Zeke copied many pages, examples and exercises from Yolly's textbook with only minor changes. That is a substantial portion of her work, used in a competing book. Neither the incompleteness of the copying nor his lack of intent excuses him.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Zeke is liable for copyright infringement, and Yolly may obtain an injunction and damages.

keyPoints: Exclusive right of reproduction, including substantial portions (Sec. 177.1)
Copying a substantial portion suffices; intent not required (Habana v. Robles)
Remedies: injunction and damages (Sec. 216)
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 177 and 216; Habana v. Robles, G.R. No. 131522, July 19, 1999

q: Under Section 180.2 of the IP Code, copyright is not deemed assigned inter vivos, in whole or in part, unless:
choices: There is a written indication of such intention
hints: Transfer of the copy is not transfer of the copyright (Sec. 181).
Submission to a periodical is only a license for a single publication (Sec. 180.3).
why: IP Code Sec. 180.1: copyright may be assigned in whole or in part; Sec. 180.2: no inter vivos assignment without a written indication of such intention; Sec. 180.3: submission to a periodical is only a license for a single publication; co-owners cannot license without the others' prior written consent.
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Secs. 180 and 181

q: Ana submitted a short story to a magazine, which published it. A year later, without asking Ana, the magazine's sister company republished the story in an anthology for sale. Separately, Ben, a co-owner of a song's copyright with Carlo, licensed a TV network to use the song without Carlo's written consent. Are these acts valid?

alac.answer: No; the anthology republication and Ben's license are both unauthorized.
alac.basis: Section 180.3 of the IP Code provides that the submission of a literary, photographic or artistic work to a newspaper, magazine or periodical for publication shall constitute only a license to make a single publication unless a greater right is expressly granted, and that if two or more persons jointly own a copyright, neither of the owners shall be entitled to grant licenses without the prior written consent of the other owner or owners. Section 180.2 provides that copyright is not deemed assigned unless there is a written indication of such intention.
alac.application: Here, Ana's submission gave the magazine only a license for a single publication, which it used. Republication in an anthology, by the magazine's sister company, was not authorized. Ben, a co-owner, licensed the song without Carlo's prior written consent.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the anthology infringes Ana's copyright, and Ben's license is invalid without Carlo's written consent.

keyPoints: Submission to a periodical: license for a single publication only (Sec. 180.3)
Co-owners cannot license without the others' prior written consent
No assignment without a written indication (Sec. 180.2)
cite: Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293, as amended), Sec. 180

q: Under the Howey test, as applied in Securities and Exchange Commission v. Prosperity.Com, Inc., an investment contract exists when there is:
choices: A partnership with equal management by all
An investment of money in a common enterprise with expectation of profits primarily from the efforts of others
hints: Investment contracts are securities (SRC Sec. 3.1(b)).
The key is profits from the efforts of others.
why: SRC Sec. 3.1 defines securities to include investment contracts. Under the Howey test, an investment contract requires (1) an investment of money, (2) in a common enterprise, (3) with expectation of profits, (4) arising primarily from the efforts of others (SEC v. Prosperity.Com, Inc., G.R. No. 164197, January 25, 2012).
cite: Securities Regulation Code (RA 8799), Sec. 3; Securities and Exchange Commission v. Prosperity.Com, Inc., G.R. No. 164197, January 25, 2012

q: Agri Corp. invited the public to "buy" a share in a mango farm for P50,000 each. Investors would do nothing; Agri Corp. would plant, manage and sell the harvest, and pay investors 30% returns a year. Agri Corp. did not register anything with the SEC, arguing that it sells farm shares, not securities. Is it correct?

alac.answer: No, Agri Corp. is selling securities in the form of investment contracts, which must be registered.
alac.basis: Section 3.1(b) of the Securities Regulation Code includes investment contracts among securities. In Securities and Exchange Commission v. Prosperity.Com, Inc., G.R. No. 164197, January 25, 2012, the Supreme Court applied the Howey test: an investment contract exists where there is an investment of money in a common enterprise with an expectation of profits primarily from the efforts of others. Section 8.1 provides that securities shall not be sold or offered for sale to the public without a registration statement duly filed with and approved by the SEC.
alac.application: Here, investors pay money into a common farm venture, expect 30% annual returns, and rely entirely on Agri Corp.'s efforts to plant, manage and sell the harvest. All the elements of the Howey test are present, whatever the scheme is called.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Agri Corp. is offering investment contracts, which are securities requiring SEC registration before being offered to the public.

keyPoints: Investment contracts are securities (SRC Sec. 3.1(b))
Howey test elements (SEC v. Prosperity.Com)
Registration required before public offering (Sec. 8.1)
cite: Securities Regulation Code (RA 8799), Secs. 3 and 8; Securities and Exchange Commission v. Prosperity.Com, Inc., G.R. No. 164197, January 25, 2012

q: Which of the following is included in the definition of securities under Section 3.1 of the Securities Regulation Code?
choices: Proprietary or non-proprietary membership certificates in corporations
hints: Sec. 3.1 lists the classes.
Golf club shares are a common example.
why: SRC Sec. 3.1: securities are shares, participation or interests in a corporation or profit-making venture evidenced by a certificate or contract; they include shares, bonds, notes, investment contracts, fractional interests in mineral rights, derivatives, certificates of assignment or participation, membership certificates, and others the SEC may determine.

q: Bia, a promoter, sold to the public "fractional undivided interests" in an oil exploration venture, as well as stock options in a mining company. She argues that only shares of stock are securities, so she needs no SEC registration. Is she correct?

alac.answer: No, Bia is not correct; both are securities.
alac.basis: Section 3.1 of the Securities Regulation Code defines securities as shares, participation or interests in a corporation or in a commercial enterprise or profit-making venture, evidenced by a certificate, contract, or instrument, whether written or electronic, and expressly includes fractional undivided interests in oil, gas or other mineral rights, and derivatives like options and warrants.
alac.application: Here, the fractional undivided interests in the oil exploration venture and the stock options in the mining company are both expressly listed in Section 3.1. The definition is not limited to shares of stock.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, both are securities, and Bia must register them before offering them to the public, unless an exemption applies.

keyPoints: Broad definition of securities (Sec. 3.1)
Fractional interests in mineral rights included
Derivatives like options and warrants included

q: Under Section 9 of the Securities Regulation Code, which of the following is an exempt security that need not be registered?
choices: Bonds of a private company sold to the public
Shares of a new private corporation sold to the public
Any security issued or guaranteed by the Government of the Philippines or its political subdivisions or agencies
hints: Exempt securities (Sec. 9) differ from exempt transactions (Sec. 10).
Government securities are exempt.
why: SRC Sec. 9.1 exempts certain classes of securities from registration, such as government securities, certain foreign government securities on reciprocity, and receiver's certificates; Sec. 10.1 exempts certain transactions, such as judicial sales, isolated transactions, and sales to fewer than 20 persons in 12 months.

q: Cita, the owner of 1,000 shares in a corporation, sold them in a single private deal to her friend Dan, not as part of any business of selling securities. Separately, a sheriff sold shares of a judgment debtor at a public auction. Neither sale was registered with the SEC. Were registrations required?

alac.answer: No, both are exempt transactions, so no registration was required.
alac.basis: Section 8.1 of the Securities Regulation Code generally requires registration before securities are sold to the public. Section 10.1 provides that the registration requirement shall not apply to the sale of any security (a) at any judicial sale, and (c) in an isolated transaction in which any security is sold by the owner, or by his representative for the owner's account, not made in the course of repeated and successive transactions of a like character.
alac.application: Here, Cita's single private sale of her own shares to Dan is an isolated transaction by the owner, not part of a business of selling securities. The sheriff's auction of a judgment debtor's shares is a judicial sale.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, neither sale required registration with the SEC.

keyPoints: Registration requirement (Sec. 8.1)
Exempt transaction: judicial sale (Sec. 10.1(a))
Exempt transaction: isolated transaction by the owner (Sec. 10.1(c))

q: Under Section 4(p) of the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act (FRIA), a debtor is insolvent when it:
choices: Is generally unable to pay its liabilities as they fall due in the ordinary course of business or has liabilities greater than its assets
hints: There are two alternative tests.
FRIA policy: timely, fair, transparent, effective and efficient rehabilitation or liquidation (Sec. 2).
why: FRIA Sec. 4(p): insolvent refers to the financial condition of a debtor that is generally unable to pay its liabilities as they fall due in the ordinary course of business or has liabilities greater than its assets; Sec. 2 sets the policy of timely, fair and efficient rehabilitation or liquidation.
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Secs. 2 and 4

q: Eco Corp. has assets worth P500 million and liabilities of P300 million, but most of its assets are idle land, and for six months it has been unable to pay its suppliers and bank loans as they fall due. It filed a petition for rehabilitation. A creditor argues that Eco Corp. is not insolvent because its assets exceed its liabilities. Is the creditor correct?

alac.answer: No, the creditor is not correct; Eco Corp. is insolvent under FRIA.
alac.basis: Section 4(p) of the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 defines insolvent as the financial condition of a debtor that is generally unable to pay its liabilities as they fall due in the ordinary course of business or has liabilities that are greater than its assets. The two tests are alternative. Section 2 declares the policy of encouraging debtors and creditors to collectively and realistically resolve competing claims through timely rehabilitation or liquidation.
alac.application: Here, although Eco Corp.'s assets exceed its liabilities, it has been generally unable to pay its suppliers and bank loans as they fall due for six months. That satisfies the first test, liquidity insolvency, even if the balance-sheet test is not met.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Eco Corp. is insolvent and may file for rehabilitation under FRIA.

keyPoints: Two alternative tests of insolvency (Sec. 4(p))
Inability to pay debts as they fall due suffices
Policy of collective resolution (Sec. 2)
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Secs. 2 and 4

q: Under Section 16 of FRIA, rehabilitation proceedings commence upon:
choices: The approval of the Rehabilitation Plan
The issuance of the Commencement Order
hints: The court issues an order.
Its effects include a stay of enforcement of claims.
why: FRIA Sec. 16: rehabilitation proceedings commence upon the issuance of the Commencement Order, which includes a Stay or Suspension Order; Sec. 17: it renders void extrajudicial seizure or sale of the debtor's property, among other effects.
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Secs. 16 and 17

q: After the rehabilitation court issued a Commencement Order with a stay order for Fab Corp., Bank G, a mortgagee, proceeded with the extrajudicial foreclosure of Fab Corp.'s factory and bought it at the auction. Is the foreclosure valid?

alac.answer: No, the foreclosure is void.
alac.basis: Section 16 of the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 provides that rehabilitation proceedings commence upon the issuance of the Commencement Order, which includes a Stay or Suspension Order. Section 17(b) provides that the Commencement Order shall prohibit or otherwise serve as the legal basis rendering null and void the results of any extrajudicial activity or process to seize property, sell encumbered property, or otherwise attempt to collect or enforce a claim against the debtor after the commencement date.
alac.application: Here, Bank G foreclosed extrajudicially and sold Fab Corp.'s encumbered factory after the Commencement Order and stay order were issued. That is exactly the kind of extrajudicial enforcement that the order prohibits and renders void.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the foreclosure sale is null and void; Bank G must instead pursue its claim as a secured creditor in the rehabilitation proceedings.

keyPoints: Proceedings commence upon the Commencement Order (Sec. 16)
Stay of enforcement of claims
Extrajudicial seizure or sale after commencement is void (Sec. 17(b))
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Secs. 16 and 17

q: Under Section 31 of FRIA, the rehabilitation receiver is:
choices: An agent of the creditors only
An officer of the court, with the principal duty of preserving and maximizing the value of the debtor's assets
hints: The receiver works for the court.
The receiver also prepares and recommends the Rehabilitation Plan.
why: FRIA Sec. 31: the rehabilitation receiver is an officer of the court whose principal duty is to preserve and maximize the value of the debtor's assets, determine viability, prepare and recommend the Rehabilitation Plan, and implement it; Sec. 62 sets the minimum contents of the Plan.
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Secs. 31 and 62

q: In the rehabilitation of Hub Corp., the rehabilitation receiver prepared a plan. A creditor objected that the plan does not compare what creditors will receive under the plan with what they would receive in immediate liquidation. Is the objection meritorious?

alac.answer: Yes, the objection is meritorious; the plan lacks a required content.
alac.basis: Section 31 of the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 provides that the rehabilitation receiver is an officer of the court with the duty of preserving and maximizing the value of the debtor's assets, determining viability, and preparing and recommending a Rehabilitation Plan. Section 62 provides that the Rehabilitation Plan shall, as a minimum, compare the amounts expected to be received by the creditors under the Plan with those they will receive if liquidation ensues within the next 120 days, and contain information sufficient to give creditors a reasonable basis for deciding whether supporting the Plan is in their financial interest.
alac.application: Here, Hub Corp.'s plan omits the comparison with immediate liquidation. Without it, creditors cannot fairly decide whether supporting the plan serves their interest, and the court cannot assess whether it should be confirmed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the objection is meritorious, and the receiver should revise the plan to include the required comparison.

keyPoints: Rehabilitation receiver as officer of the court (Sec. 31)
Minimum contents of the Rehabilitation Plan (Sec. 62)
Comparison with liquidation within 120 days
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Secs. 31 and 62

q: Under Section 64 of FRIA, the court may confirm a rehabilitation plan despite its rejection by a class of creditors (cram down) if, among other conditions:
choices: The objecting creditors receive less than in liquidation
The debtor's owners keep full control
The shareholders, owners or partners of the debtor lose at least their controlling interest as a result of the plan
hints: All four conditions must be present.
Objecting creditors must get more than in liquidation.
why: FRIA Sec. 64: a plan is approved by a class if members holding more than 50% of the class's claims vote for it; notwithstanding rejection, the court may confirm it if it complies with the Act, the receiver recommends it, the owners lose at least their controlling interest, and the objecting class would likely receive more than in liquidation.
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Sec. 64

q: In Ion Corp.'s rehabilitation, the secured creditors' class rejected the plan, while the other classes approved it. The receiver recommends confirmation. Under the plan, Ion Corp.'s owners will lose their controlling interest to creditors, and the secured creditors will likely receive more than in a liquidation. May the court confirm the plan?

alac.answer: Yes, the court may confirm the plan under the cram-down provision.
alac.basis: Section 64 of the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 provides that the plan shall be deemed rejected unless approved by all classes of creditors whose rights are adversely affected. However, notwithstanding the rejection, the court may confirm the plan if all of the following are present: (a) the plan complies with the Act; (b) the rehabilitation receiver recommends its confirmation; (c) the shareholders, owners or partners of the debtor lose at least their controlling interest as a result of the plan; and (d) the plan would likely provide the objecting class with compensation having a net present value greater than what it would receive in liquidation. Section 69 makes the confirmed plan binding on all creditors.
alac.application: Here, the secured class rejected the plan, but the receiver recommends it, the owners will lose their controlling interest, and the secured creditors will likely receive more than in liquidation. Assuming the plan complies with the Act, all the conditions for cram down are present.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court may confirm the plan, and it will bind the secured creditors despite their rejection.

keyPoints: Approval by all adversely affected classes, majority of claims per class (Sec. 64)
Cram-down conditions: compliance, receiver's recommendation, loss of control by owners, better than liquidation
Confirmed plan binds all creditors (Sec. 69)
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Secs. 64 and 69

q: Under Section 113 of FRIA, upon the issuance of the Liquidation Order:
choices: The debtor continues business as usual
The juridical debtor is deemed dissolved and its corporate existence terminated
hints: Liquidation ends the juridical debtor.
Assets vest in the liquidator.
why: FRIA Sec. 113: upon the Liquidation Order, the juridical debtor is deemed dissolved; title to its assets vests in the liquidator; its contracts are deemed terminated unless the liquidator declares otherwise; and no separate action for an unsecured claim is allowed. Sec. 90: an insolvent debtor may petition for voluntary liquidation.
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Secs. 90 and 113

q: After the court issued a Liquidation Order against Jet Corp., an unsecured creditor filed a separate collection suit against Jet Corp. in another court. Another unsecured creditor's collection case against Jet Corp. was already pending before the order. What happens to the two cases?

alac.answer: The new suit is not allowed, and the pending case will be transferred to the liquidator.
alac.basis: Section 113(d) of the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 provides that upon the issuance of the Liquidation Order, no separate action for the collection of an unsecured claim shall be allowed, and such actions already pending will be transferred to the liquidator for him to accept and settle or contest. Section 113(a) and (b) provides that the juridical debtor is deemed dissolved and legal title to its assets vests in the liquidator.
alac.application: Here, the first creditor filed a separate collection suit after the Liquidation Order, which the law prohibits. The second creditor's case was already pending, so it will be transferred to the liquidator, who may accept and settle or contest the claim.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the new suit should be dismissed, and the pending case should be transferred to the liquidator; both creditors must pursue their claims in the liquidation proceedings.

keyPoints: Debtor dissolved and assets vest in the liquidator (Sec. 113(a)-(b))
No separate action for unsecured claims after the order (Sec. 113(d))
Pending actions transferred to the liquidator
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Sec. 113

q: Under Section 94 of FRIA, a petition for suspension of payments may be filed by:
choices: A corporation with liabilities greater than its assets
An individual debtor who has sufficient property to cover all his debts but foresees the impossibility of meeting them when they fall due
hints: Suspension of payments is for individuals.
The debtor is solvent but illiquid.
why: FRIA Sec. 94: an individual debtor possessing sufficient property to cover all his debts, but foreseeing the impossibility of meeting them when they fall due, may petition to be declared in a state of suspension of payments, attaching a schedule of debts, an inventory of assets and a proposed agreement with creditors.
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Sec. 94

q: Kiko, a sole proprietor, owns properties worth P30 million and owes P20 million. Because his properties are not easily sold, he foresees that he cannot pay his loans when they fall due next month. Separately, Lux Corp., a corporation in a similar situation, wants to file a petition for suspension of payments. What remedies are available to each?

alac.answer: Kiko may file a petition for suspension of payments; Lux Corp. may not, but it may seek rehabilitation.
alac.basis: Section 94 of the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 provides that an individual debtor who, possessing sufficient property to cover all his debts but foreseeing the impossibility of meeting them when they respectively fall due, may file a verified petition to be declared in a state of suspension of payments, attaching a schedule of debts and liabilities, an inventory of assets, and a proposed agreement with his creditors. Juridical debtors in financial distress use the rehabilitation proceedings under the Act instead.
alac.application: Here, Kiko, an individual, has P30 million in property against P20 million in debts, but foresees that he cannot pay his debts on time. He fits the remedy of suspension of payments. Lux Corp. is a juridical person, for which the Act provides rehabilitation, not suspension of payments.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Kiko may petition for suspension of payments with the required attachments, while Lux Corp. should file for rehabilitation.

keyPoints: Suspension of payments is for individual debtors (Sec. 94)
Sufficient property but foreseeable inability to pay on time
Juridical debtors use rehabilitation
cite: Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act of 2010 (RA 10142), Sec. 94

q: Under Section 8 of the Electronic Commerce Act, an electronic signature is equivalent to the signature of a person on a written document if:
choices: It is proved that a prescribed procedure, not alterable by the parties, existed to identify the party and indicate his approval, and the method is reliable
It is typed in capital letters
hints: Reliability and identification are key.
Electronic documents have the same legal effect as paper (Sec. 7).
why: E-Commerce Act Sec. 6: information is not denied legal effect solely because it is in a data message; Sec. 7: electronic documents have the same legal effect as written documents; Sec. 8: an electronic signature is equivalent to a handwritten one if a reliable prescribed procedure identifies the signer and indicates his approval.

q: Mila and Nato agreed by email to the sale of Nato's car for P800,000. Nato's email ended with his name and the phrase "I agree to sell." Mila paid, but Nato refused to deliver, arguing that there is no valid written contract with a signature. Is the contract unenforceable for lack of a written document?

alac.answer: No, the electronic document satisfies the writing requirement, and the contract may be enforced.
alac.basis: Section 7 of the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000 provides that electronic documents shall have the legal effect, validity or enforceability as any other document or legal writing, and where the law requires a document to be in writing, that requirement is met by an electronic document that maintains its integrity and reliability and can be authenticated. Section 8 provides that an electronic signature is equivalent to a handwritten signature if a reliable method identifies the party and indicates his approval. Section 6 provides that information shall not be denied legal effect solely because it is in a data message.
alac.application: Here, the email exchange is an electronic document recording the sale of the car for P800,000. Nato's typed name with "I agree to sell," sent from his email account, can identify him and show his approval, subject to proof of authenticity and reliability. Mila has also paid, so the contract has been partly performed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Nato cannot avoid the contract merely because it was made by email; Mila may enforce it.

keyPoints: Legal recognition of data messages and electronic documents (Secs. 6-7)
Writing requirement met by reliable electronic documents
Electronic signature equivalent to handwritten if reliable (Sec. 8)

q: Under Section 32 of the Electronic Commerce Act, a person who obtained access to an electronic document pursuant to powers conferred by the Act:
choices: Shall not convey to or share it with any other person, except for purposes authorized under the Act
hints: There is a duty of confidentiality.
Lawful access is limited to those with a legal right (Sec. 31).
why: E-Commerce Act Sec. 31: access to an electronic file or key is authorized only in favor of those with a legal right to it; Sec. 32: persons who obtained access under the Act shall not share it with others except for authorized purposes.
cite: Electronic Commerce Act of 2000 (RA 8792), Secs. 31 and 32

q: Oli, an IT contractor hired by a bank to audit its system, was given access to the bank's encrypted customer files and electronic keys. After the audit, he gave copies of the files and a key to a marketing company. Has Oli violated the Electronic Commerce Act?

alac.answer: Yes, Oli violated the rules on lawful access and confidentiality.
alac.basis: Section 31 of the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000 provides that access to an electronic file or electronic key shall only be authorized in favor of the individual or entity having a legal right to it or solely for authorized purposes, and that the electronic key shall not be made available to any person without the consent of the person in lawful possession of it. Section 32 provides that any person who obtained access to any electronic key or electronic document pursuant to powers conferred under the Act shall not convey to or share the same with any other person.
alac.application: Here, Oli was given access only for the authorized purpose of auditing the bank's system. Giving the customer files and an electronic key to a marketing company was outside that purpose and without the bank's consent.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Oli violated Sections 31 and 32 and may be penalized, without prejudice to liability under data privacy and bank secrecy laws.

keyPoints: Lawful access only for those with legal right or authorized purposes (Sec. 31)
Electronic keys not to be given without consent
Obligation of confidentiality (Sec. 32)
cite: Electronic Commerce Act of 2000 (RA 8792), Secs. 31 and 32

q: Under the Internet Transactions Act (RA 11967), an online merchant is a person:
choices: Who buys goods online for personal use
Selling non-financial goods or services to online consumers through an e-marketplace or third-party digital platforms
hints: Online consumers buy; online merchants sell.
Consumer-to-consumer transactions are not covered.
why: Internet Transactions Act Sec. 4: an online consumer purchases, leases or subscribes to goods or services over the internet for a fee; an online merchant sells non-financial goods or services through an e-marketplace or third-party digital platforms. Digital platforms may be subsidiarily or solidarily liable in certain cases.
cite: Internet Transactions Act of 2023 (RA 11967), Secs. 3 and 4

q: Pia bought a phone through an online marketplace app from a merchant who turned out to be using a fake identity; the phone was never delivered. The marketplace had not verified the merchant's identity as required by law. Can Pia hold the marketplace liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the marketplace may be held subsidiarily liable to Pia.
alac.basis: The Internet Transactions Act of 2023 defines an online consumer as a person who purchases goods or services over the internet for a fee, and an online merchant as a person selling non-financial goods or services through an e-marketplace or third-party digital platforms. It provides that the e-marketplace or digital platform that facilitated the transaction shall be subsidiarily liable to the online consumer if, among others, it failed to exercise ordinary diligence in complying with its obligations, such as verifying the identity of online merchants, resulting in loss or damage to the consumer.
alac.application: Here, Pia is an online consumer, and the merchant used the marketplace to sell her a phone. The marketplace failed to verify the merchant's identity, a failure of ordinary diligence that allowed the fraud and caused Pia's loss.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Pia may hold the marketplace subsidiarily liable for her loss if she cannot recover from the merchant.

keyPoints: Online consumer and online merchant defined (Sec. 4)
Subsidiary liability of e-marketplaces and digital platforms
Failure of ordinary diligence in complying with obligations
cite: Internet Transactions Act of 2023 (RA 11967), Secs. 4 and 26

q: Under Section 3 of the Internet Transactions Act, the law applies to internet transactions where one of the parties is situated in the Philippines, or where the digital platform, e-retailer or online merchant:
choices: Is availing of the Philippine market and has minimum contacts therein
Has its head office in the Philippines only
hints: The law reaches foreign platforms.
C2C transactions and online media content are excluded.
why: Internet Transactions Act Sec. 3: it covers B2B and B2C internet transactions within DTI's mandate where one party is in the Philippines or the platform, e-retailer or merchant avails of the Philippine market and has minimum contacts there; online media content and C2C transactions are excluded.

q: Q-Shop, an e-retailer incorporated and based in Singapore, has no office in the Philippines but targets Filipino buyers with ads in Filipino, accepts pesos, and ships to Philippine addresses. A Filipino buyer filed a DTI complaint over defective goods. Q-Shop argues that Philippine law does not apply to it. Also, a Filipino who sold a used bag to another individual online is the subject of a separate complaint under the same law. Rule on both.

alac.answer: The Internet Transactions Act applies to Q-Shop, but not to the individual's sale of a used bag.
alac.basis: Section 3 of the Internet Transactions Act of 2023 provides that it shall apply to all business-to-business and business-to-consumer internet transactions within the mandate of the DTI, where one of the parties is situated in the Philippines or where the digital platform, e-retailer, or online merchant is availing of the Philippine market and has minimum contacts therein, but that online media content and consumer-to-consumer (C2C) transactions shall not be covered.
alac.application: Here, Q-Shop is an e-retailer selling to a Filipino buyer situated in the Philippines, and it deliberately avails of the Philippine market by advertising in Filipino, accepting pesos and shipping locally, which are minimum contacts. The sale of a used bag between two individuals is a consumer-to-consumer transaction.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Q-Shop is covered by the law despite being based abroad, while the C2C sale of the used bag is outside its coverage.

keyPoints: Coverage of B2B and B2C internet transactions (Sec. 3)
Foreign platforms availing of the Philippine market with minimum contacts are covered
C2C transactions excluded

q: Under Section 14(a) of the Philippine Competition Act, which agreement between competitors is per se prohibited?
choices: A supply contract with a customer
A joint research project that improves production
Fixing prices at an auction or bid rigging
A merger reviewed by the PCC
hints: Per se: no need to prove anti-competitive effect.
Sec. 14(b) agreements require proof of object or effect.
why: PCA Sec. 14(a): agreements between competitors restricting competition as to price or terms of trade, and bid manipulation, are per se prohibited; Sec. 14(b): agreements limiting production or dividing markets are prohibited if they have the object or effect of substantially lessening competition.

q: Three cement companies agreed to take turns submitting the lowest bid in government infrastructure projects, with the others submitting higher "cover" bids. Separately, two bakeries agreed that one would sell only in Quezon City and the other only in Manila. The companies argue that the PCC must first prove harm to competition in both cases. Are they correct?

alac.answer: They are correct only as to the bakeries; the bid rotation is per se prohibited.
alac.basis: Section 14(a) of the Philippine Competition Act provides that agreements between competitors fixing price at an auction or in any form of bidding, including cover bidding, bid suppression and bid rotation, are per se prohibited. Section 14(b) provides that agreements between competitors dividing or sharing the market by territory or other means are prohibited if they have the object or effect of substantially preventing, restricting or lessening competition.
alac.application: Here, the cement companies' bid rotation and cover bidding are per se prohibited, so the PCC need not prove any effect on competition. The bakeries' territorial division falls under Section 14(b), so the PCC must show that it has the object or effect of substantially lessening competition.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the cement companies are liable without proof of harm, while the bakeries' agreement is prohibited only upon such proof.

keyPoints: Per se prohibited agreements: price fixing and bid manipulation (Sec. 14(a))
Market division: prohibited if it substantially lessens competition (Sec. 14(b))
Burden differs

q: Under Section 14(c) of the Philippine Competition Act, agreements not covered by Sec. 14(a) and (b) that substantially lessen competition are prohibited, except those that:
choices: Contribute to improving production or distribution or promoting technical or economic progress, while allowing consumers a fair share of the resulting benefits
hints: This is an efficiency defense.
Consumers must share in the benefits.
why: PCA Sec. 14(c): other agreements with the object or effect of substantially lessening competition are prohibited, but those contributing to improving production or distribution or promoting technical or economic progress, while allowing consumers a fair share of the benefits, may not necessarily be deemed prohibited.

q: Two small rice millers agreed to share a single modern drying facility and delivery trucks. This cut their costs, and both lowered rice prices for consumers. The PCC questions the agreement as anti-competitive. How should the PCC determine whether it is prohibited?

alac.answer: The PCC should evaluate the agreement under Section 14(c), considering its object and effect and its efficiency benefits to consumers; it is likely not prohibited.
alac.basis: Section 14(c) of the Philippine Competition Act provides that agreements other than those under Section 14(a) and (b) which have the object or effect of substantially preventing, restricting or lessening competition shall be prohibited, provided that those which contribute to improving the production or distribution of goods or services or to promoting technical or economic progress, while allowing consumers a fair share of the resulting benefits, may not necessarily be deemed a violation.
alac.application: Here, the agreement is not price fixing, bid rigging, output limitation or market division, so it is not per se prohibited and falls under Section 14(c). The shared facility and trucks improve production and distribution, and consumers receive a fair share of the benefits through lower rice prices. There is no showing that competition is substantially lessened.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the agreement is likely not a prohibited anti-competitive agreement.

keyPoints: Other agreements judged by object or effect (Sec. 14(c))
Efficiency defense: improved production or distribution
Consumers must share in the benefits

q: Under Section 15 of the Philippine Competition Act, which of the following is an abuse of dominant position?
choices: Lowering prices in good faith to meet a competitor's price
Having a large market share because of a superior product
Selling goods below cost with the object of driving competition out of the relevant market
hints: Dominance itself is not prohibited; abuse is.
Good-faith price matching is allowed.
why: PCA Sec. 15: one or more entities may not abuse their dominant position through conduct that substantially lessens competition, such as predatory pricing, imposing barriers to entry, tying, and price discrimination; dominance from a superior product or business acumen is not prohibited.

q: Rex Telco, which dominates the market for internet services in a province, sells its plans below cost for a year after a new competitor entered, publicly stating that it will "drive the newcomer out." It also requires customers who buy its internet plans to also buy its cable TV service. Has Rex Telco committed abuse of dominant position?

alac.answer: Yes, Rex Telco abused its dominant position.
alac.basis: Section 15 of the Philippine Competition Act prohibits entities from abusing their dominant position by engaging in conduct that would substantially prevent, restrict or lessen competition, including (a) selling goods or services below cost with the object of driving competition out of the relevant market, and (c) making a transaction subject to acceptance by the other parties of other obligations which, by their nature or according to commercial usage, have no connection with the transaction.
alac.application: Here, Rex Telco is dominant in the provincial market. It sold below cost with the stated object of driving out the new competitor, which is predatory pricing, not good-faith price matching. Requiring internet customers to also buy cable TV makes the transaction subject to an unconnected obligation, which is tying.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rex Telco committed abuse of dominant position on both counts and may be penalized by the PCC.

keyPoints: Abuse of dominant position prohibited (Sec. 15)
Predatory pricing with the object of driving out competition
Tying unconnected obligations

q: Under Section 24 of the Philippine Competition Act, the relevant market is determined by considering, among others:
choices: The possibilities of substituting the goods or services in question with others of domestic or foreign origin
hints: Relevant market has product and geographic dimensions.
Substitutability is the key.
why: PCA Sec. 24: in determining the relevant market, factors affecting substitutability and the geographic area are considered, such as the possibility of substitution, costs of distribution, the cost and probability of consumers seeking other markets, and restrictions on access to alternative sources.

q: Sun Ferry is the only ferry operator between two islands, but travelers may also take a daily plane at a similar price and travel time. In a PCC case, Sun Ferry argues that the relevant market is "transport between the two islands," not "ferry services." How should the relevant market be determined?

alac.answer: The relevant market should be determined by substitutability; if air travel is a reasonable substitute, the market is transport between the islands, not ferry services alone.
alac.basis: Section 24 of the Philippine Competition Act provides that, in determining the relevant market, the factors affecting the substitutability among goods or services and the geographic area shall be considered, including the possibilities of substituting the goods or services in question with others, the extent to which substitutes are available to consumers and the time required for substitution, and the cost and probability of users seeking other markets.
alac.application: Here, travelers can take a daily plane at a similar price and travel time, which suggests that air travel is a reasonable substitute for the ferry from the consumers' point of view. If so, Sun Ferry competes with the airline, and the relevant market is transport between the two islands.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the PCC should define the market by examining substitutability, and if air travel is a substitute, Sun Ferry's market share should be measured in the wider transport market.

keyPoints: Relevant market determined by substitutability (Sec. 24)
Availability of substitutes, price and time
Product and geographic dimensions

q: Under Section 27 of the Philippine Competition Act, there is a rebuttable presumption of market dominant position if an entity's market share in the relevant market is at least:
choices: 50%, unless the PCC sets a new threshold for the sector
hints: The presumption can be rebutted.
Other factors matter, such as barriers to entry.
why: PCA Sec. 27: the PCC considers market share, ability to fix prices or restrict supply, barriers to entry, competitors, access to inputs, customers' power to switch, and recent conduct; a market share of at least 50% creates a rebuttable presumption of dominance.

q: Tala Corp. has a 55% share of the relevant market for instant noodles. It proves that new brands easily enter the market, that two strong competitors hold 40% combined, that retailers and consumers switch brands freely, and that it cannot raise prices without losing sales. Is Tala Corp. in a market dominant position?

alac.answer: No, Tala Corp. has rebutted the presumption of dominance.
alac.basis: Section 27 of the Philippine Competition Act provides that, in determining whether an entity has a market dominant position, the PCC shall consider its market share and whether it can fix prices unilaterally or restrict supply, the existence of barriers to entry, the existence and power of competitors, access to inputs, the power of customers to switch, and its recent conduct. There is a rebuttable presumption of market dominant position if its market share is at least fifty percent.
alac.application: Here, Tala Corp.'s 55% share raises the presumption of dominance. But it showed low barriers to entry, strong competitors, customers who switch freely, and its inability to raise prices without losing sales. These factors show that it cannot act independently of competitors and consumers.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the presumption is rebutted, and Tala Corp. is not in a market dominant position.

keyPoints: Factors in determining dominance (Sec. 27)
Rebuttable presumption at 50% market share
Rebuttal: low barriers, strong rivals, switching customers, no pricing power

q: Under the Public Service Act, as amended by RA 11659, which of the following is a public utility subject to the constitutional 60-40 nationality requirement?
hints: RA 11659 limited the list of public utilities.
Telecommunications, airlines and shipping are public services but not public utilities.
why: CA 146 Sec. 13(d), as amended by RA 11659: public utility refers to a public service that operates, manages or controls for public use the distribution and transmission of electricity, petroleum pipeline transmission, water and wastewater pipeline systems, seaports, and public utility vehicles. Other public services are not public utilities.
cite: Public Service Act (CA 146, as amended by RA 11659), Sec. 13

q: A company 70% owned by foreigners wants to operate (a) an inter-island airline and (b) a water pipeline distribution system in a city. It asks whether the 40% constitutional limit on foreign ownership of public utilities applies to each. Advise it.

alac.answer: The 40% limit does not apply to the airline, but it applies to the water pipeline distribution system.
alac.basis: Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution limits foreign ownership of public utilities to 40%. Section 13(d) of the Public Service Act, as amended by RA 11659, defines public utility as a public service that operates, manages or controls for public use only the following: distribution of electricity, transmission of electricity, petroleum pipeline transmission systems, water pipeline distribution systems and wastewater pipeline systems, seaports, and public utility vehicles. No other person shall be deemed a public utility unless provided by law.
alac.application: Here, an airline is a public service but is not in the list of public utilities, so the 40% limit does not apply to it (subject to other laws and the rules on critical infrastructure). A water pipeline distribution system is expressly a public utility.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the company may own 70% of the airline business, but its ownership of the water pipeline utility must comply with the 60-40 requirement.

keyPoints: Constitutional 60-40 rule applies only to public utilities
Exclusive list of public utilities (Sec. 13(d), as amended)
Airlines are public services, not public utilities
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 11; Public Service Act (CA 146, as amended by RA 11659), Sec. 13

q: Under RA 11659, critical infrastructure refers to any public service which owns, uses or operates systems and assets so vital that their incapacity or destruction would have a detrimental impact on:
choices: National security, including telecommunications and other vital services declared by the President
hints: Critical infrastructure is about national security.
Telecommunications is expressly mentioned.
why: RA 11659 Sec. 2(e): critical infrastructure refers to any public service with systems and assets so vital that their incapacity or destruction would have a detrimental impact on national security, including telecommunications and other vital services declared by the President; special rules apply to foreign investment in it.
cite: Public Service Act (CA 146, as amended by RA 11659), Sec. 2(e)

q: Following RA 11659, a foreign-owned company wishes to acquire 100% of a Philippine telecommunications company. A legislator argues that telecommunications is no longer regulated at all for foreign investors because it is no longer a public utility. Is the legislator correct?

alac.answer: No; although telecommunications is no longer a public utility, it is critical infrastructure subject to national security safeguards.
alac.basis: Section 2(e) of the Public Service Act, as amended by RA 11659, defines critical infrastructure as any public service which owns, uses or operates systems and assets so vital that their incapacity or destruction would have a detrimental impact on national security, including telecommunications. The law subjects investments in critical infrastructure to safeguards, such as the President's power to suspend or prohibit transactions on national security grounds, the reciprocity requirement for foreign ownership above 50%, and the prohibition on investments by foreign state-owned enterprises.
alac.application: Here, telecommunications is not among the listed public utilities, so the 60-40 constitutional limit does not apply. But it is expressly critical infrastructure. The foreign company's acquisition of 100% is subject to national security review and to the reciprocity rule.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the legislator is wrong; the acquisition is allowed in principle, but subject to the safeguards for critical infrastructure.

keyPoints: Critical infrastructure includes telecommunications (Sec. 2(e))
Not a public utility, so no 60-40 limit
Subject to national security review, reciprocity, and the state-owned enterprise ban
cite: Public Service Act (CA 146, as amended by RA 11659), Secs. 2(e), 23-25

q: Under Section 23 of the Public Service Act, as amended by RA 11659, the President may suspend or prohibit a transaction or investment in a public service in the interest of national security, within how many days from receipt of the recommendation of the relevant agency?
hints: The power covers transactions resulting in foreign control.
The PCC may be consulted on mergers.
why: RA 11659 Sec. 23: in the interest of national security, the President, after review and recommendation of the relevant agency, may within 60 days suspend or prohibit any proposed merger, acquisition or investment in a public service that effectively grants control to a foreigner or foreign corporation.
cite: Public Service Act (CA 146, as amended by RA 11659), Sec. 23

q: A foreign corporation proposed to acquire control of a Philippine power transmission service provider. The relevant agency reviewed the deal and recommended its prohibition on national security grounds. Forty days later, the President prohibited the acquisition. The foreign corporation argues that the President has no such power over private transactions. Is it correct?

alac.answer: No, the President validly prohibited the acquisition.
alac.basis: Section 23 of the Public Service Act, as amended by RA 11659, provides that in the interest of national security, the President, after review, evaluation and recommendation of the relevant government department or administrative agency, may, within sixty days from the receipt of such recommendation, suspend or prohibit any proposed merger or acquisition transaction, or any investment in a public service, that effectively results in the grant of control, whether direct or indirect, to a foreigner or a foreign corporation.
alac.application: Here, the acquisition would give control of a public service to a foreign corporation. The relevant agency reviewed and recommended prohibition on national security grounds, and the President acted within forty days, within the sixty-day period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the President validly exercised the power to prohibit the acquisition.

keyPoints: President's power to suspend or prohibit transactions (Sec. 23)
Ground: national security; grant of control to a foreigner
After agency recommendation, within 60 days
cite: Public Service Act (CA 146, as amended by RA 11659), Sec. 23

q: Under Section 24 of the Public Service Act, as amended by RA 11659, entities controlled by foreign governments or foreign state-owned enterprises are prohibited from owning capital in a public service classified as public utility or critical infrastructure, except that:
choices: They may own any amount with PCC approval
Sovereign wealth funds and independent pension funds may collectively own up to 30% of the capital
hints: The ban applies to investments made after the law took effect.
Existing state-owned investors cannot add capital.
why: RA 11659 Sec. 24: foreign government-controlled entities and foreign state-owned enterprises may not own capital in public utilities or critical infrastructure for investments after the law's effectivity; existing ones cannot invest additional capital; sovereign wealth funds and independent pension funds may collectively own up to 30%.
cite: Public Service Act (CA 146, as amended by RA 11659), Sec. 24

q: After RA 11659 took effect, Corp. S, more than 50% of whose capital is owned by a foreign State, sought to buy 20% of a Philippine seaport operator. Separately, a foreign State's independent pension fund sought to buy 25% of a Philippine water pipeline utility. May each invest?

alac.answer: Corp. S may not invest, but the pension fund may, as long as the collective cap of 30% for such funds is respected.
alac.basis: Section 2(g) of the Public Service Act, as amended by RA 11659, defines a foreign state-owned enterprise to include an entity in which a foreign State directly or indirectly owns more than fifty percent of the capital. Section 24 provides that an entity controlled by or acting on behalf of a foreign government, or a foreign state-owned enterprise, shall be prohibited from owning capital in any public service classified as public utility or critical infrastructure, for investments made after the law's effectivity, but that sovereign wealth funds and independent pension funds of each state may collectively own up to thirty percent of the capital of such public services.
alac.application: Here, Corp. S is a foreign state-owned enterprise, since a foreign State owns more than 50% of it, and a seaport is a public utility; its proposed investment after the law took effect is prohibited. The independent pension fund falls within the exception, and its 25% is within the 30% collective cap, assuming other such funds do not push the total above 30%.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Corp. S's investment is prohibited, while the pension fund's 25% investment is allowed within the 30% limit.

keyPoints: Foreign state-owned enterprise: foreign State owns over 50% (Sec. 2(g))
Prohibited from owning capital in public utilities or critical infrastructure (Sec. 24)
Exception: sovereign wealth and independent pension funds, up to 30% collectively
cite: Public Service Act (CA 146, as amended by RA 11659), Secs. 2(g) and 24

q: Under the reciprocity clause of RA 11659, foreign nationals may own more than 50% of the capital of entities operating critical infrastructure only if:
choices: Their country accords reciprocity to Philippine nationals, as provided by foreign law, treaty or international agreement
hints: Reciprocity may be satisfied by rights of similar value in other sectors.
NEDA issues the implementing rules.
why: RA 11659 Sec. 25: foreign nationals shall not own more than 50% of the capital of entities operating critical infrastructure unless their country accords reciprocity to Philippine nationals; reciprocity may be satisfied by rights of similar value in other economic sectors.
cite: Public Service Act (CA 146, as amended by RA 11659), Sec. 25

q: Investors from Country X want to own 80% of a Philippine telecommunications company. Country X does not allow Filipinos to own telecommunications companies there, but it allows Filipinos to own 100% of power and banking companies. May the Country X investors own 80%?

alac.answer: Yes, they may, if the NEDA finds that Country X's grant of rights in power and banking satisfies reciprocity.
alac.basis: Section 25 of the Public Service Act, as amended by RA 11659, provides that foreign nationals shall not be allowed to own more than fifty percent of the capital of entities engaged in the operation and management of critical infrastructure unless the country of such foreign national accords reciprocity to Philippine nationals as provided by foreign law, treaty or international agreement, and that reciprocity may be satisfied by according rights of similar value in other economic sectors. The NEDA promulgates the implementing rules.
alac.application: Here, a telecommunications company is critical infrastructure, and the investors want more than 50%. Country X does not give reciprocity in telecommunications, but it gives Filipinos full ownership rights in power and banking. Under the law, rights of similar value in other sectors may satisfy reciprocity.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the Country X investors may own 80% if the NEDA determines that the rights granted in power and banking are of similar value; otherwise, they are limited to 50%.

keyPoints: Foreign ownership above 50% of critical infrastructure requires reciprocity (Sec. 25)
Reciprocity may be satisfied by rights of similar value in other sectors
NEDA implementing rules
cite: Public Service Act (CA 146, as amended by RA 11659), Sec. 25

q: Under Section 2 of the Revised Corporation Code, a corporation is:
choices: A natural person engaged in business
An artificial being created by operation of law, with the right of succession and the powers, attributes and properties authorized by law
A partnership of two or more persons
hints: A corporation is created by the State, not merely by agreement.
It has the right of succession.
why: RCC Sec. 2: a corporation is an artificial being created by operation of law, having the right of succession and the powers, attributes and properties expressly authorized by law or incidental to its existence.

q: Arturo, the majority stockholder and president of Golden Grains Corp., died. His heirs claim that the corporation was dissolved by his death and that its properties should be distributed to them. Are they correct?

alac.answer: No, the heirs are not correct. The corporation continues to exist.
alac.basis: Section 2 of the Revised Corporation Code defines a corporation as an artificial being created by operation of law, having the right of succession and the powers, attributes and properties authorized by law. The right of succession means that the corporation continues to exist despite changes in its stockholders, including their death.
alac.application: Here, Arturo's death changed only the ownership of his shares, which pass to his heirs. It did not affect the existence of Golden Grains Corp., which has a personality and a right of succession of its own. Its properties belong to the corporation, not to its stockholders.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the corporation is not dissolved; the heirs succeed only to Arturo's shares, not to the corporate properties.

keyPoints: Corporation is an artificial being created by law (RCC Sec. 2)
Right of succession: existence continues despite changes in stockholders
Heirs inherit the shares, not corporate assets

q: Under Section 3 of the Revised Corporation Code, a stock corporation is one that:
choices: Has capital stock divided into shares and is authorized to distribute dividends or surplus profits to shareholders on the basis of the shares held
hints: Stock and nonstock are the two classes under the Code.
The key is the authority to distribute profits.
why: RCC Sec. 3: stock corporations have capital stock divided into shares and are authorized to distribute dividends or allotments of surplus profits on the basis of shares held; all other corporations are nonstock.

q: Bayanihan Foundation, Inc., a nonstock corporation organized for charitable purposes, earned a large surplus from its fund-raising events. Its trustees voted to distribute the surplus to its members as dividends. Is the distribution valid?

alac.answer: No, the distribution is not valid.
alac.basis: Section 3 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that stock corporations are those which have capital stock divided into shares and are authorized to distribute to the holders of such shares dividends or allotments of the surplus profits; all other corporations are nonstock corporations. A nonstock corporation, by its nature, is not authorized to distribute its income to its members as dividends; any surplus must be used for the purposes for which it was organized.
alac.application: Here, Bayanihan Foundation is a nonstock corporation organized for charitable purposes. It has no shares and no authority to distribute profits to members. Distributing the surplus as dividends would contradict its nature as a nonstock corporation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the distribution is invalid, and the surplus must be applied to the foundation's charitable purposes.

keyPoints: Stock vs nonstock corporations (RCC Sec. 3)
Only stock corporations may distribute dividends
Nonstock income goes to the corporation's purposes

q: In Gamboa v. Teves, the Supreme Court held that the term "capital" in the 60-40 Filipino ownership requirement of the Constitution refers to:
choices: Shares of stock entitled to vote in the election of directors
Only common shares, voting or not
hints: The purpose is Filipino control of the corporation.
Control comes through voting for the board.
why: In Gamboa v. Teves, G.R. No. 176579, June 28, 2011, "capital" refers only to shares entitled to vote in the election of directors; Filipinos must own at least 60% of those shares.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Secs. 2 and 11; Gamboa v. Teves, G.R. No. 176579, June 28, 2011

q: Prime Power Corp., which seeks to operate a public utility, has 1,000 common voting shares and 2,000 non-voting preferred shares. Filipinos own 2,000 of the preferred shares and 400 of the common shares; foreigners own the other 600 common shares. Prime Power argues that Filipinos own 80% of its total shares. Is it qualified as a Filipino corporation?

alac.answer: No, Prime Power Corp. is not qualified.
alac.basis: Article XII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution reserves the operation of public utilities to Filipino citizens or corporations at least sixty per centum of whose capital is owned by Filipinos. In Gamboa v. Teves, G.R. No. 176579, June 28, 2011, the Supreme Court held that "capital" refers only to shares of stock entitled to vote in the election of directors, so that Filipinos must own at least 60% of the voting shares, ensuring Filipino control.
alac.application: Here, although Filipinos own 2,400 of the 3,000 total shares, the preferred shares cannot vote for directors. Of the 1,000 voting common shares, Filipinos own only 400, or 40%, while foreigners own 60%. Control of the board is therefore in foreign hands.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Prime Power Corp. does not meet the 60% Filipino ownership requirement and cannot operate a public utility.

keyPoints: 60-40 rule for nationalized activities (Const., Art. XII)
"Capital" means voting shares (Gamboa v. Teves)
Filipinos own only 40% of voting shares
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 11; Gamboa v. Teves, G.R. No. 176579, June 28, 2011

q: Under Narra Nickel Mining v. Redmont, the Grandfather Rule applies:
choices: When there is doubt as to the actual Filipino ownership and control of the corporation, as in layered corporate structures
Never; only the Control Test applies
hints: The Control Test is applied first.
The Grandfather Rule looks through the layers to the real owners.
why: In Narra Nickel Mining and Development Corp. v. Redmont Consolidated Mines Corp., G.R. No. 195580, April 21, 2014, the Court held that the Control Test is the prevailing mode, but the Grandfather Rule applies when there is doubt as to the true Filipino ownership and control, e.g., when Filipino equity is less than 60% at any level or layered structures suggest foreign control.
cite: Narra Nickel Mining and Development Corp. v. Redmont Consolidated Mines Corp., G.R. No. 195580, April 21, 2014

q: Mina Corp. applies for a mining agreement. Its shares are 60% owned by Holdco, Inc. and 40% by foreigners. Holdco, in turn, is 60% owned by Filipinos and 40% by the same foreign group, which also funds all of Holdco's capital. Is Mina Corp. a qualified Filipino corporation?

alac.answer: No, Mina Corp. is not qualified, applying the Grandfather Rule.
alac.basis: Article XII, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution limits mining agreements to Filipino citizens or corporations at least 60% of whose capital is owned by Filipinos. In Narra Nickel Mining and Development Corp. v. Redmont Consolidated Mines Corp., G.R. No. 195580, April 21, 2014, the Supreme Court held that while the Control Test is generally applied, the Grandfather Rule is used when there is doubt as to the true Filipino ownership and control, by computing the Filipino equity through each layer of ownership.
alac.application: Here, the layered structure and the foreign group's funding of Holdco raise doubt about real Filipino control, so the Grandfather Rule applies. Filipino ownership of Mina Corp. is only 60% (Holdco's share) x 60% (Filipino share in Holdco) = 36%, while the foreign group effectively owns the rest. That is far below 60%.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Mina Corp. is not a qualified Filipino corporation and cannot enter into the mining agreement.

keyPoints: 60% Filipino ownership for natural resources (Const., Art. XII, Sec. 2)
Grandfather Rule when there is doubt about real control (Narra Nickel v. Redmont)
Effective Filipino equity: 60% x 60% = 36%
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 2; Narra Nickel Mining and Development Corp. v. Redmont Consolidated Mines Corp., G.R. No. 195580, April 21, 2014

q: Under the doctrine of separate juridical personality, a corporation's property:
choices: Belongs to its stockholders in proportion to their shares
Belongs to the corporation, distinct from its stockholders, and cannot be taken for their personal debts
hints: The corporation has a personality of its own.
Stockholders own shares, not the corporate assets.
why: A corporation has a juridical personality separate and distinct from its stockholders; its property is its own and is not answerable for the personal debts of its stockholders, and vice versa.
cite: Revised Corporation Code, Sec. 2; Civil Code, Art. 44(3)

q: Celso owns 70% of the shares of Celso Trading Corp. A creditor of Celso, holding a judgment for Celso's personal debt, levied on a delivery truck registered in the name of Celso Trading Corp. The corporation filed a third-party claim. Should the levy be lifted?

alac.answer: Yes, the levy on the corporation's truck should be lifted.
alac.basis: Under Article 44(3) of the Civil Code, a corporation for private interest is a juridical person with a personality separate and distinct from that of each shareholder. Section 2 of the Revised Corporation Code defines a corporation as an artificial being created by operation of law. As a rule, the property of a corporation cannot be held liable for the personal obligations of its stockholders.
alac.application: Here, the judgment is for Celso's personal debt, while the truck belongs to Celso Trading Corp., a separate juridical person. Celso's 70% shareholding does not make the corporation's assets his. Nothing shows that the corporation is a mere alter ego used to defraud creditors.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the corporation's truck cannot be levied upon for Celso's personal debt; the creditor may instead levy on Celso's shares.

keyPoints: Separate juridical personality (Civil Code Art. 44(3); RCC Sec. 2)
Corporate property not liable for stockholders' personal debts
Creditor may levy on the debtor's shares
cite: Civil Code, Art. 44(3); Revised Corporation Code, Sec. 2

q: The corporate veil may be pierced when the separate personality of the corporation is used to:
choices: Defeat public convenience, justify a wrong, protect fraud, or defend a crime, or when the corporation is a mere alter ego of a person
hints: The doctrine is applied with caution.
There are three broad classes of cases.
why: The veil is pierced in cases of (1) defeat of public convenience, (2) fraud, or (3) alter ego, where the corporation is a mere conduit of a person or another corporation (Concept Builders, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. No. 108734, May 29, 1996).
cite: Concept Builders, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. No. 108734, May 29, 1996

q: After losing an illegal dismissal case to its workers, Delta Builders, Inc. stopped operating and transferred all its equipment, office and staff to a new company, Delta Construction, Inc., owned by the same family, managed by the same officers, at the same address, in the same business. The workers cannot collect their award from the empty Delta Builders. What can they do?

alac.answer: The workers may ask the labor tribunal to pierce the corporate veil and enforce the award against Delta Construction, Inc.
alac.basis: The separate personality of a corporation may be disregarded when it is used as a shield to defeat public convenience, justify a wrong, protect fraud, or when the corporation is a mere alter ego or business conduit of another. In Concept Builders, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. No. 108734, May 29, 1996, on similar facts, the Supreme Court pierced the veil of a new corporation created by the same owners to evade a labor judgment against the old one.
alac.application: Here, Delta Builders closed right after losing the case and moved everything, including its equipment, staff, officers and address, to Delta Construction, owned by the same family and engaged in the same business. The new company was used to evade the workers' judgment.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the corporate veil may be pierced, and the award may be enforced against Delta Construction, Inc.

keyPoints: Veil pierced to prevent fraud or evasion of obligations
Same owners, officers, address and business: alter ego (Concept Builders v. NLRC)
Judgment enforceable against the new corporation
cite: Concept Builders, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. No. 108734, May 29, 1996

q: Under Section 10 of the Revised Corporation Code, how many incorporators may organize a corporation?
choices: Not more than fifteen, and even one (a One Person Corporation)
hints: The Code removed the old minimum of five.
There is still a maximum.
why: RCC Sec. 10: any person, partnership, association or corporation, singly or jointly with others but not more than fifteen, may organize a corporation; natural persons must be of legal age; each incorporator of a stock corporation must own or subscribe to at least one share.

q: Five doctors want to organize "Healing Hands Medical Practice, Inc." to practice medicine as a corporation, with each doctor as an incorporator. No special law allows it. May the SEC register the corporation?

alac.answer: No, the SEC should not register it.
alac.basis: Section 10 of the Revised Corporation Code allows any person, partnership, association or corporation, singly or jointly with others but not more than fifteen, to organize a corporation for any lawful purpose, provided that natural persons who are licensed to practice a profession, and partnerships or associations organized for the purpose of practicing a profession, shall not be allowed to organize as a corporation unless otherwise provided under special laws.
alac.application: Here, the doctors are licensed professionals who want to organize a corporation for the purpose of practicing medicine, and no special law allows it. The proviso of Section 10 prohibits this.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the corporation cannot be registered for the practice of medicine; the doctors may instead form a professional partnership.

keyPoints: Up to fifteen incorporators (RCC Sec. 10)
Licensed professionals cannot incorporate to practice their profession
Unless a special law allows it

q: As a rule, a promoter who enters into a contract on behalf of a corporation still to be formed is:
choices: Liable only if the corporation fails
Personally liable on the contract, unless the corporation, once formed, adopts it and the other party agrees to release the promoter
hints: A corporation not yet in existence cannot be bound or be a principal.
The promoter acts without an existing principal.
why: A promoter who contracts for a corporation not yet formed is personally liable, since there is no existing principal; he is released only if the corporation adopts the contract and the other party agrees to substitute it (novation).
cite: Revised Corporation Code, Sec. 18; Civil Code, Art. 1293

q: Before "Ever Fresh Foods, Inc." was incorporated, its promoter, Edgar, signed a lease of a warehouse "for and in behalf of Ever Fresh Foods, Inc., a corporation to be organized." The corporation was never organized, and the lessor sued Edgar for unpaid rent. Edgar argues he signed only as an agent of the corporation. Is he liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Edgar is personally liable.
alac.basis: Under Section 18 of the Revised Corporation Code, a private corporation commences its corporate existence and juridical personality only upon issuance of the certificate of incorporation. Before that, there is no principal that can be represented or bound. A promoter who contracts in the name of a corporation still to be formed is therefore personally liable on the contract, unless the corporation, once formed, adopts it and the other party agrees to release him.
alac.application: Here, Ever Fresh Foods, Inc. was never organized, so it never existed to adopt the lease. Edgar could not have acted as agent of a non-existent principal. He signed the lease and is bound by it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Edgar is personally liable to the lessor for the unpaid rent.

keyPoints: Corporate existence begins upon the SEC certificate (RCC Sec. 18)
No principal before incorporation; promoter personally liable
Released only by adoption plus the creditor's consent

q: When does a corporation become liable on a pre-incorporation contract made by its promoter?
choices: When, after incorporation, it adopts or ratifies the contract, expressly or impliedly, as by knowingly accepting its benefits
hints: The corporation did not exist when the contract was made.
It can make the contract its own after it is formed.
why: A corporation is not bound by its promoter's pre-incorporation contracts unless, after incorporation, it adopts or ratifies them, expressly or impliedly, such as by knowingly accepting their benefits.

q: Promoters of "Bright Tech, Inc." hired an engineer to prepare a feasibility study before the corporation was formed. After incorporation, the board used the study to secure a bank loan and start operations, but refused to pay the engineer, saying it never contracted with him. Is Bright Tech liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Bright Tech, Inc. is liable to the engineer.
alac.basis: A corporation is not bound by contracts made by its promoters before it came into existence, because it could not have consented. However, once incorporated, it may adopt or ratify such contracts, expressly or impliedly, as when it knowingly accepts and uses their benefits. Corporate existence begins upon the issuance of the certificate of incorporation (Section 18 of the Revised Corporation Code).
alac.application: Here, the feasibility study was ordered by the promoters before incorporation. But after Bright Tech came into existence, its board, with knowledge of the study, used it to obtain a loan and start operations. By knowingly accepting the benefits, the corporation impliedly adopted the contract.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Bright Tech is liable to pay the engineer for the feasibility study.

keyPoints: Corporation not bound by promoter contracts before incorporation
Bound upon adoption or ratification after incorporation
Knowing acceptance of benefits is implied adoption

q: Under Section 11 of the Revised Corporation Code, a corporation has:
choices: A term fixed by the SEC
Perpetual existence, unless its articles of incorporation provide otherwise
hints: The Code changed the old 50-year term.
A specific term may still be stated in the articles.
why: RCC Sec. 11: a corporation has perpetual existence unless its articles of incorporation provide otherwise; existing corporations also have perpetual existence unless they elect to retain their term.

q: Fortune Corp.'s articles of incorporation provide for a term of 25 years, expiring on 31 December 2035. In January 2026, the board and stockholders approved an amendment extending the term by another 25 years, without giving any special reason. Will the SEC approve the extension now?

alac.answer: Not yet, unless Fortune Corp. shows justifiable reasons for an early extension.
alac.basis: Section 11 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that a corporate term for a specific period may be extended or shortened by amending the articles of incorporation, provided that no extension may be made earlier than three years prior to the original or subsequent expiry date, unless there are justifiable reasons for an earlier extension as may be determined by the Commission.
alac.application: Here, Fortune Corp.'s term expires on 31 December 2035. In January 2026, it is almost ten years before expiry, far earlier than the three-year window, and no justifiable reason was given.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the SEC should not approve the extension at this time; Fortune Corp. may apply within three years before expiry, or convert to perpetual existence, or show justifiable reasons for an earlier extension.

keyPoints: Term may be extended or shortened by amendment (RCC Sec. 11)
Not earlier than three years before expiry
Unless justifiable reasons are shown
