q: Under Section 13 of the Revised Corporation Code, the principal office of a corporation stated in its articles of incorporation must be located:
choices: In the place of the majority stockholder
hints: Philippine corporations are domestic.
Read Sec. 13(c).
why: RCC Sec. 13(c): the articles of incorporation must state the place where the principal office is to be located, which must be within the Philippines.

q: Global Link Corp. filed articles of incorporation stating that its principal office is in Singapore, where most of its Filipino incorporators work, and that its purposes are "any lawful business." Should the SEC accept the articles?

alac.answer: No, the SEC should require corrections before accepting the articles.
alac.basis: Section 13 of the Revised Corporation Code requires the articles of incorporation to state, among others, the specific purpose or purposes for which the corporation is being formed, indicating the primary and secondary purposes, and the place where the principal office is to be located, which must be within the Philippines.
alac.application: Here, Global Link stated a principal office in Singapore, which violates the requirement that the principal office be within the Philippines. It also stated only "any lawful business," which does not specify its purposes or identify its primary purpose.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the SEC should not accept the articles until they state a principal office in the Philippines and specific primary and secondary purposes.

keyPoints: Principal office must be within the Philippines (RCC Sec. 13(c))
Specific primary and secondary purposes required (Sec. 13(b))
Defective articles may be returned for correction

q: Under Section 17 of the Revised Corporation Code, is "Sunrise Trading, Inc." distinguishable from a registered "Sunrise Trading Corporation"?
choices: Yes, if the owners are different
No; words like "corporation" or "incorporated" do not make a name distinguishable
hints: The test is whether the names are distinguishable.
Corporate suffixes are disregarded.
why: RCC Sec. 17: a name is not distinguishable even if it contains words such as "corporation," "company," "incorporated," or "limited," or differences in punctuation, articles or abbreviations.

q: "Golden Harvest Foods, Inc." was registered in 2015. In 2025, a new company managed to register "Golden Harvest Food Corp." and began selling similar products. Golden Harvest Foods complains to the SEC. What may the SEC do?

alac.answer: The SEC may order the new company to cease and desist from using the name and require it to register a new one.
alac.basis: Section 17 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that no corporate name shall be allowed if it is not distinguishable from one already reserved or registered for another corporation, and that a name is not distinguishable even if it contains words such as "corporation" or "incorporated," or differences in number of the same word. Upon determining that a name is not distinguishable, the Commission may summarily order the corporation to immediately cease and desist from using it and require it to register a new one.
alac.application: Here, "Golden Harvest Food Corp." differs from the earlier "Golden Harvest Foods, Inc." only in the corporate suffix and in the singular form of "Foods," differences the law disregards. The names are not distinguishable, and the earlier registrant has the prior right.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the SEC may order the new company to stop using the name and to adopt a new one.

keyPoints: Names must be distinguishable (RCC Sec. 17)
Suffixes and number of the same word are disregarded
SEC may summarily order cease and desist and a new name

q: Under Section 19 of the Revised Corporation Code, the due incorporation of a de facto corporation may be questioned:
choices: By any private party in any suit
Only by the Solicitor General in a quo warranto proceeding, not collaterally in a private suit
hints: A de facto corporation claims in good faith to be a corporation.
Its existence is attacked directly by the State.
why: RCC Sec. 19: the due incorporation of a corporation claiming in good faith to be one shall not be inquired into collaterally in a private suit; such inquiry may be made by the Solicitor General in a quo warranto proceeding.

q: Harbor Supply Corp., which has an SEC certificate but whose articles contain a technical defect in the incorporators' acknowledgment, sued Ivan to collect payment for goods delivered. Ivan moved to dismiss, arguing that Harbor Supply was not validly incorporated and has no capacity to sue. Should the motion be granted?

alac.answer: No, the motion should be denied.
alac.basis: Section 19 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that the due incorporation of any corporation claiming in good faith to be a corporation under the Code, and its right to exercise corporate powers, shall not be inquired into collaterally in any private suit to which such corporation may be a party; such inquiry may be made by the Solicitor General in a quo warranto proceeding.
alac.application: Here, Harbor Supply has a certificate of incorporation and claims in good faith to be a corporation, despite a technical defect in its articles. It is at least a de facto corporation. Ivan, a private party, is questioning its incorporation collaterally, as a defense in a collection suit.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ivan cannot attack Harbor Supply's corporate existence in this suit, and he must pay for the goods; only the Solicitor General may question it in a quo warranto case.

keyPoints: De facto corporation: good-faith claim to be a corporation (RCC Sec. 19)
No collateral attack in a private suit
Only the Solicitor General, through quo warranto

q: Under Section 20 of the Revised Corporation Code, persons who assume to act as a corporation knowing it to be without authority to do so are liable:
choices: As general partners for all debts, liabilities and damages incurred
hints: They cannot hide behind a non-existent corporation.
Their liability is like that of general partners.
why: RCC Sec. 20: all persons who assume to act as a corporation knowing it to be without authority are liable as general partners for all debts, liabilities and damages incurred; the ostensible corporation cannot use its lack of personality as a defense, and one who contracts with it cannot resist performance on that ground.
cite: Revised Corporation Code, Sec. 20; Lim Tong Lim v. Philippine Fishing Gear Industries, Inc., G.R. No. 136448, November 3, 1999

q: Three friends bought fishing nets on credit in the name of "Ocean Catch Corporation," which they knew had never been registered. They used the nets in their joint fishing business. When the debt went unpaid, the seller sued all three. One of them, who never signed the purchase documents, argues he cannot be liable. Decide.

alac.answer: All three are liable as general partners, including the one who did not sign.
alac.basis: Section 20 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that all persons who assume to act as a corporation knowing it to be without the authority to do so shall be liable as general partners for all debts, liabilities and damages incurred or arising as a result thereof. In Lim Tong Lim v. Philippine Fishing Gear Industries, Inc., G.R. No. 136448, November 3, 1999, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held that a person who benefited from the use of fishing nets bought in the name of a non-existent corporation is liable as a general partner, even if he did not sign the contract.
alac.application: Here, the three friends acted as Ocean Catch Corporation knowing that it was never registered, and all three used the nets in their joint business. The one who did not sign still took part in the business and benefited from the purchase.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, all three are liable as general partners for the price of the nets.

keyPoints: Corporation by estoppel (RCC Sec. 20)
Those who act as a corporation knowing it has no authority are liable as general partners
Benefiting from the transaction suffices (Lim Tong Lim v. Philippine Fishing Gear)
cite: Revised Corporation Code, Sec. 20; Lim Tong Lim v. Philippine Fishing Gear Industries, Inc., G.R. No. 136448, November 3, 1999

q: Under Section 47 of the Revised Corporation Code, who may amend or repeal the bylaws?
choices: A majority of the board, together with the owners of at least a majority of the outstanding capital stock (or majority of members)
hints: Both the board and the stockholders act.
The power may be delegated to the board by a 2/3 vote.
why: RCC Sec. 47: a majority of the board and the owners of at least a majority of the outstanding capital stock (or majority of members) may amend or repeal the bylaws; owners of 2/3 may delegate the power to the board.

q: The board of directors of Kalayaan Corp., acting alone, amended the bylaws to raise the quorum for stockholders' meetings. The stockholders had never delegated to the board the power to amend the bylaws. A stockholder questions the amendment. Is it valid?

alac.answer: No, the amendment is not valid.
alac.basis: Section 47 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that a majority of the board of directors and the owners of at least a majority of the outstanding capital stock, at a regular or special meeting duly called for the purpose, may amend or repeal the bylaws. The owners of two-thirds of the outstanding capital stock may delegate to the board the power to amend or repeal the bylaws.
alac.application: Here, only the board voted on the amendment, without the approval of stockholders owning a majority of the outstanding capital stock. The stockholders had not delegated the power to amend the bylaws to the board.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the board's amendment of the bylaws is invalid.

keyPoints: Amendment requires board majority plus stockholders' majority (RCC Sec. 47)
Board may act alone only if the power was delegated by 2/3 of stockholders
No delegation here

q: Under Section 21 of the Revised Corporation Code, if a corporation does not formally organize and commence business within five years from incorporation:
choices: Its certificate of incorporation is deemed revoked as of the day following the end of the five-year period
hints: Non-use of the charter has consequences.
The revocation is automatic.
why: RCC Sec. 21: failure to formally organize and commence business within five years from incorporation results in the certificate of incorporation being deemed revoked; a corporation that becomes inoperative for five consecutive years may be placed under delinquent status.

q: Lumen Corp. operated for ten years, then stopped all business operations for six consecutive years without filing any reports. The SEC, after notice and hearing, placed it under delinquent status. What must Lumen Corp. do to avoid revocation?

alac.answer: Lumen Corp. must resume operations and comply with all SEC requirements within two years.
alac.basis: Section 21 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that if a corporation has commenced its business but subsequently becomes inoperative for a period of at least five consecutive years, the Commission may, after due notice and hearing, place it under delinquent status. A delinquent corporation has two years to resume operations and comply with all requirements; upon compliance, the delinquent status is lifted, but failure to comply causes the revocation of its certificate of incorporation.
alac.application: Here, Lumen Corp. had commenced business but became inoperative for six consecutive years, so it was properly placed under delinquent status after notice and hearing.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Lumen Corp. must resume operations and comply with the SEC's requirements within two years; otherwise, its certificate of incorporation will be revoked.

keyPoints: Inoperative for five consecutive years: delinquent status (RCC Sec. 21)
Two years to resume operations and comply
Failure leads to revocation

q: Under Section 12 of the Revised Corporation Code, stock corporations are required to have a minimum capital stock:
choices: Only when specially provided by special law
hints: The Code removed the general minimum capital.
Some businesses, like banks, have minimum capital under special laws.
why: RCC Sec. 12: stock corporations are not required to have a minimum capital stock, except as otherwise specially provided by special law.

q: Two incorporators want to form (a) a small trading corporation with a capital stock of P10,000, and (b) a commercial bank with the same capital. They argue that the Revised Corporation Code no longer requires any minimum capital. Are they correct as to both?

alac.answer: They are correct as to the trading corporation, but not as to the bank.
alac.basis: Section 12 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that stock corporations shall not be required to have minimum capital stock, except as otherwise specially provided by special law. Banks are governed by special banking laws and regulations of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, which prescribe minimum capital requirements.
alac.application: Here, the trading corporation is an ordinary stock corporation, so no minimum capital stock is required under the Code. The bank, however, falls under special laws that require a much higher minimum capital.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the trading corporation may be formed with P10,000 in capital, but the bank must meet the minimum capital required by the special banking laws.

keyPoints: No minimum capital stock in general (RCC Sec. 12)
Except when required by special law
Banks have special minimum capital requirements

q: Under Section 59 of the Revised Corporation Code, a contract for the acquisition of unissued stock of a corporation is:
choices: A subscription, even if the parties refer to it as a purchase or another contract
A sale, if the parties call it a sale
hints: Substance prevails over the label.
Unissued stock can only be acquired from the corporation.
why: RCC Sec. 59: any contract for the acquisition of unissued stock in an existing corporation or one still to be formed is deemed a subscription, notwithstanding that the parties call it a purchase or some other contract.

q: Under a "Deed of Sale of Shares," Mario agreed to buy 10,000 unissued shares from Apex Corp. for P1 million, paying P250,000 upfront. Apex later became insolvent, and its creditors demand that Mario pay the unpaid P750,000. Mario argues that he merely bought shares under a sale, not a subscription, so he owes nothing more to creditors. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Mario is not correct. He is a subscriber liable for the unpaid balance.
alac.basis: Section 59 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that any contract for the acquisition of unissued stock in an existing corporation shall be deemed a subscription, notwithstanding the fact that the parties refer to it as a purchase or some other contract. Under the trust fund doctrine, unpaid subscriptions form part of the assets that answer for corporate debts.
alac.application: Here, the shares Mario acquired were unissued shares of Apex Corp. Though called a "deed of sale," the contract is in law a subscription. His unpaid P750,000 is an unpaid subscription, which is a corporate asset that may be collected for the benefit of creditors.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Mario is liable for the P750,000 balance of his subscription.

keyPoints: Acquisition of unissued stock is a subscription (RCC Sec. 59)
Label of the contract does not control
Unpaid subscriptions answer for corporate debts (trust fund doctrine)

q: Under Section 60 of the Revised Corporation Code, a pre-incorporation subscription is irrevocable for at least:
choices: Six months from the date of subscription, unless all other subscribers consent to revocation or the corporation fails to incorporate within that period
hints: The rule protects the corporation being formed and the other subscribers.
There are two exceptions.
why: RCC Sec. 60: a subscription to shares of a corporation still to be formed is irrevocable for at least six months from subscription, unless all other subscribers consent to the revocation or the corporation fails to incorporate within that period or a longer stipulated period.

q: Ninety days after subscribing to shares of a corporation still to be formed, Ofelia wanted to withdraw her subscription because she found a better investment. The corporation had not yet been incorporated, and the other subscribers refused to consent. May she revoke her subscription?

alac.answer: No, Ofelia may not revoke her subscription at this time.
alac.basis: Section 60 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that a subscription of shares in a corporation still to be formed shall be irrevocable for a period of at least six months from the date of subscription, unless all of the other subscribers consent to the revocation, or the corporation fails to incorporate within the same period or within a longer period stipulated in the contract of subscription.
alac.application: Here, only ninety days have passed since Ofelia subscribed, within the six-month irrevocability period. The other subscribers did not consent to her revocation, and the period for incorporation has not yet lapsed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ofelia's subscription remains irrevocable for now; she may withdraw only if all other subscribers consent or the corporation is not incorporated within the period.

keyPoints: Pre-incorporation subscription irrevocable for six months (RCC Sec. 60)
Unless all other subscribers consent
Or the corporation fails to incorporate within the period

q: Under Section 61 of the Revised Corporation Code, which of the following is NOT valid consideration for the issuance of stock?
choices: Previously incurred indebtedness of the corporation
Actual cash paid to the corporation
Labor performed for or services actually rendered to the corporation
A promise to render services in the future
hints: Stocks must be paid with value actually received.
Services must already have been rendered.
why: RCC Sec. 61 allows cash, property actually received, labor performed or services actually rendered, previously incurred corporate debt, retained earnings, exchanged shares, shares of another corporation, and other accepted forms; future services are not listed.

q: Star Media Corp. issued 50,000 shares worth P500,000 to a celebrity, Pia, in exchange for her promise to endorse the company's products over the next two years. A stockholder questions the issuance. Is it valid?

alac.answer: No, the issuance is not valid.
alac.basis: Section 61 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that stocks shall not be issued for a consideration less than their par or issued price, and lists the valid forms of consideration, including labor performed for or services actually rendered to the corporation. Services to be rendered in the future are not included.
alac.application: Here, the shares were issued in exchange for Pia's promise to endorse products over the next two years. These are future services, not services actually rendered to the corporation at the time of issuance. The corporation received nothing of value for the shares.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the issuance of the shares for future services is invalid.

keyPoints: Valid consideration for stocks (RCC Sec. 61)
Only services actually rendered qualify
Promise of future services is not valid consideration

q: Under Section 6 of the Revised Corporation Code, which shares may be deprived of voting rights?
choices: Only preferred or redeemable shares, unless the Code provides otherwise, and there must always be a class with complete voting rights
hints: Voting rights may be restricted only for certain classes.
Someone must always be able to vote.
why: RCC Sec. 6: no share may be deprived of voting rights except preferred or redeemable shares, unless otherwise provided; there must be a class with complete voting rights; non-voting shares still vote on fundamental matters.

q: Rosa holds non-voting preferred shares of Trident Corp. The board called a stockholders' meeting to amend the articles of incorporation to change the corporation's primary purpose, and informed Rosa that, as a non-voting shareholder, she could not vote. Is the board correct?

alac.answer: No, the board is not correct. Rosa may vote on the amendment.
alac.basis: Section 6 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that no share may be deprived of voting rights except preferred or redeemable shares, but holders of non-voting shares shall nevertheless be entitled to vote on certain fundamental matters, including the amendment of the articles of incorporation.
alac.application: Here, Rosa's preferred shares are non-voting in ordinary matters. But the meeting concerns an amendment of the articles of incorporation, one of the matters on which the law gives even non-voting shares the right to vote.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rosa is entitled to vote on the proposed amendment.

keyPoints: Non-voting shares limited to preferred or redeemable shares (RCC Sec. 6)
Non-voting shares still vote on fundamental matters
Amendment of the articles is one of them

q: Under the doctrine of equality of shares (Section 6 of the Revised Corporation Code):
choices: Each share is equal in all respects to every other share, except as otherwise provided in the articles of incorporation and certificate of stock
Shares of directors have more rights
All shares always have identical rights
hints: Differences must be stated in the articles.
Absent such provisions, shares are equal.
why: RCC Sec. 6: each share shall be equal in all respects to every other share, except as otherwise provided in the articles of incorporation and in the certificate of stock.

q: Sapphire Corp. has only one class of common shares. Its board declared a cash dividend of P10 per share for stockholders who are also employees, and P5 per share for all other stockholders. The articles of incorporation say nothing about different classes. Is the dividend declaration valid?

alac.answer: No, the dividend declaration is not valid.
alac.basis: Section 6 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that each share shall be equal in all respects to every other share, except as otherwise provided in the articles of incorporation and in the certificate of stock. This is the doctrine of equality of shares.
alac.application: Here, Sapphire Corp. has only one class of common shares, and its articles do not provide for different rights. Paying a higher dividend to some holders of the same shares, based on their being employees, treats equal shares unequally.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the declaration violates the doctrine of equality of shares; all common shares must receive the same dividend per share.

keyPoints: Doctrine of equality of shares (RCC Sec. 6)
Differences only if provided in the articles and certificate
Same class must receive the same dividend

q: Under Section 63 of the Revised Corporation Code, when may a certificate of stock be issued to a subscriber?
choices: At any time the board wishes
Only after the full amount of the subscription, with interest and expenses if any, has been paid
hints: A subscription is one entire contract.
The certificate evidences fully paid shares.
why: RCC Sec. 63: no certificate of stock shall be issued to a subscriber until the full amount of the subscription, with interest and expenses (for delinquent shares), has been paid.

q: Tomas subscribed to 1,000 shares of Vista Corp. and has paid for 400. He demands a certificate of stock for the 400 shares he has fully paid, so he can sell them. Must Vista Corp. issue the certificate?

alac.answer: No, Vista Corp. need not issue a certificate for the 400 shares.
alac.basis: Section 63 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that no certificate of stock shall be issued to a subscriber until the full amount of the subscription, together with interest and expenses if any, has been paid. A subscription is treated as one entire and indivisible contract.
alac.application: Here, Tomas subscribed to 1,000 shares under one subscription and has paid only part of it. Until the full subscription is paid, no certificate may be issued, even for the portion corresponding to his payments.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Vista Corp. may refuse to issue a certificate until Tomas pays his entire subscription.

keyPoints: No certificate until full payment of the subscription (RCC Sec. 63)
Subscription is indivisible
Partial payment does not entitle him to a certificate for part

q: Under Section 64 of the Revised Corporation Code, a director who consents to the issuance of stocks for less than their par or issued value is liable:
choices: Solidarily with the stockholder concerned, to the corporation or its creditors, for the difference between the value received and the par or issued value
hints: These are watered stocks.
The liability is solidary with the stockholder.
why: RCC Sec. 64: a director or officer who consents to issuing stocks below par or issued value, or for overvalued non-cash consideration, or who fails to object in writing despite knowledge, is solidarily liable with the stockholder for the difference.

q: The board of Wave Corp. approved the issuance of 100,000 shares with a par value of P10 each to Ursula in exchange for a lot that the directors knew was worth only P400,000. Director Vic voted in favor. Wave Corp. later became insolvent. Can its creditors hold Vic liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Vic is liable to the creditors for P600,000, solidarily with Ursula.
alac.basis: Section 64 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that a director or officer who consents to the issuance of stocks for a consideration other than cash, valued in excess of its fair value, shall be liable to the corporation or its creditors, solidarily with the stockholder concerned, for the difference between the value received at the time of issuance and the par or issued value of the stock.
alac.application: Here, 100,000 shares with a par value of P10 each have a total par value of P1 million, but they were issued for a lot worth only P400,000, an overvaluation the directors knew of. Vic consented to the issuance. The shortfall is P600,000.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Vic is solidarily liable with Ursula to Wave Corp.'s creditors for the P600,000 difference.

keyPoints: Watered stock: issued for less than par or for overvalued property (RCC Sec. 64)
Consenting director solidarily liable with the stockholder
Liability is for the difference: P1,000,000 - P400,000

q: Under the trust fund doctrine, the subscribed capital stock of a corporation:
choices: Is a trust fund for the payment of corporate creditors, which cannot be returned to stockholders to the prejudice of creditors
Belongs to the stockholders and may be returned at any time
hints: Creditors rely on the corporation's capital.
Unpaid subscriptions are corporate assets.
why: Trust fund doctrine: the capital stock, property and assets of a corporation, including unpaid subscriptions, are a trust fund for the payment of its creditors; the corporation may not release subscribers or return capital to stockholders to their prejudice (Ong Yong v. Tiu, G.R. No. 144476, April 8, 2003).
cite: Ong Yong v. Tiu, G.R. No. 144476, April 8, 2003

q: While insolvent, Xenon Corp.'s board passed a resolution condoning the P2 million unpaid subscription of its majority stockholder, Yuri. Xenon's creditors, who cannot be paid from other assets, sue Yuri for the P2 million. Can they collect?

alac.answer: Yes, the creditors can collect the unpaid subscription from Yuri.
alac.basis: Under the trust fund doctrine, the subscribed capital stock of a corporation, including unpaid subscriptions, is a trust fund for the payment of its creditors. The corporation cannot release subscribers from their obligation to pay or otherwise return capital to stockholders to the prejudice of creditors (Ong Yong v. Tiu, G.R. No. 144476, April 8, 2003). Section 69 of the Revised Corporation Code allows unpaid subscriptions to be collected by court action.
alac.application: Here, Xenon was insolvent when its board condoned Yuri's unpaid subscription. The condonation diminished the trust fund available to creditors, who cannot be paid from other assets. It cannot prejudice them.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the condonation is ineffective as against the creditors, and they may collect the P2 million from Yuri.

keyPoints: Unpaid subscriptions are a trust fund for creditors
Corporation cannot condone them to the prejudice of creditors (Ong Yong v. Tiu)
Collection by court action (RCC Sec. 69)
cite: Revised Corporation Code, Sec. 69; Ong Yong v. Tiu, G.R. No. 144476, April 8, 2003

q: Under Section 66 of the Revised Corporation Code, unpaid subscriptions become due and payable:
choices: On the date specified in the subscription contract or in a call made by the board
hints: The board may make a call.
Failure to pay makes the whole balance due.
why: RCC Sec. 66: the board may declare unpaid subscriptions due and payable; payment is due on the date in the subscription contract or in the call; failure to pay makes the entire balance due with legal interest, and the stock becomes delinquent if unpaid within 30 days.

q: Zenaida subscribed to P1 million worth of shares, paid P250,000, and the subscription contract set no due date for the balance. The board then called for payment of 50% of the unpaid balance on 1 March. Zenaida did not pay on that date. What are the consequences?

alac.answer: The entire unpaid balance became due, with legal interest, and her shares may become delinquent if she does not pay within thirty days.
alac.basis: Section 66 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that, subject to the subscription contract, the board may at any time declare unpaid subscriptions due and payable. Payment shall be made on the date stated in the call, and failure to pay on that date shall render the entire balance due and payable and make the stockholder liable for interest at the legal rate, unless a different rate is provided; if no payment is made within thirty days from that date, the stock becomes delinquent.
alac.application: Here, the subscription contract set no due date, so the board validly called for payment. Zenaida did not pay on 1 March. As a result, not only the called 50% but the entire unpaid balance of P750,000 became due, with interest.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Zenaida owes the whole P750,000 balance with legal interest, and her shares become delinquent if unpaid within thirty days, subject to a delinquency sale.

keyPoints: Board may call unpaid subscriptions (RCC Sec. 66)
Failure to pay on the date makes the entire balance due, with interest
Stock becomes delinquent after thirty days

q: Under Section 67 of the Revised Corporation Code, the delinquency sale of shares must be set on a date:
choices: Not less than thirty days nor more than sixty days from the date the stock became delinquent
The day after the shares become delinquent
hints: The law gives the stockholder time to pay.
Notice and publication are also required.
why: RCC Sec. 67: the board resolution must state the amount due and the date, time and place of sale, which shall be not less than 30 nor more than 60 days from the date the stock became delinquent; notice must be sent and published.

q: Aldo's delinquent shares were sold at a delinquency sale. Seven months later, he sued to recover them, claiming the notice of sale was defective, without paying or tendering anything. Will his action prosper?

alac.answer: No, Aldo's action will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 68 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that no action to recover delinquent stock sold can be sustained upon the ground of irregularity or defect in the notice of sale, or in the sale itself, unless the party seeking to maintain such action first pays or tenders to the party holding the stock the sum for which it was sold, with interest from the date of sale at the legal rate; and no such action shall be maintained unless the complaint is filed within six months from the date of sale.
alac.application: Here, Aldo did not pay or tender the amount for which his shares were sold, with interest. He also filed his action seven months after the sale, beyond the six-month period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Aldo's action to recover the shares must be dismissed.

keyPoints: Action to question a delinquency sale requires prior payment or tender (RCC Sec. 68)
Must be filed within six months from the sale
Both requirements unmet

q: Under Section 62 of the Revised Corporation Code, a transfer of shares is valid as against the corporation and third persons only when:
choices: The transfer is recorded in the books of the corporation
hints: Between the parties, delivery of the indorsed certificate suffices.
As to others, recording is needed.
why: RCC Sec. 62: shares are transferred by delivery of the certificate indorsed by the owner; but no transfer is valid, except as between the parties, until recorded in the books of the corporation.

q: Bert sold his fully paid shares in Coral Corp. to Cris by delivering the duly indorsed stock certificate. Cris never had the transfer recorded in the corporation's books. At the next stockholders' meeting, Cris sought to vote the shares, but the corporation recognized only Bert. Was the corporation correct?

alac.answer: Yes, the corporation was correct.
alac.basis: Section 62 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that shares of stock may be transferred by delivery of the certificate indorsed by the owner, but no transfer shall be valid, except as between the parties, until the transfer is recorded in the books of the corporation.
alac.application: Here, the sale and delivery of the indorsed certificate made the transfer valid between Bert and Cris. But the transfer was never recorded in Coral Corp.'s books. As far as the corporation is concerned, Bert remains the stockholder of record entitled to vote.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the corporation properly recognized Bert; Cris must first have the transfer recorded to exercise rights as a stockholder against the corporation.

keyPoints: Transfer by delivery of the indorsed certificate (RCC Sec. 62)
Valid only between the parties until recorded
Corporation recognizes the stockholder of record

q: Under Section 35 of the Revised Corporation Code, which is among the express powers of every corporation?
choices: To sue and be sued in its corporate name
hints: A corporation acts through its corporate name.
The list starts with litigation capacity.
why: RCC Sec. 35 lists express powers, beginning with the power to sue and be sued in the corporate name, perpetual existence, a corporate seal, and amending the articles and bylaws.

q: Sunrise Bakeries, Inc., whose primary purpose is baking, wants to invest P50 million of its funds in a resort company. The board approved the investment by majority vote, but the stockholders were never asked. A stockholder objects. Is the investment valid? What right does a dissenting stockholder have?

alac.answer: The investment is not yet valid without stockholder ratification; a dissenting stockholder may exercise the right of appraisal.
alac.basis: Section 41 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that a private corporation may invest its funds in any other corporation or business, or for any purpose other than its primary purpose, when approved by a majority of the board and ratified by the stockholders representing at least two-thirds of the outstanding capital stock, at a meeting duly called for the purpose. Any dissenting stockholder shall have the appraisal right.
alac.application: Here, investing in a resort is a purpose other than Sunrise's primary purpose of baking. The board approved it, but the required ratification by two-thirds of the outstanding capital stock was not obtained.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the investment cannot validly proceed without the stockholders' two-thirds ratification, and any stockholder who dissents may demand payment of the fair value of his shares.

keyPoints: Investment in another business requires board majority and 2/3 stockholder ratification (RCC Sec. 41)
Dissenting stockholders have the appraisal right
No ratification yet

q: Under Section 22 of the Revised Corporation Code, who exercises the corporate powers, conducts all business, and controls all properties of a corporation?
choices: The board of directors or trustees, unless otherwise provided in the Code
hints: The board is the repository of corporate powers.
Stockholders act only on matters the Code reserves to them.
why: RCC Sec. 22: unless otherwise provided in the Code, the board of directors or trustees shall exercise the corporate powers, conduct all business, and control all properties of the corporation.

q: At the annual meeting of Topaz Corp., the stockholders passed a resolution directing the board to cancel a supply contract with a long-time supplier and award it to a stockholder's relative. The board, after study, refused, finding the existing contract more advantageous. Is the board bound by the stockholders' resolution?

alac.answer: No, the board is not bound by the resolution.
alac.basis: Section 22 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that, unless otherwise provided in the Code, the board of directors shall exercise the corporate powers, conduct all business, and control all properties of the corporation. Stockholders act only on matters the Code specifically reserves to them, such as amendments to the articles, mergers, or the sale of all or substantially all assets.
alac.application: Here, the choice of a supplier is an ordinary business decision within the board's authority, not a matter reserved to the stockholders. The board studied the matter and decided in good faith that the existing contract is better.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the stockholders' resolution cannot compel the board, which validly retains the existing supply contract.

keyPoints: Board is the repository of corporate powers (RCC Sec. 22)
Stockholders act only on matters reserved to them by law
Ordinary business decisions belong to the board

q: Under Section 26 of the Revised Corporation Code, a person is disqualified from being a director if, within five years before election, he was convicted by final judgment of:
choices: A crime punishable by a fine only
An offense punishable by imprisonment exceeding six years, or a violation of the Code or of the Securities Regulation Code
hints: The disqualification looks back five years.
Fraud-related administrative liability also disqualifies.
why: RCC Sec. 26: a person convicted by final judgment within five years before election of an offense punishable by more than six years, or of violating the Code or the SRC, or found administratively liable for fraudulent acts, is disqualified.

q: Two years ago, Ulysses was convicted by final judgment of estafa and sentenced to imprisonment of eight years; he was later paroled. He owns 1,000 shares of Wave Corp. and was elected director at the last annual meeting. Is his election valid?

alac.answer: No, Ulysses is disqualified from being a director.
alac.basis: Section 26 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that a person shall be disqualified from being a director, trustee or officer of any corporation if, within five years prior to the election, the person was convicted by final judgment of an offense punishable by imprisonment for a period exceeding six years. Section 22 requires that directors be elected from among the holders of stock registered in the corporation's books.
alac.application: Here, Ulysses owns shares, so he meets the shareholding requirement. But two years ago, within the five-year period, he was convicted by final judgment of estafa and sentenced to eight years, an offense punishable by imprisonment exceeding six years. His parole does not erase the disqualification.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ulysses is disqualified, and his election as director is invalid.

keyPoints: Directors must own stock (RCC Sec. 22)
Disqualified if convicted within five years of an offense punishable by over six years (Sec. 26)
Parole does not remove the disqualification

q: Under Section 22 of the Revised Corporation Code, corporations vested with public interest must have independent directors constituting at least:
hints: Examples: listed companies, banks, and large companies with many shareholders.
The minimum is one-fifth.
why: RCC Sec. 22: the board of corporations vested with public interest shall have independent directors constituting at least twenty percent (20%) of the board.

q: Vega Holdings, Inc. is listed on the stock exchange and has a board of ten directors, only one of whom is independent. A minority stockholder complains to the SEC. Is Vega compliant?

alac.answer: No, Vega Holdings is not compliant.
alac.basis: Section 22 of the Revised Corporation Code requires the board of corporations vested with public interest to have independent directors constituting at least twenty percent (20%) of the board. These include corporations covered by Section 17.2 of the Securities Regulation Code, such as those listed with an exchange.
alac.application: Here, Vega Holdings is listed on the stock exchange, so it is vested with public interest. With a ten-member board, it needs at least two independent directors (20% of 10). It has only one.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Vega Holdings violates the independent director requirement and must elect at least one more independent director.

keyPoints: Corporations vested with public interest need independent directors (RCC Sec. 22)
At least 20% of the board
10-member board needs at least 2

q: Under Section 27 of the Revised Corporation Code, a director may be removed by a vote of stockholders holding at least:
choices: A majority of the outstanding capital stock
Two-thirds of the outstanding capital stock, at a regular or special meeting with prior notice of the intent to remove
hints: Removal needs a higher vote than election.
Prior notice of the proposed removal is required.
why: RCC Sec. 27: a director may be removed by the vote of stockholders holding at least two-thirds of the outstanding capital stock, at a regular or special meeting, after previous notice of the intention to propose the removal.

q: The stockholders of Opal Corp., by a two-thirds vote at a special meeting duly called for the purpose, removed director Wilma. The remaining directors, still a quorum, then elected Wilma's replacement themselves. Is the replacement's election valid?

alac.answer: No, the replacement's election by the board is not valid.
alac.basis: Section 28 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that a vacancy in the board, other than by removal or expiration of term, may be filled by a majority of the remaining directors if still constituting a quorum; but when the vacancy arises as a result of removal by the stockholders, the election may be held on the same day of the meeting authorizing the removal by the stockholders. Section 27 lays down the requirements for removal.
alac.application: Here, Wilma's removal was valid. But the resulting vacancy arose from removal by the stockholders, a case excluded from the board's power to fill vacancies. Only the stockholders could elect her replacement.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the board's election of Wilma's replacement is void; the stockholders must elect the new director.

keyPoints: Removal by 2/3 of outstanding capital stock with prior notice (RCC Sec. 27)
Board may fill vacancies other than by removal or expiration of term (Sec. 28)
Vacancy from removal is filled by the stockholders

q: Under Section 29 of the Revised Corporation Code, absent a bylaw provision fixing their compensation, directors:
choices: Shall not receive compensation in their capacity as such, except reasonable per diems, unless granted by stockholders owning a majority of the outstanding capital stock
Receive the same pay as officers
hints: Directors cannot freely pay themselves.
Total yearly compensation is capped at 10% of net income before tax.
why: RCC Sec. 29: absent a bylaw provision, directors receive no compensation as such except reasonable per diems; stockholders owning a majority may grant compensation; total yearly compensation may not exceed 10% of net income before income tax of the preceding year.

q: The bylaws of Indigo Corp. are silent on directors' compensation. The board voted to give each director an annual bonus totaling 15% of the previous year's net income before tax, without any stockholder vote. Is the bonus valid?

alac.answer: No, the bonus is not valid.
alac.basis: Section 29 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that in the absence of any bylaw provision fixing their compensation, directors shall not receive any compensation in their capacity as such, except reasonable per diems; stockholders representing at least a majority of the outstanding capital stock may grant compensation; and in no case shall the total yearly compensation of directors exceed ten percent of the net income before income tax of the corporation during the preceding year.
alac.application: Here, the bylaws do not fix directors' compensation, and no stockholder vote granted it; the directors voted the bonus to themselves. Moreover, 15% of net income exceeds the 10% cap.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the bonus is invalid, and the directors may be required to return the amounts received.

keyPoints: No compensation as directors absent bylaws, except per diems (RCC Sec. 29)
Stockholders' majority may grant compensation
Cap: 10% of preceding year's net income before tax

q: Under Section 33 of the Revised Corporation Code, a director who, by virtue of his office, acquires a business opportunity that should belong to the corporation must:
choices: Keep the profits if he used his own money
Account for and refund all profits to the corporation, unless ratified by stockholders owning at least two-thirds of the outstanding capital stock
Pay a fine to the SEC
hints: This is the corporate opportunity doctrine.
Using his own funds is no defense.
why: RCC Sec. 33: a director who acquires a business opportunity belonging to the corporation must account for and refund the profits, unless ratified by 2/3 of the outstanding capital stock, even if he risked his own funds.

q: Xander, a director of Pearl Shipping Corp., learned at a board meeting that a ship the corporation needed was for sale at a bargain. He bought it himself using his own money and leased it to a competitor at a large profit. The corporation demands his profits. Must he account for them?

alac.answer: Yes, Xander must account for and refund the profits to Pearl Shipping Corp.
alac.basis: Section 33 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that where a director, by virtue of such office, acquires a business opportunity which should belong to the corporation, thereby obtaining profits to the prejudice of the corporation, the director must account for and refund to it all such profits, unless the act has been ratified by stockholders owning at least two-thirds of the outstanding capital stock. The rule applies even if the director risked his own funds.
alac.application: Here, Xander learned of the bargain through his position as director, and the ship was an opportunity the corporation needed. He took it for himself and profited to the corporation's prejudice. No ratification by the stockholders took place, and his use of his own money is no defense.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Xander must account for and refund his profits to the corporation.

keyPoints: Corporate opportunity acquired by virtue of office (RCC Sec. 33)
Must account for profits unless ratified by 2/3
Use of own funds is no defense

q: Under the business judgment rule:
choices: Directors are liable for every loss
Courts will not interfere with or substitute their judgment for the board's good-faith business decisions within its powers, absent bad faith, fraud or gross negligence
Courts may replace any board decision with their own
hints: Business decisions involve risk.
Liability attaches only for bad faith, fraud or gross negligence (RCC Sec. 30).
why: Business judgment rule: contracts and decisions of the board made in good faith and within its powers are not subject to judicial review; directors are liable only for patently unlawful acts, gross negligence or bad faith (RCC Sec. 30).

q: After studying market reports and consulting experts, the board of Ruby Foods, Inc. decided in good faith to expand into Mindanao. The expansion lost money because of an unexpected price war. A stockholder sues the directors for the losses. Will the suit prosper?

alac.answer: No, the suit will not prosper.
alac.basis: Under the business judgment rule, questions of policy and management are left to the honest decision of the board, and courts will not interfere with decisions made in good faith and within the board's authority. Section 30 of the Revised Corporation Code makes directors liable only when they wilfully and knowingly vote for patently unlawful acts, are guilty of gross negligence or bad faith, or acquire interests in conflict with their duty.
alac.application: Here, the board studied market reports and consulted experts before deciding to expand. The decision was within its authority and made in good faith. The losses resulted from an unexpected price war, a normal business risk, not from bad faith or gross negligence.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the directors are protected by the business judgment rule and are not personally liable for the losses.

keyPoints: Business judgment rule protects good-faith decisions
Liability only for unlawful acts, gross negligence or bad faith (RCC Sec. 30)
Business losses alone do not create liability

q: Under Section 30 of the Revised Corporation Code, directors who wilfully and knowingly vote for patently unlawful acts of the corporation are liable:
choices: Only if the corporation is insolvent
Jointly and severally for all resulting damages suffered by the corporation, its stockholders or members and other persons
hints: The liability is personal and solidary.
It covers damage to the corporation and others.
why: RCC Sec. 30: directors who wilfully and knowingly assent to patently unlawful acts, or are guilty of gross negligence or bad faith, or acquire conflicting interests, are jointly and severally liable for resulting damages.

q: Knowing that Zircon Corp. had no unrestricted retained earnings, its board declared and paid a large cash dividend out of the corporation's capital. The corporation later could not pay its creditors. Are the directors personally liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the directors who voted for the dividend are personally liable.
alac.basis: Section 30 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that directors who wilfully and knowingly vote for or assent to patently unlawful acts of the corporation, or who are guilty of gross negligence or bad faith, shall be liable jointly and severally for all damages resulting therefrom suffered by the corporation, its stockholders and other persons. Dividends may be declared only out of unrestricted retained earnings, and capital is a trust fund for creditors.
alac.application: Here, the directors knew that there were no unrestricted retained earnings, yet declared and paid a dividend out of capital. That is a patently unlawful act that impaired the trust fund and prejudiced the creditors.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the directors who voted for the dividend are jointly and severally liable for the resulting damages to the corporation and its creditors.

keyPoints: Directors liable for patently unlawful acts or bad faith (RCC Sec. 30)
Dividends only from unrestricted retained earnings
Paying dividends out of capital prejudices creditors

q: Under the special fact doctrine, a director or officer who buys shares from a stockholder must:
choices: Disclose special facts known to him by virtue of his position that materially affect the value of the shares
hints: The director has inside information.
Concealment of such facts is fraud.
why: Special fact doctrine: a director or officer who, by reason of his position, knows special facts affecting the value of shares (such as a pending profitable sale) must disclose them before buying shares from a stockholder; otherwise the sale may be annulled for fraud.
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 1338 and 1390; Revised Corporation Code, Sec. 30

q: Arnel, president of Coral Mines, Inc., learned that the corporation was about to sell its mining claims to a foreign company at a price that would quadruple the value of its shares. Before this was announced, he bought shares from Bella, an elderly stockholder, at the old market price, without telling her. Can Bella annul the sale?

alac.answer: Yes, Bella may annul the sale.
alac.basis: Under the special fact doctrine, a director or officer who, by reason of his position, has knowledge of special facts materially affecting the value of the shares is under a duty to disclose them before buying shares from a stockholder; failure to do so is fraud. Under Article 1338 of the Civil Code, there is fraud when, through insidious words or machinations of one party, the other is induced to enter into a contract, and Article 1390 makes a contract voidable when consent is vitiated by fraud.
alac.application: Here, Arnel, as president, knew of the pending sale of the mining claims that would quadruple the value of the shares. Bella did not know of it. By buying her shares at the old price without disclosing this special fact, Arnel took unfair advantage of his position.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Bella may annul the sale for fraud and recover her shares or their true value.

keyPoints: Duty to disclose special facts known by virtue of position
Concealment is fraud (Civil Code Art. 1338)
Contract voidable (Art. 1390)

q: Under Section 31 of the Revised Corporation Code, a contract between the corporation and one of its directors is, as a rule:
choices: Voidable at the option of the corporation, unless all the conditions in Section 31 are present
hints: The conditions protect the corporation from self-dealing.
Fairness and the director's non-essential vote matter.
why: RCC Sec. 31: a contract of the corporation with its directors, trustees, officers or their spouses and relatives within the fourth civil degree is voidable at the corporation's option, unless the director's presence and vote were not necessary, the contract is fair and reasonable, and other conditions are met.

q: The five-member board of Jade Corp. approved, by a vote of 3-2, the purchase of a lot owned by director Carlo at a price 40% above market value. Carlo attended and voted in favor; without him, there would have been no quorum. A stockholder questions the contract. What is its status?

alac.answer: The contract is voidable at the option of Jade Corp.
alac.basis: Section 31 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that a contract of the corporation with one or more of its directors is voidable at the option of the corporation, unless all of the following are present: the director's presence was not necessary to constitute a quorum; his vote was not necessary for approval; the contract is fair and reasonable; and other conditions applicable to corporations vested with public interest or to officers.
alac.application: Here, Carlo's presence was necessary for a quorum, his vote was needed to reach three votes, and the price, 40% above market value, is not fair and reasonable. The conditions of Section 31 are not met.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the contract is voidable at the option of Jade Corp., which may have it annulled.

keyPoints: Contracts with directors are voidable unless the Sec. 31 conditions are met
Director's presence and vote were necessary
Contract not fair and reasonable

q: Under Section 32 of the Revised Corporation Code, a director's stockholding is considered "substantial" for purposes of interlocking directors when it exceeds:
hints: Interlocking directorship alone does not void a contract.
But a substantial-versus-nominal interest triggers Sec. 31.
why: RCC Sec. 32: a contract between corporations with interlocking directors is not invalidated on that ground alone, absent fraud and if fair; but if the director's interest is substantial (over 20%) in one and nominal in the other, Sec. 31 applies to the latter.

q: Delia is a director of both Alpha Corp., where she owns 35% of the shares, and Beta Corp., where she owns only 1%. Beta Corp. bought equipment from Alpha Corp. at a fair price, with Delia's vote being necessary to approve the purchase in Beta's board. Is the contract valid as to Beta Corp.?

alac.answer: The contract is voidable at Beta Corp.'s option, because the Section 31 conditions are not met as to Beta.
alac.basis: Section 32 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that, except in cases of fraud and provided the contract is fair and reasonable, a contract between corporations with interlocking directors shall not be invalidated on that ground alone; but if the interest of the interlocking director in one corporation is substantial (stockholding exceeding 20%) and merely nominal in the other, the contract shall be subject to Section 31 insofar as the latter corporation is concerned. Under Section 31, the contract is voidable unless, among others, the director's vote was not necessary for approval.
alac.application: Here, Delia's interest in Alpha (35%) is substantial, while her interest in Beta (1%) is nominal. Section 31 therefore applies as to Beta. Although the price was fair, Delia's vote was necessary to approve the contract in Beta's board.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the contract is voidable at the option of Beta Corp.

keyPoints: Interlocking directorship alone does not invalidate a contract (RCC Sec. 32)
Substantial (over 20%) in one, nominal in the other: Sec. 31 applies to the latter
Director's vote was necessary: voidable

q: Under Section 80 of the Revised Corporation Code, a stockholder may exercise the right of appraisal when:
choices: He disagrees with any board decision
The corporation sells all or substantially all of its assets, among other instances provided by law
hints: Appraisal lets a dissenter exit at fair value.
It applies only in instances listed by law.
why: RCC Sec. 80: appraisal right arises on amendments changing or restricting rights or extending/shortening the term, sale of all or substantially all assets, merger or consolidation, and investment in another business, among others.

q: The board and two-thirds of the stockholders of Garnet Corp. approved the sale of all its operating assets to another company. Ely, who owns 5% and voted against the sale, asks what he can do. Advise him.

alac.answer: Ely may exercise his right of appraisal and demand payment of the fair value of his shares.
alac.basis: Section 80 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that any stockholder of a corporation shall have the right to dissent and demand payment of the fair value of the shares in case of sale, lease, exchange, transfer, mortgage, pledge or other disposition of all or substantially all of the corporate property and assets. The dissenting stockholder must vote against the action and make a written demand for payment within the period provided by law.
alac.application: Here, Garnet Corp. is selling all its operating assets, one of the instances that give rise to the appraisal right. Ely voted against the sale.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ely may make a written demand on Garnet Corp. for the fair value of his shares, and upon payment he must surrender his shares.

keyPoints: Appraisal right on sale of all or substantially all assets (RCC Sec. 80)
Dissenter must vote against and make a written demand
Payment of fair value upon surrender of shares

q: Under Section 23 of the Revised Corporation Code, stockholders may vote through remote communication or in absentia when:
choices: Only if the SEC approves each time
Authorized in the bylaws or by a majority of the board (and in corporations vested with public interest, even without a bylaw provision)
hints: The Code modernized participation.
Those who vote remotely are deemed present for quorum.
why: RCC Sec. 23: when authorized in the bylaws or by a majority of the board, stockholders may vote through remote communication or in absentia; in corporations vested with public interest this is allowed even without a bylaw provision; such stockholders are deemed present for quorum.

q: Fely owns 1,000 shares of Onyx Corp., which is electing five directors. Fely wants to make sure that her nominee wins a seat. The bylaws are silent on voting methods. How many votes may she cast for her nominee?

alac.answer: Fely may cast all 5,000 votes for her nominee through cumulative voting.
alac.basis: Under Section 23 of the Revised Corporation Code, in stock corporations, stockholders entitled to vote may vote the number of shares registered in their names for as many persons as there are directors to be elected, or may cumulate their shares by giving one candidate as many votes as the number of directors to be elected multiplied by the number of their shares, or distribute them on the same principle among as many candidates as they may see fit. This right cannot be taken away by the bylaws.
alac.application: Here, Fely owns 1,000 shares and five directors are to be elected. She therefore has 1,000 x 5 = 5,000 votes, which she may cast entirely for one nominee to improve the chance of minority representation on the board.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Fely may cast all 5,000 votes for her nominee.

keyPoints: Cumulative voting in stock corporations (RCC Sec. 23)
Votes = shares x number of directors to be elected
May be cast for one or distributed among candidates

q: Under Section 51 of the Revised Corporation Code, unless otherwise provided, a quorum at stockholders' meetings consists of:
choices: Stockholders representing a majority of the outstanding capital stock
Two-thirds of the outstanding capital stock
hints: The bylaws may provide otherwise.
Remote participants count if allowed.
why: RCC Sec. 51: unless otherwise provided in the Code or bylaws, a quorum consists of stockholders representing a majority of the outstanding capital stock, or a majority of members in nonstock corporations.

q: The articles of Quartz Corp. provide for a seven-member board. At a board meeting, only four directors attended, and they elected a new corporate president by a vote of 3-1. A stockholder questions the election. Is it valid?

alac.answer: No, the election of the president is not valid.
alac.basis: Section 52 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that, unless the articles or bylaws require a greater majority, a majority of the directors as stated in the articles of incorporation constitutes a quorum, and every decision of at least a majority of the directors constituting a quorum is a valid corporate act, except for the election of officers, which requires the vote of a majority of all the members of the board.
alac.application: Here, four of the seven directors attended, which is a quorum. But the election of an officer requires the vote of a majority of all members of the board, that is, at least four of seven. The new president received only three votes.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the election of the president is invalid.

keyPoints: Board quorum: majority of directors in the articles (RCC Sec. 52)
Ordinary acts: majority of the quorum
Election of officers: majority of all board members

q: A derivative suit is filed by a stockholder:
choices: On behalf of the corporation, to enforce a corporate right that the board refuses or fails to enforce
To recover his own personal damages
hints: The corporation is the real party in interest.
Any recovery goes to the corporation.
why: A derivative suit is brought by a stockholder on behalf of the corporation to redress wrongs done to it when the board fails or refuses to act; requisites include being a stockholder at the time of the acts, exhaustion of intra-corporate remedies, no available appraisal right, and that the suit is not a nuisance or harassment suit (Interim Rules of Procedure for Intra-Corporate Controversies, Rule 8, Sec. 1).
cite: Interim Rules of Procedure for Intra-Corporate Controversies, Rule 8, Sec. 1

q: Gerry, a stockholder of Lapis Corp. since 2015, discovered that the president had diverted P20 million of corporate funds to his own company. Gerry wrote the board demanding action; the board, controlled by the president's allies, did nothing. Gerry then sued the president in his own name for the P20 million to be paid to him. Is this the proper action?

alac.answer: No. Gerry should file a derivative suit on behalf of the corporation, with any recovery going to Lapis Corp.
alac.basis: A derivative suit is an action brought by a stockholder on behalf of the corporation to enforce a corporate cause of action when the board refuses or fails to act. Under Rule 8, Section 1 of the Interim Rules of Procedure for Intra-Corporate Controversies, the stockholder must have been a stockholder at the time of the acts complained of, must have exerted all reasonable efforts to exhaust intra-corporate remedies, no appraisal rights must be available, and the suit must not be a nuisance or harassment suit.
alac.application: Here, the diversion of funds injured the corporation, not Gerry personally, so the cause of action belongs to Lapis Corp. Gerry was a stockholder when the acts occurred, demanded action from the board, which refused, and no appraisal right applies. The proper remedy is a derivative suit in the name of the corporation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Gerry should sue derivatively for the corporation, and any amount recovered will go to Lapis Corp., not to him personally.

keyPoints: Wrong to the corporation: derivative suit, not individual suit
Requisites under the Interim Rules, Rule 8
Recovery goes to the corporation
cite: Interim Rules of Procedure for Intra-Corporate Controversies, Rule 8, Sec. 1

q: Under Section 73 of the Revised Corporation Code, corporate records are open to inspection by:
choices: Any director, trustee, stockholder or member, in person or by a representative, at reasonable hours on business days
hints: Stockholders have a right to information.
Confidentiality rules still bind the inspecting party.
why: RCC Sec. 73: corporate records shall be open to inspection by any director, trustee, stockholder or member, in person or by a representative, at reasonable hours on business days, and copies may be demanded at their expense, subject to confidentiality rules.

q: Hilda, a minority stockholder of Beryl Corp., wrote the corporate secretary asking to inspect the minutes of board meetings and the financial records, to check suspected mismanagement. The secretary refused, saying Hilda owns too few shares. Was the refusal proper?

alac.answer: No, the refusal was not proper.
alac.basis: Section 73 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that corporate records, regardless of the form in which they are stored, shall be open to inspection by any director, trustee, stockholder or member of the corporation in person or by a representative at reasonable hours on business days, and a written demand may be made for copies at their expense. The inspecting party remains bound by confidentiality rules. The right does not depend on the size of one's shareholding.
alac.application: Here, Hilda is a stockholder seeking to inspect board minutes and financial records for a legitimate purpose, to check suspected mismanagement. The number of her shares is irrelevant to her right of inspection.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the corporate secretary must allow Hilda to inspect the records at reasonable hours on business days.

keyPoints: Right of inspection of any stockholder (RCC Sec. 73)
Not dependent on the size of shareholding
Subject to confidentiality and good faith

q: As a rule, in an asset-only transfer (sale of assets for cash in good faith), the buyer:
choices: Must pay the seller's taxes always
Becomes a partner of the seller
Does not become liable for the seller's debts, unless it expressly or impliedly assumed them, or the transaction is a fraud, a de facto merger, or a business-enterprise transfer
hints: Buying assets is different from taking over a business.
Exceptions prevent evasion of creditors.
why: In an asset-only transfer, the transferee is generally not liable for the transferor's debts, except when it agreed to assume them, the transaction amounts to a merger, the transferee is a mere continuation of the transferor, or the transfer is fraudulent. In a business-enterprise transfer, the transferee takes over the business and is liable for its obligations.

q: Iolite Corp. sold its entire bakery business to Jasper Corp., including the brand, the outlets, the employees and the supplier contracts, and Iolite stopped operating. Jasper continued the same bakery under the same name. A supplier with unpaid bills from Iolite now sues Jasper. Is Jasper liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Jasper Corp. may be held liable for Iolite's business obligations.
alac.basis: Corporate law distinguishes an asset-only transfer, where the transferee generally takes the assets free of the transferor's debts, from a business-enterprise transfer, where the transferee acquires the business itself as a going concern and is liable for the obligations of the business transferred. A transferee is also liable when it is a mere continuation of the transferor or the transfer is a de facto merger.
alac.application: Here, Jasper did not merely buy some assets. It took over the entire bakery business as a going concern, with its brand, outlets, employees and supplier contracts, while Iolite ceased operating. Jasper is a continuation of the business.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the transfer is a business-enterprise transfer, and Jasper may be held liable to Iolite's supplier.

keyPoints: Asset-only transfer: buyer generally not liable for seller's debts
Business-enterprise transfer: buyer liable for the business's obligations
Continuation of the same business

q: Under Section 17 of the Philippine Competition Act, what happens to a merger agreement that meets the notification threshold but is consummated without notifying the Philippine Competition Commission?
choices: It is considered void, and the parties are subject to an administrative fine
hints: Parties must wait 30 days after notice before closing.
The law imposes a serious consequence.
why: PCA Sec. 17: parties to a covered merger or acquisition must not consummate it until 30 days after notifying the PCC; an agreement consummated in violation is void and subjects the parties to an administrative fine.

q: Kappa Corp. agreed to acquire all the shares of Lambda Corp. in a deal whose value exceeds the notification threshold set by the Philippine Competition Act and the PCC. To save time, the parties closed the deal the next day without notifying the PCC. What is the effect?

alac.answer: The acquisition is void, and the parties are liable to an administrative fine.
alac.basis: Section 17 of the Philippine Competition Act (RA 10667) provides that parties to a merger or acquisition whose value exceeds the threshold are prohibited from consummating their agreement until thirty days after providing notification to the Philippine Competition Commission, and that an agreement consummated in violation of this requirement shall be considered void and subject the parties to an administrative fine.
alac.application: Here, the deal exceeds the notification threshold, so the parties had to notify the PCC and wait thirty days before closing. They closed the next day without notification.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the acquisition is void, and Kappa and Lambda may be fined by the PCC.

keyPoints: Notification required above the threshold (RA 10667, Sec. 17)
Thirty-day waiting period
Consummation without notice is void, with a fine

q: Under Section 21 of the Philippine Competition Act, a merger that would otherwise be prohibited may be exempted when, among others:
choices: It brings efficiency gains greater than the effects of any limitation on competition
hints: Efficiency can justify a merger.
So can a failing firm with no better alternative.
why: PCA Sec. 21: a prohibited merger may be exempted if it brings efficiency gains greater than its anti-competitive effects, or if a party faces actual or imminent financial failure and the deal is the least anti-competitive alternative.

q: The only two cement makers in a region plan to merge. The PCC finds that the merger would substantially lessen competition. The parties show that one of them is about to become insolvent and that no other buyer has offered to acquire it or its plants. Can the merger be allowed?

alac.answer: Yes, the merger may be exempted under the failing-firm defense if the conditions are proved.
alac.basis: Section 20 of the Philippine Competition Act prohibits merger agreements that substantially prevent, restrict or lessen competition in the relevant market. Section 21 allows the Commission to exempt such a merger when a party to the agreement is faced with actual or imminent financial failure, and the agreement represents the least anti-competitive arrangement among the known alternative uses for the failing entity's assets.
alac.application: Here, the merger would substantially lessen competition, so it is prohibited under Section 20. But one party faces imminent insolvency, and no other buyer is available, which suggests that the merger may be the least anti-competitive use of its assets.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the PCC may exempt the merger if the parties prove the failing firm's condition and the absence of less anti-competitive alternatives.

keyPoints: Mergers that substantially lessen competition are prohibited (RA 10667, Sec. 20)
Failing-firm exemption (Sec. 21(b))
Must be the least anti-competitive alternative

q: Under Section 79 of the Revised Corporation Code, upon a merger, the separate existence of the constituent corporations:
choices: Ceases for all, including the surviving one
Ceases, except that of the surviving corporation, which takes over all rights and liabilities
hints: A merger leaves one surviving corporation.
Liabilities follow the assets.
why: RCC Sec. 79: the constituent corporations become a single corporation; their separate existence ceases except that of the surviving or consolidated corporation, which possesses all their rights and is responsible for all their liabilities.

q: Mica Corp. merged into Nacre Corp., the surviving corporation. Before the merger, Mica owed P5 million to a supplier and had a pending collection case against a customer. After the merger, the supplier sued Nacre, and Nacre wanted to continue Mica's case. What are their positions?

alac.answer: Nacre is liable to the supplier and may continue Mica's case against the customer.
alac.basis: Section 79 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that upon a merger, the constituent corporations become a single corporation, the separate existence of the absorbed corporation ceases, and the surviving corporation possesses all the rights, privileges, immunities and powers of the constituent corporations and is responsible for all their liabilities and obligations, and any pending claim by or against a constituent corporation may be prosecuted by or against the surviving corporation.
alac.application: Here, Mica merged into Nacre, so Mica ceased to exist, and Nacre succeeded to all its rights and obligations. Mica's debt to the supplier and its claim against the customer both passed to Nacre by operation of law.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the supplier may collect from Nacre, and Nacre may substitute for Mica in the collection case against the customer.

keyPoints: Absorbed corporation ceases to exist (RCC Sec. 79)
Surviving corporation takes all rights and liabilities
Pending claims continue by or against it

q: Under Section 95 of the Revised Corporation Code, a close corporation is one whose articles provide that its issued stock is held of record by not more than:
choices: Twenty persons, with restrictions on transfer and no public offering
hints: Close corporations are like incorporated partnerships.
Three features: limited holders, transfer restrictions, no public offering.
why: RCC Sec. 95: a close corporation's articles provide that its stock is held by not more than a specified number of persons not exceeding twenty, all stock is subject to transfer restrictions, and it shall not list or publicly offer its stock.

q: Olga owns 20% of Petal Corp., a close corporation with ample assets and no significant debts. After disagreements with the other stockholders, she wants to leave and get her money out. What can she do?

alac.answer: Olga may compel Petal Corp. to purchase her shares at fair value.
alac.basis: Section 104 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that any stockholder of a close corporation may, for any reason, compel the corporation to purchase shares held at fair value, which shall not be less than the par or issued value, when the corporation has sufficient assets in its books to cover its debts and liabilities exclusive of capital stock.
alac.application: Here, Petal Corp. is a close corporation with ample assets and no significant debts, so it can cover its liabilities exclusive of capital stock. Olga may withdraw for any reason, including disagreements with the other stockholders.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Olga may compel Petal Corp. to buy her shares at fair value, not less than their par or issued value.

keyPoints: Close corporation features (RCC Sec. 95)
Stockholder may compel purchase of shares for any reason (Sec. 104)
If assets cover debts exclusive of capital stock

q: Under Section 106 of the Revised Corporation Code, the trustees of educational institutions organized as nonstock corporations shall number:
choices: Not less than five nor more than fifteen, in multiples of five
hints: Their terms are staggered.
One-fifth of the trustees' terms expire every year.
why: RCC Sec. 106: trustees of nonstock educational institutions shall be not less than five nor more than fifteen, in multiples of five; their terms are staggered so that one-fifth expire every year, unless otherwise provided.

q: A group organized "Lakan College, Inc." as a nonstock educational corporation with eight trustees, all serving one-year terms. The SEC returned the articles for correction. What is wrong?

alac.answer: The number of trustees and their terms do not comply with the rules for educational corporations.
alac.basis: Section 106 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that trustees of educational institutions organized as nonstock corporations shall not be less than five nor more than fifteen, in multiples of five, and that, unless otherwise provided in the articles or bylaws, the board shall classify themselves so that the term of office of one-fifth of their number expires every year. Educational corporations are also governed by special laws.
alac.application: Here, eight trustees is within five to fifteen but is not a multiple of five. The board should have five, ten, or fifteen trustees, with staggered terms in which one-fifth of the trustees' terms expire each year.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Lakan College must amend its articles to provide for five, ten or fifteen trustees, with staggered terms.

keyPoints: Five to fifteen trustees in multiples of five (RCC Sec. 106)
Staggered terms: one-fifth expire every year
Also governed by special laws
