q: Under Section 108 of the Revised Corporation Code, a corporation sole may be formed by:
choices: The chief archbishop, bishop, priest, minister, rabbi, or other presiding elder of a religious denomination, sect or church
hints: A corporation sole has one member.
It administers the temporalities of the church.
why: RCC Sec. 108: a corporation sole may be formed by the chief archbishop, bishop, priest, minister, rabbi, or other presiding elder of a religious denomination, to administer its affairs, property and temporalities as trustee.

q: The members of the Grace Fellowship, a religious society that is part of a larger denomination, want to incorporate to manage their properties. The denomination's rules do not forbid it. At a meeting called for the purpose, 60% of the members voted to incorporate. Can they incorporate as a religious society?

alac.answer: Not yet; they need the affirmative vote or written consent of at least two-thirds of the membership.
alac.basis: Section 114 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that, unless forbidden by competent authority or by the rules or discipline of the religious denomination of which it is part, any religious society may, upon written consent and/or by an affirmative vote at a meeting called for the purpose of at least two-thirds of its membership, incorporate for the administration of its temporalities or the management of its affairs and properties.
alac.application: Here, the denomination's rules do not forbid incorporation, but only 60% of the members voted in favor, short of the required two-thirds.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Grace Fellowship cannot yet incorporate; it must secure the vote or written consent of at least two-thirds of its members.

keyPoints: Religious societies may incorporate (RCC Sec. 114)
Unless forbidden by the denomination's rules
Requires 2/3 of the membership

q: Under Section 116 of the Revised Corporation Code, who may form a One Person Corporation?
choices: Only a natural person, a trust, or an estate
hints: An OPC has a single stockholder.
Some businesses, like banks and insurance companies, cannot be OPCs.
why: RCC Sec. 116: only a natural person, trust, or estate may form an OPC; banks, quasi-banks, preneed, trust, insurance, public and publicly-listed companies, and non-chartered GOCCs may not; licensed professionals may not form an OPC to practice their profession unless a special law allows.

q: Rachel formed "Rachel Trading OPC" and appointed herself president, treasurer and corporate secretary. The SEC questions her appointments. What is wrong, and what must she do as treasurer?

alac.answer: Rachel cannot be the corporate secretary, and as self-appointed treasurer she must post a bond.
alac.basis: Section 122 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that a One Person Corporation shall appoint a treasurer, corporate secretary, and other officers within fifteen days from the issuance of its certificate of incorporation; the single stockholder may not be appointed as the corporate secretary; and a single stockholder who is likewise the self-appointed treasurer shall give a bond to the Commission in such sum as may be required.
alac.application: Here, Rachel is the single stockholder, so she may not serve as corporate secretary. She may be treasurer, but as a self-appointed treasurer she must post a bond with the SEC.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rachel must appoint another person as corporate secretary and post the required bond as treasurer.

keyPoints: OPC must appoint a treasurer and corporate secretary (RCC Sec. 122)
Single stockholder cannot be the corporate secretary
Self-appointed treasurer must post a bond

q: Under Section 139 of the Revised Corporation Code, after dissolution, a corporation remains a body corporate for how long to wind up its affairs?
choices: Three years after the effective date of dissolution
hints: Winding up needs time.
The corporation may sue and be sued but may not continue its business.
why: RCC Sec. 139: every dissolved corporation (except banks) continues as a body corporate for three years after the effective date of dissolution to prosecute and defend suits, settle and close its affairs, dispose of property, and distribute its assets, but not to continue its business.

q: Sapphire Corp., which has no debts, wants to dissolve voluntarily. Its board approved the dissolution by majority vote, and stockholders owning 55% of the outstanding capital stock voted in favor at a duly called meeting. Is the vote sufficient, and what happens after dissolution?

alac.answer: Yes, the vote is sufficient; after dissolution, Sapphire continues as a body corporate for three years to wind up its affairs.
alac.basis: Section 134 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that if dissolution does not prejudice the rights of any creditor, it may be effected by majority vote of the board and by a resolution adopted by the affirmative vote of the stockholders owning at least a majority of the outstanding capital stock at a meeting called for the purpose. Section 139 provides that the dissolved corporation shall remain as a body corporate for three years after the effective date of dissolution for the purpose of winding up its affairs.
alac.application: Here, Sapphire has no debts, so no creditor is prejudiced. The board approved by majority, and stockholders owning 55%, more than a majority, voted in favor. After dissolution, it may continue only to settle its affairs, not to carry on its business.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the dissolution is validly approved, and Sapphire has three years to wind up and distribute its assets.

keyPoints: Voluntary dissolution with no creditors affected: board majority plus majority of outstanding capital stock (RCC Sec. 134)
Winding up for three years (Sec. 139)
No continuation of business

q: Under Section 3(d) of the Foreign Investments Act, which of the following is considered "doing business" in the Philippines?
choices: A single isolated sale to a Philippine buyer
Investing in shares of a domestic corporation only
Opening an office, whether called a liaison office or a branch, or appointing representatives domiciled in the Philippines
hints: Doing business implies continuity of commercial dealings.
Mere investment as a shareholder is excluded.
why: FIA Sec. 3(d): doing business includes soliciting orders, service contracts, opening offices, appointing representatives or distributors domiciled in the Philippines, participating in the management of a domestic business, and acts implying continuity of commercial dealings.
cite: Foreign Investments Act (RA 7042), Sec. 3(d), as amended

q: A Japanese company, without a Philippine license, sold one shipment of machine parts to a Manila factory in a single deal negotiated entirely in Japan. A year later, the factory refused to pay, and the Japanese company sued in a Philippine court. The factory argues the company cannot sue because it is unlicensed. Is the factory correct?

alac.answer: No. The Japanese company was not doing business in the Philippines and may sue.
alac.basis: Section 150 of the Revised Corporation Code bars a foreign corporation transacting business in the Philippines without a license from maintaining any suit in Philippine courts. Under Section 3(d) of the Foreign Investments Act, doing business refers to acts that imply a continuity of commercial dealings, such as opening offices or appointing representatives; an isolated transaction is not doing business.
alac.application: Here, the Japanese company made a single sale, negotiated entirely in Japan, with no office, representative or continuing dealings in the Philippines. It was not doing business here, so the license requirement does not bar its suit.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the Japanese company may sue the factory to collect the price.

keyPoints: Doing business requires continuity of dealings (FIA Sec. 3(d))
An isolated transaction is not doing business
License requirement for suits applies only to those doing business (RCC Sec. 150)
cite: Foreign Investments Act (RA 7042), Sec. 3(d); Revised Corporation Code, Sec. 150

q: Under Section 150 of the Revised Corporation Code, a foreign corporation transacting business in the Philippines without a license:
choices: May sue and be sued freely
Cannot maintain or intervene in any action in Philippine courts or agencies, but may be sued
hints: The rule penalizes doing business without a license.
It cannot benefit, but it can still be held liable.
why: RCC Sec. 150: no unlicensed foreign corporation transacting business in the Philippines may maintain or intervene in any suit, but it may be sued on any valid cause of action under Philippine law.

q: Omega Ltd., a Hong Kong company, has for years maintained a Manila office and sales agents, but never obtained a license. When a Philippine distributor refused to pay, Omega sued it. The distributor also filed a separate suit against Omega for damages. Which suits may proceed?

alac.answer: The distributor's suit against Omega may proceed, but Omega's suit against the distributor may not.
alac.basis: Section 150 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that no foreign corporation transacting business in the Philippines without a license shall be permitted to maintain or intervene in any action, suit or proceeding in any court or administrative agency of the Philippines, but such corporation may be sued or proceeded against before Philippine courts on any valid cause of action recognized under Philippine laws.
alac.application: Here, Omega has been doing business in the Philippines through a Manila office and sales agents for years, without a license. It therefore lacks capacity to sue. But the distributor may sue Omega, since an unlicensed foreign corporation may be sued.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Omega's collection suit should be dismissed for lack of capacity, while the distributor's suit against Omega may proceed.

keyPoints: Unlicensed foreign corporation doing business cannot sue (RCC Sec. 150)
But it may be sued
Office and agents show doing business

q: Under Section 3(c) of the Foreign Investments Act, "foreign investment" means:
choices: An equity investment made by a non-Philippine national in the form of foreign exchange and/or other assets actually transferred to the Philippines and duly registered
Any loan from a foreign bank
hints: It is an equity investment.
The assets must actually be transferred and registered.
why: FIA Sec. 3(c): foreign investment is an equity investment by a non-Philippine national in the form of foreign exchange and/or other assets actually transferred to the Philippines and duly registered.

q: A Korean company lent P50 million to a Philippine manufacturing corporation, payable in five years with interest, without acquiring any shares. Separately, it bought 30% of the shares of another Philippine company, remitting the price from Korea. Which of these is a "foreign investment" under the Foreign Investments Act?

alac.answer: Only the purchase of 30% of the shares is a foreign investment; the loan is not.
alac.basis: Section 3(b) of the Foreign Investments Act defines "investment" as equity participation in any enterprise organized or existing under Philippine laws, and Section 3(c) defines "foreign investment" as an equity investment made by a non-Philippine national in the form of foreign exchange and/or other assets actually transferred to the Philippines and duly registered.
alac.application: Here, the loan gives the Korean company only a creditor's right to repayment with interest, not equity participation. The purchase of 30% of the shares, paid for with funds remitted from Korea, is equity participation by a non-Philippine national through foreign exchange transferred to the Philippines.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, only the share purchase is a foreign investment under the Act (subject to registration), while the loan is a foreign loan, not a foreign investment.

keyPoints: Investment means equity participation (FIA Sec. 3(b))
Foreign investment: equity by a non-Philippine national, with assets actually transferred (Sec. 3(c))
A loan is not equity

q: Under Section 5 of the Foreign Investments Act, as amended by RA 11647, a non-Philippine national may invest up to 100% in a domestic enterprise:
choices: Without need of prior approval, upon registration with the SEC (or DTI for sole proprietorships), unless foreign participation is prohibited or limited by law
hints: The law liberalized foreign investment.
The Negative List still applies.
why: FIA Sec. 5, as amended by RA 11647: without prior approval, a non-Philippine national not otherwise disqualified may, upon registration with the SEC (or DTI for single proprietorships), do business or invest up to 100% of capital, unless foreign participation is prohibited or limited by law.
cite: Foreign Investments Act (RA 7042), Sec. 5, as amended by RA 11647, Sec. 6

q: Pierre, a French citizen, wants to set up a wholly owned software development company in the Philippines, an activity not on the Foreign Investment Negative List. He asks whether he needs prior approval from any government office. Advise him.

alac.answer: Pierre needs no prior approval; he must register the company with the SEC.
alac.basis: Section 5 of the Foreign Investments Act, as amended by RA 11647, provides that without need of prior approval, a non-Philippine national not otherwise disqualified by law may, upon registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission, or the DTI in the case of single proprietorships, do business or invest in a domestic enterprise up to one hundred percent of its capital, unless participation of non-Philippine nationals in the enterprise is prohibited or limited by law.
alac.application: Here, software development is not on the Negative List, so foreign participation is not prohibited or limited. Pierre may own 100% of the company, and the only requirement is registration with the SEC, not prior approval.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Pierre may set up the wholly owned company upon SEC registration, subject to other applicable requirements such as minimum paid-in capital for certain foreign-owned domestic market enterprises.

keyPoints: No prior approval needed (FIA Sec. 5, as amended)
Registration with the SEC (or DTI)
Up to 100% unless prohibited or limited by law
cite: Foreign Investments Act (RA 7042), Sec. 5, as amended by RA 11647

q: Under Section 8 of the Foreign Investments Act, List A of the Foreign Investment Negative List enumerates:
choices: Areas of activities reserved to Philippine nationals by mandate of the Constitution and specific laws
hints: List B covers defense, health and morals, and small domestic enterprises.
List A rests on the Constitution and specific laws.
why: FIA Sec. 8: the Negative List has List A (areas reserved to Philippine nationals by the Constitution and specific laws) and List B (areas limited by law for security, defense, health, morals, and protection of small and medium enterprises).
cite: Foreign Investments Act (RA 7042), Sec. 8, as amended

q: Two American investors want to own 100% of a Philippine company that will (a) operate a radio station and (b) manufacture solar panels for export. Neither activity has a special law allowing full foreign ownership, except that the Constitution reserves mass media to Filipinos. Can they own 100% of both businesses?

alac.answer: No. They cannot own any part of the radio station, but they may own 100% of the solar panel manufacturing business.
alac.basis: Section 8 of the Foreign Investments Act provides that List A of the Foreign Investment Negative List enumerates the areas of activities reserved to Philippine nationals by mandate of the Constitution and specific laws. Article XVI, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution reserves the ownership and management of mass media to Filipino citizens or corporations wholly owned and managed by them. Activities not on the Negative List may be 100% foreign-owned, upon registration.
alac.application: Here, a radio station is mass media, which the Constitution reserves entirely to Filipinos, so it falls under List A. Manufacturing solar panels for export is not a reserved or limited activity.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the Americans cannot own the radio station, but they may own 100% of the solar panel manufacturing company.

keyPoints: List A: areas reserved by the Constitution and laws (FIA Sec. 8)
Mass media is reserved wholly to Filipinos (Const., Art. XVI, Sec. 11)
Activities not on the list may be 100% foreign-owned
cite: Foreign Investments Act (RA 7042), Sec. 8; 1987 Constitution, Art. XVI, Sec. 11
